News.title: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
News.content:
The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

News.title: Police in Scotland arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human trafficking
News.content:
One of Scotland's biggest police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms.

About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations.

In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders.

Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime.

The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year.

Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth Â£26m were seized.

News.title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
News.content:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it in their manufacturing processes until 2012.

Sam Hammond and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

News.title: 781 migrants arrive in small boats in 2026 record
News.content:
A total of 781 migrants arrived in 10 small boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year, Home Office figures show.

So far this year 18,565 people have made the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

The government said its "progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable" but it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".

French authorities reported on Thursday that a man had died after having a cardiac arrest while people attempted to board a vessel at a beach south of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

Wednesday's figures include a dinghy carrying 51 people which departed from Normandy, much further west than small boats typically set off, on Monday morning and spent more than 33 hours at sea.

About 150 people crossed from France in three small boats on both Monday and Tuesday. This followed five days with no crossings at all.

Wednesday's figure was the highest daily total since 803 people arrived on 20 December 2025.

The highest total in one day in recent years was on 3 September 2022, when 1,305 migrants made the crossing.

News.title: Ministers reject dog ownership licence scheme
News.content:
The Responsible Dog Ownership Taskforce was established by the government in 2022, following a series of high-profile dog attacks.

The taskforce's report noted that since 2011 the dog population in the UK had grown by 35%, while hospital admissions relating to dog bites in England had risen by 77%.

It said pet ownership had spiked during the Covid pandemic at a time when it was harder to access support services.

"This led to less experienced owners struggling to access services and finding it harder to get help," the report said.

Until 1987, dog owners in England, Wales and Scotland had to pay an annual fee to get an ownership licence.

The scheme was scrapped on the grounds that the amount of money it raised was outweighed by the operating costs.

Dog owners in Northern Ireland still have to buy a licence of Â£12.50, or Â£5 if the owner receives an income-related benefit.

In France, owners of the most dangerous dogs have to get special permits which can involve passing a training course and putting the dog through a behavioural assessment.

Switzerland previously required potential dog owners to complete a knowledge test, followed by a practical, but this condition has been scrapped.

The report said that most members of the taskforce backed introducing legal requirements for dog owners but "further consideration would be needed regarding the form that this should take".

"Any legal requirement would need careful consideration of its objective and not appear as a tax on already responsible dog owners.

"Reintroducing a universal dog licence may amount to another database of responsible owners or an administrative exercise with little public safety benefit or opportunity to promote responsible dog ownership."

It said options could include focusing a scheme on high-risk dogs, introducing background checks on owners and requiring potential owners to pass a knowledge test.

The Dogs Trust and the RSPCA have commissioned research into the costs and benefits of different systems and their conclusions are due to be published later this year.

In a ministerial foreword to the report, environment minister Baroness Hayman of Ullock said: "In recent years, we have seen a concerning rise in dog attacks, alongside changes in patterns of dog ownership."

She said the taskforce's report was an "important and timely contribution", adding: "As ministers, we are carefully considering the recommendations alongside the wider programme of work already under way."

Cody Gakpo denied his former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp a win in his first game in charge of Germany.

Felix Nmecha had put Germany ahead with what looked set to be the only goal of an intense Nations League match against the Netherlands at the Johan Cruyff Arena in Amsterdam.

But Gakpo scored a spectacular volley at the death to earn the Dutch a deserved point.

open image in gallery Cody Gakpo’s spectacular volley earned the Netherlands a point late on ( AP )

A controversial game saw Virgil van Dijk have a goal harshly disallowed while Germany’s Kai Havertz and Dutch striker Brian Brobbey both suffered hamstring injuries.

Erling Haaland scored twice as Norway secured a 3-2 win over Denmark.

Oscar Bobb put the hosts ahead and Haaland doubled the lead with only 18 minutes on the clock.

Mikkel Damsgaard pulled one back for the Danes and Rasmus Hojlund equalised on the hour mark.

But Haaland grabbed a 74th-minute winner when he crashed home a first-time shot from a short corner.

open image in gallery Erling Haaland bagged a brace in Norway’s win over Denmark ( Getty )

Norway finished with 10 men after David Moller Wolfe was shown a second yellow card in stoppage time.

Cristiano Ronaldo had a goal disallowed in Portugal’s 1-0 win over Wales.

The 41-year-old thought he had tucked away career goal number 980 to double Portugal’s lead, but a VAR check showed he was just offside.

The hosts had to settle for Joao Felix’s 22nd-minute strike despite a dominant display.

open image in gallery Joao Felix (second left) celebrates scoring for Portugal (Zed Jameson/PA) ( PA Wire )

Israel’s Sayed Abu Farchi was sent off for his celebration during a 3-1 defeat against Austria.

The Colorado Rapids forward was already on a yellow card when he equalised before picking up the corner flag and aiming it like a gun.

Austria, who led through Romano Schmid’s penalty, won it in stoppage time through goals from Phillipp Mwene and Sasa Kalajdzic.

Late goals from Christos Tzolis and Anastasios Douvikas saw Greece snatch a 2-1 win in Serbia, who led through Andrija Zivkovic.

The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in Pristina thanks to a goal seven minutes from time from Vedat Muriqi.

Elsewhere. Lithuania won 2-0 in Liechtenstein and Andorra were beaten 2-1 at home to Malta.

A man has been charged in connection with an incident that took place in the English Channel earlier this week.

Far-right activist Daniel Thomas – known to his supporters as Danny Tommo – has been charged with criminal damage and failing to disclose the PIN to his phone after he was filmed slashing a boat with an emergency responder on board.

The 37-year-old, of no fixed abode, was remanded into custody to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court on Friday, Hampshire police said in a statement.

The force said in a statement on Thursday evening: “The charges follow an allegation made to police that damage had been caused to a boat in the Channel whilst an emergency responder was on board.”

On Thursday evening, Chris Derrick from the Crown Prosecution Service said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire Constabulary into an incident on Tuesday September 22.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.”

It comes after around 300 people gathered outside a police investigation centre calling for his release.

The protesters, who were mostly in black, and some with hoods or face coverings, arrived at the centre in Basingstoke, Hampshire, just before 6.30pm after social media posts urged them to be there at that time.

open image in gallery Protesters gathered calling for the release of Danny Tommo ( PA )

The group mainly consisted of men, with some carrying Union flags.

Some chanted “free DT”, with others taking mobile phone footage of the protest.

About a dozen police officers stood between the crowd and the entrance to the police investigation centre but the demonstration was peaceful.

It follows an anti-migrant protest in Gosport on Tuesday, when hundreds gathered in the belief that a boat of asylum-seekers, which had travelled from France, would be brought to shore.

open image in gallery Supporters of Danny Tommo gather outside Basingstoke Police Station ( Getty )

Six people were arrested by officers during the evening, the force said.

The boat eventually docked in Dover, Kent, at around 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 migrants on board reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea.

The government on Wednesday said it must “push further and harder” to stop migrants crossing the Channel after more than 700 people arrived in the UK – the highest number for a single day so far this year.

Education secretary Lucy Powell said not every migrant boat could be intercepted after two vessels landed undetected on British shores within two days.

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood said the failure to intercept the two boats was “not acceptable” and has ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command.

The Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, suggesting an average of 78 people per boat.

It brings the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565.

Arsenal have been dealt an injury blow on the first night of the international break after Kai Havertz limped off during Germany’s clash with the Netherlands.

Havertz was chosen to start by Jurgen Klopp for the former Liverpool manager’s first outing in the Germany dugout, but his night was cut short after going down with what appeared to be a muscle problem.

After receiving treatment on his hamstring, which was heavily taped up, the forward was replaced by Younes Ebnoutalib on the half-hour mark.

It came minutes after Havertz was caught by a heavy challenge by Crystal Palace summer signing Quinten Timber on the knee, a foul the midfielder saw yellow for but could have realistically warranted a red.

open image in gallery Kai Havertz limps off against the Netherlands ( Getty )

Havertz spent much of the first half of last season sidelined with a knee injury, so Mikel Arteta will be praying that Havertz has not suffered any sort of recurrence with that issue.

Havertz was not the only injury casualty of the game that concerned a Premier League club, with Sunderland striker Brian Brobbey forced off with a hamstring issue.

The Dutch frontman came into the game off the back of his stunning hat-trick against Manchester City, taking home the match ball despite his side losing 5-3 at the Etihad Stadium.

However, he now faces a spell on the sidelines, pulling up and requiring help from the team doctor when leaving the field.

Brobbey was injured in the build-up to Germany’s goal, which was scored in controversial fashion after it appeared Klopp’s side were going to adhere to the Netherlands’ request to stop play, only to continue and find the net through Felix Nmecha.

Jamal Musiala, meanwhile, was forced out of the match before the game even got underway despite being named in the starting XI, picking up a thigh problem in the warm-up. He was replaced by Nadiem Amiri.

Hospitals and health insurance companies' use of AI may be driving Americans' healthcare costs up by nearly a billion dollars, according to a new report.

The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, which represents Blue Cross insurance plans, released a report on Thursday that found that codes used for billing were more complex in 2024 and 2025 than they were in 2023, even when there was no evidence suggesting the patients were receiving different treatments from their hospitals.

The association claims that hospitals, using AI tools, are collecting more information about their patients and submitting bigger claims, which eventually rolls back onto the patient, according to The New York Times.

Costs for Blue Cross companies increased by $653 million between 2024 and 2025, according to the report.

When AI tools add more conditions to patients' claims — noting conditions like low sodium or anemia — it can drive the cost of a treatment up. Hospitals were paid, on average, nearly $12,000 more per case because of the way AI tools are sending codes.

The use of AI tools by both hospitals and insurance companies may be driving prices for healthcare higher by the millions, according to a new report ( Getty )

The report highlights an example in individuals undergoing bowel surgery. Billing codes that include secondary conditions like partial blockages in the intestines or an increase in acid increased by 55 percent and 33 percent, respectively, between the first quarter of 2023 and the fourth quarter of 2025.

While insurers are pointing the finger at hospitals for driving up costs, hospitals in turn are pointing the finger at insurers for using AI to reject their patients' claims.

“All the insurers are using A.I. to scan our charts to look for claims to deny. For the same reason, we’re looking at the same charts today,” Dave Mazurkiewicz, the chief financial officer for McLaren Health Care in Michigan, told The New York Times.

He told the paper that AI tools can help doctors better record their patients’ conditions and make suggestions for procuring higher payments from insurance companies.

In theory, the use of AI should streamline the process of billing and payouts and produce more accurate results, with the ideal result of lowering healthcare costs for patients — but some doctors fear the battle of the bots will do the opposite.

“That’s the danger,” Dr. Shiv Rao, who founded AI patient care records company Abridge, told the paper, “where it’s bots fighting bots, agents fighting agents, a horrible dystopian future nobody wants to live in.”

Some of the experts who spoke to The New York Times described a tug of war between bots that prioritize the profits of the companies using them over the overall health and well-being of the patients who will ultimately be impacted by their decisions.

Luke Chalker, who represents Blue Cross, has pushed back on that notion, though, describing the struggle as "not a war" but a "completely one-sided bloodbath."

He said that Blue Cross does not use AI to process claims, but does use it to guard against what he calls inappropriate billing.

Basys.ai, owned by Amber Nigam, provides advisement to private insurers and the Medicare program on how to review and flag potential abuses of the billing system.

He told the paper that there are other versions of AI that are "optimizing for revenue," adding that he is "really, really concerned about what I'm seeing right now."

Donald Trump proudly showed off his additions to the White House wall of presidents to a visiting Xi Jinping on Thursday, which under his domain has become a sideshow pathway used to attack two of his predecessors: Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

Xi was at the White House for the second day of a state visit to the United States, which began Wednesday with a red-carpet rollout at Maryland’s Joint Base Andrews, a welcome described as unduly “lavish” by some of the U.S. president’s critics on both sides of the aisle.

On Thursday, the president gave his guest the grand tour, showing off his various additions and changes to the White House grounds, including the new helipad for Marine One on the lawn. He told reporters that his counterpart “loves good granite” as they inspected the landing pad.

Xi also strolled through the “Presidential Walk of Fame” with Trump, who excitedly showed him that his face was on the wall not just once, but twice — because of his non-consecutive election wins.

The Chinese president and his aides laughed hard as Trump pointed to Biden and said, “This is the autopen,” referring to Biden’s use of an automated signing tool, which Trump has used to mock his physical condition as well as mental acuity while in office.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump shows off his ‘Presidential Walk of Fame’ China’s leader Xi Jinping, including a portrait of an autopen that he has standing in for his predecessor Joe Biden on Thursday ( AFP via Getty Images )

The moment was captured as a Thursday court ruling turned the grounds of the White House into a legal battlefield.

CNN, MS Now and Politico were readmitted to the premises on Thursday around noon after initially being turned away, with reporters receiving security badges that were confiscated by Secret Service at the beginning of the week. News agencies continued to hold out on providing television pool coverage as White House officials left the issue of readmitting CNN and MS Now to the pool rotation unclear.

Video of the moment Trump mocked his predecessor was shared by the official White House account on X, with a crying-laughing emoji.

Chinese officials and White House aides, as well as Secret Service agents, reportedly also got into a heated dispute minutes before Xi’s arrival Thursday over the placement of photographers working for the White House and the visiting Chinese delegation around the White House entranceway.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

The president’s focus on the White House’s physical transformation was unsurprising. Trump frequently gives guests tours of the White House, with the wall of presidential portraits — and his Trump-ified additions — a main stop.

The president also frequently shows guests the site and plans for the ballroom and “DronePort” he hopes to finish constructing on the former grounds of the White House East Wing, a project which like his renovations to the Kennedy Center is mired in court battles. As he has battled with Congress and mostly failed to enact his agenda through legislation, the president has focused on radically transforming the White House and the broader District of Columbia as he has sought another way to make his mark during his second term.

Biden and Xi met several times during the former’s presidency. Unlike Trump, the 46th president met the visiting Xi in San Francisco, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in 2023 and focused entirely on politics, leaving with agreements to cooperate on AI development, defense issues, and efforts to curb fentanyl trafficking.

open image in gallery Joe Biden and Xi Jinping met in 2023 on the sidelines of a summit in San Francisco, rather than during a state visit ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery Trump and Xi pose for photos with their spouses Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan outside of the White House ( AFP/Getty )

Xi’s visit to the U.S. was marked by a welcome ceremony Wednesday at a Maryland military base that was packed with pomp, complete with a military flyover, an artillery salute, and the playing of the national anthem. The Chinese president watched the proceedings placidly while his U.S. counterpart, wearing full winter weather garb, winced in surprise as the planned flyover took place.

Trump’s over-the-top welcome for Xi drew immediate condemnation from one of his Republican allies on the Hill, Sen. Roger Wicker. The Mississippi senator said in a floor speech that he would have advised the president not to put on such a show for the Chinese president given the U.S.’s ongoing concerns with China’s human rights record, among other topics of dispute.

“I would not have scheduled such a thing. But as guests converse over the meal, the president might inquire about the purposes of China's massive military build-up, or about China's clear support for Iran,” said Wicker on Tuesday.

"Our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America," he added.

open image in gallery A red-carpet arrival ceremony for Xi Jinping on Wednesday came complete with a military flyover and an artillery salute ( Getty Images )

His reception of Xi at the White House follows Trump’s speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. The president’s poll numbers on foreign and domestic affairs are plunging, linked in both cases to the war in Iran the administration launched in late February with the stated assumption that the conflict would end in a few weeks. Nearly seven months on, fuel prices including gasoline and diesel remain at record highs across the United States while the overall cost of the war itself has surpassed $80 billion and continues to climb, with no signs of a negotiated end in sight.

Trump’s speech Tuesday to world leaders at the U.N. was centered around his administration’s willingness to make tough foreign policy decisions, but as the midterm elections approach America still appears isolated from not just its European allies but from Canada, where Trump has launched a trade war, as well.

“We inherited a dark age of America from the previous administration, and we turned it into the golden age of America,” Trump insisted during his speech Tuesday. “The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit, and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America.”

Wales fell to an opening 1-0 Nations League defeat to Portugal as Cristiano Ronaldo drew a blank in Lisbon.

On an evening when Ronaldo missed a slew of chances and had a second-half effort ruled out by a VAR intervention, it was his Al Nassr teammate Joao Felix who settled the contest.

Ronaldo was winning cap number 234 after deciding to prolong his international career following a disappointing World Cup, but his contribution ended when substituted after 67 minutes.

The manner of Felix’s 22nd minute goal was cruel on Wales, deflecting off Ben Davies, but it could not be denied that Portugal deserved their victory by having 22 shots to five.

Wales fell to an opening 1-0 Nations League defeat to Portugal as Cristiano Ronaldo drew a blank in Lisbon.

On an evening when Ronaldo missed a slew of chances and had a second-half effort ruled out by a VAR intervention, it was his Al Nassr team-mate Joao Felix who settled the contest.

Ronaldo was winning cap number 234 after deciding to prolong his international career following a disappointing World Cup, but his contribution ended when substituted after 67 minutes.

The manner of Felix’s 22nd minute goal was cruel on Wales, deflecting off Ben Davies, but it could not be denied that Portugal deserved their victory by having 23 shots to five.

open image in gallery Joao Felix's deflected strike proved the difference against Wales ( AP )

Being pitched into a tough Nations League A group with Portugal, Norway and Denmark was Wales’ reward for promotion two years ago.

But boss Craig Bellamy – who was on the brink of leaving in the summer to join Burnley – had welcomed the challenge as an opportunity to improve their seeding for the 2028 European Championship.

Ronaldo was back at the Jose Alvalde Stadium, where he began his career with Sporting Lisbon, as the septuagenarian Jorge Jesus took charge for the first time.

open image in gallery Cristiano Ronaldo had a goal disallowed for the home side (Zed Jameson/PA)

On paper it looked a mismatch with Portugal ranked seventh in the world and 31 places higher than Wales, and their players drawn from major European clubs while Craig Bellamy’s squad had been ravaged by injuries and withdrawals.

Key pair Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon were missing and the absence of goalkeeper Karl Darlow saw Wrexham’s Danny Ward make only his second appearance of the season.

The first half was a tale of Felix’s strike and rising Ronaldo frustration.

Wales actually started in composed fashion, with Lewis Koumas occupying Portugal defenders and showing why he has impressed at Liverpool this season.

But Portugal gradually took control and Ronaldo fired wide from a tight angle before his poor touch allowed Neco Williams to recover.

open image in gallery Portugal’s Renato Veiga (left) and Wales’ Lewis Koumas battle for the ball (Zed Jameson/PA)

Pedro Neto missed at the far post before Felix’s 20-yard shot nicked off Davies to take the ball beyond Ward.

Ronaldo sent another opening wide before an untidy strike from 12 yards allowed Ward to collect, leaving the Portugal captain kicking the air in disgust.

The script stayed the same after the break as Ruben Neves set up a Ronaldo tap-in from four yards.

The wait for Ronaldo’s 147th international goal seemed over, but his connection sent the ball sailing over to the bewilderment of home fans.

There was even more despair for Ronaldo when racing onto a Bruno Fernandes pass after 59 minutes.

Ronaldo slid the ball home and raced towards the corner flag for his trademark ‘Siuuu’ celebration, but VAR disallowed the goal for offside.

Wales almost produced an equaliser from nowhere as Brennan Johnson broke through and, from the byline, looped his effort on to the bar.

Koumas attempted to prod home the rebound but Ruben Dias made a superb clearance to deny Wales.

News.title: Buttler injury derails England chase and sends Sri Lanka series to decider
News.content:
Enter Buttler to play a wonderful counter-attack, whacking Wellalage for four and six and dumping leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage over the rope twice as he raced to 41 off 22 balls.

Buttler was at a crossroads after the T20 World Cup in February. Despite England making the semi-finals, he averaged just 10 in the tournament to complete a third poor World Cup in a row. A break with his family, and a very good Indian Premier League, where he made a crucial technical correction, changed his fortunes.

Matthew Hayden, the batting coach at the Gujarat Titans, asked him whether he was watching the ball closely enough. Buttler discovered that, now 36, he is a right-eye dominant batsman, so with Hayden’s help he opened up his stance to give himself a better view of the ball. A summer rich in runs has followed with an average of 51 for England and a strut back in his body language. The injury has surely ended Buttler’s summer and there are worries that he could be out of the Pakistan ODI triangular tournament next month as well, just to add to the night’s woes.

This was not a vintage England performance. Atkinson made a crucial error on the boundary, dropping a straightforward chance off Kusal Mendis on 17. It kickstarted Mendis, who went on the charge smashing 51 in 24 balls. He put on 137 in 120 balls with Kuminda Mendis. Josh Tongue had an off day going at seven an over and Jofra Archer was given similar treatment, although he bowled better than figures suggest, as anything wayward with pace on the ball was hit away.

Overton was more effective with his cutters and slower balls, while Ahmed did at least bag a couple of wickets, credit for keeping his head after some early rough treatment. Kusal Mendis was given out leg before on 99 but overturned the decision and stroked a four next ball for a deserved hundred.

News.title: Oil jumps after Saudi thwarts missile attack
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. A global rout in bond markets deepened overnight as traders expect the US to keep raising interest rates.

Japan’s 10-year bond yield surged to 3.08pc on Thursday, its highest level since 1996, as markets responded to stronger than expected US economic data and higher oil prices.

It followed sharp rises in the US on Wednesday, when the yield on 10-year Treasuries – a benchmark of global borrowing costs – surged as high as 5.12pc, up from 4.96pc. It was the biggest jump since the “liberation day” tariff turmoil in April last year.

Bonds were sent into turmoil as traders bet that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates three times by April next year in an effort to bring down inflation. Money markets suggest there is a 70pc chance of the Fed following this month’s first rate rise in three years with a second in October.

This followed closely watched industry data on Wednesday, known as PMIs, showed US private sector activity jumped unexpectedly to a five-year high in September.

Meanwhile, oil prices spiked 3.9pc on Wednesday to move back above $100 a barrel, risking an inflationary spiral in the world economy.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The main driver was a strong batch of PMIs, along with a rebound in oil prices, which both led to mounting speculation about faster rate hikes.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) US borrowing costs hit highest since 2007 on fears economy overheating | Yield on 10-year Treasuries soars amid inflation concerns as oil prices rise

2) Diesel prices surge as Trump mulls 90-day US export ban | Pump prices could exceed £3 per litre in Britain if Washington imposes ‘catastrophic’ block on exports

3) England’s first new reservoir in 30 years delayed despite drought warnings | Havant Thicket, in Hampshire, will now be completed in 2034, five years after initially planned

4) Timpson customers ask for extra belt holes after weight-loss jabs | Boss of key cutting chain credits Ozempic and Mounjaro after surge in requests

5) Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes | Geely says its latest system is fastest in industry as brands approach ‘physical limit’

What happened overnight

Debt markets were in turmoil after Japanese bond yields hit 30-year highs.

As Tokyo markets reopened after a three-day holiday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to its highest level since 1996.

This came after a steep sell-off in the US market overnight. Oil prices remained around $103 a barrel and the dollar held gains after Tehran’s leader vowed to never surrender following a warning by Donald Trump that he could “annihilate” Iran.

Japan’s benchmark stock market, the Nikkei 225 rose 1pc to 65,645.10, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in AI. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7pc to 8,702.00.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 0.3pc to 24,762.39, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 0.9pc to 4,545.09. Trading was closed in South Korea for the Chuseok autumn harvest holiday.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

Sports.title: Breetzke ton leads South Africa to 67-run ODI win over Australia
Sports.content:
Matthew Breetzke scored a superb 112 to guide South Africa to a 67-run victory over Australia ‌in the first one-day international in Durban on Thursday, but the tourists will rue the loss of cheap wickets as they ‌faltered in their chase.

South Africa posted 297-8 in their 50 overs and Australia were well ​on course after a fast start, until poor shot selection caused their charge to collapse and they finished on 230 all out, losing ​their last nine wickets for 101 runs.

Australia will welcome the ‌likely return of captain Pat Cummins for the second match in the three-game series in Johannesburg on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, but ​if this series is a fact-finding mission ahead of the 2027 Cricket World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe, there will be much food for thought.

"I'm pretty ​disappointed," Australia captain Mitch Marsh said. "South Africa outplayed us. It was ⁠a good game of cricket but we ⁠fell well short.

"We had our opportunities, I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our ‌batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."

Johnny Fisher's heavyweight clash with Michael Pirotton in London on Saturday will be live on Sky Sports.

First they face one another at the final press conference at the Copper Box Arena from 6pm.

Heavyweight hitter Johnny Fisher is looking to kickstart a surge up the ranks, while Belgium's Pirotton is determined to make a name for himself against the hugely popular "Romford Bull".

Their fight headlines Zuffa Boxing 11 at the Copper Box that sees a raft of 50-50 fights and unbeatens matched against one another.

Zuffa Boxing 11 also features former world light-heavyweight title challenger Craig Richards against Radivoje "Hot Rod" Kalajdzic in the chief support.

British middleweights Lee Cutler and Louis Greene will go to war in an all-action bout.

Cesar Mateo Tapia, unbeaten in 19 pro contests, takes on Leo Ruiz, a Mexican based in California with a 17-1 record.

Kayla Allen will make her professional debut while Alex MacMillan will look to continue his winning run against 2-0 Frenchman Guillaume Azagier.

London-based Moldovan Aurel Ignat, who shocked Scott Forrest with a first-round KO win last year, will put his unbeaten record on the line against Mexican Olympian Rogelio Romero, a 6-0 prospect from Juarez who has a 100 per cent knockout ratio.

Fred Pullen, a national champion as an amateur, makes his pro debut against Italy's Leonardo Faretina and in a clash of unbeaten prospects, America's Alexis De La Cerda meets Ireland's Cain Lewis.

Watch Johnny Fisher vs Michael Pirotton headline Zuffa Boxing 11 live on Sky Sports on Saturday. Get Sky Sports or stream boxing with no contract.

Sports.title: Netherlands v Germany, Portugal v Wales and more: Uefa Nations League – live
Sports.content:
now 16.47 EDT “With Ruben van Bommel on for Holland,” says Louise Devries in an email I didn’t get to publish before events overtook it, “it’s a third generation playing for Oranje (grandpa Bert van Marwijk, father Mark van Bommel).” I always found it funny that Van Marwijk managed Van Bommel, so had a first-hand look at the way he went about things, then Van Bommel married his daughter. But yup, some proper naches there. Share

3m ago 16.44 EDT FULL TIME: Serbia 1-2 Greece A great contest, pilfered at the last by the better side. Share

4m ago 16.44 EDT FULL TIME: Norway 3-2 Denmark Denmark did well to come back from 2-0 down, but ultimately Norway have Erling Haaland and they don’t. Share

5m ago 16.43 EDT FULL TIME: Netherlands 1-1 Germany A fun game between two sides who are, let’s be real, way off it. Share

5m ago 16.42 EDT Van de Ven crosses, Veerman is there … AND HEADS WIDE! That should’ve been the winner! Share

6m ago 16.42 EDT FULL TIME: Portugal 1-0 Wales A creditable performance for an under-strength Wales; same old from Portugal. Share

7m ago 16.41 EDT GOAL! Serbia 1-2 Greece (Douvikas 90+4) Tsimikas hurtles down the left, crosses superbly, and Douvikas heads in a tremendous winner! These Greece boys are very, very serious. Share Updated at 16.48 EDT

8m ago 16.39 EDT GOAL! Netherlands 1-1 Germany (Gakpo 90+2) Gnabry gives it away and Van Bommel, on as sub for a debut, drives forward down the left, crosses at an awkward heigh … and a flying Gakpo makes light of it, hurling himself at it to volley home a terrific equaliser! View image in fullscreen Ooof! Cody Gakpo scores a sumptuous equaliser! Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP Share Updated at 16.43 EDT

11m ago 16.36 EDT Greece have been pushing hard for a winer but, in the final minute, Terzic bends low from the D ... and hits the post, then Zivkovic crosses back in, Lukic head down … and Tzolakis saves improbably by kicking out a leg! Share

16m ago 16.31 EDT Both Xavi and Klopp have a lot of work to do; how do they elevate their teams without players compatible with their visions? Germany are not going to outrun and overpower every team they face, nor do they have elite attackers; Netherlands don’t have the midfield to control games, even when Frenkie de Jong is fit. Share

22m ago 16.25 EDT Are we seeing the stratification of international football? Spain, France, England and Argentina now seem a fair bit better than Brazil, Germany and Holland with the rate at which they’re developing quality young players likely to maintain that hegemony for the foreseeable. Share

25m ago 16.23 EDT A ball over the top and Johnson chases, chesting down and, almost from the by-line, lifting over Costa … and on to the top of the bar. But Koumas is there for the rebound, he shoots low … and Dias blocks! That should’ve been 1-1. Share

26m ago 16.21 EDT GOAL! Serbia 1-1 Greece (Tzolis 74) It’s been coming for well over an hour and finally, it’s arrived, Pavlidis holding up before feeding Tzolis, who measures a low finish across Milinkovic-Savis and into the far corner. View image in fullscreen Christos Tzolis equalises for Greece in Belgrade. Photograph: Pedja Milosavljevic/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at 16.25 EDT

28m ago 16.20 EDT GOAL! Norway 3-2 Denmark (Haaland 74) A short corner, then a low pass to the near post – think Anderton for Sheringham, early-to-mid-90s – and Haaland turns in powerfully. He is rrrridiculous. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Share Updated at 16.26 EDT

30m ago 16.18 EDT Eeesh, Dumfries nudges the ball away from Amiri – whose nickname, I trust, is Del – but, already committed to the slide, he tanks in to knock plough through the Inter man, knocking him off his feet. The challenge, though, is with thigh not stud, which is, I imagine, why there’s no red card. Share

33m ago 16.15 EDT Oh my complete and utter days! Summerville slides Dumfries in behind, he crosses low, missing out the keeper, and Meerdink slides in to finish into the empty net from almost under the bar … and somehow sends the ball wide! That is remarkable, a miss that defies the laws of physics and makes Adeyemi’s from earlier look like a composed tuck-away. Share

35m ago 16.12 EDT In Belgrade, Greece are dominating, but still can’t score – Milinkovic-Savic has just saved from Ionnidis, but he oughtn’t to have smelled it. Share

37m ago 16.11 EDT “I wonder does ex-dentist and current Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson pack a bit of novocaine in his kitbag when fulfilling his professional duties these days,” asks Justin Kavanagh. “Watching the current squad for 90 minutes must be painful. Especially when you’ve three appointments scheduled within a week.” View image in fullscreen Heimir Hallgrímsson gets ready for training. Possibly. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Alamy Share Updated at 16.18 EDT

38m ago 16.09 EDT Back in Dam, Netherlands are chasing an equaliser, Van Dijk having a header deflected over before the ref ruins an almighty scramble from the ensuing second corner, blowing up before Meerdink fires home. Share

41m ago 16.06 EDT GOAL! Norway 2-2 Denmark (Hojlund 60) Dorgu swings a decent corner in and, though Hjulmand’s header is saved by Nyland, Hojlund pounces from close range. From 2-0 up and cruising, Norway have been pegged back. View image in fullscreen Rasmus Hojlund levels it up for Denmark in Oslo. Photograph: NTB/Reuters Share Updated at 16.13 EDT

43m ago 16.05 EDT NO GOAL! Portugal 1-0 Wales Yup, you could see that with the naked eye, and Ronaldo can barely believe the effrontery of the system. View image in fullscreen No. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters Share Updated at 16.07 EDT

44m ago 16.04 EDT But was he offside? I think he was, you know… Share

44m ago 16.04 EDT GOAL! Portugal 2-0 Wales (Ronaldo 59) Bruno disguises a lush ball in behind, striking across it and threading it through the near side of the defence, and Ronaldo slides across Ward and low into the far corner. Share

48m ago 15.59 EDT Timber powers through midfield and finds Gakpo … whose square-pass is poor. Holland’s lack of attacking class is remarkable – in 2004, say, they had Van Hooijdonk, Van Nistelrooy, Makaay, Overmars, Robben, Kluivert … and Andy van der Meyde. Share Updated at 16.33 EDT

50m ago 15.57 EDT “What could go wrong under Jesus?” returns Nelson Calvinho. “Exactly what you said, Daniel: he won’t get to develop players in international football. There’s also his hubris and stubbornness. At times his football is too attacking and leaves his teams exposed. He famously didn’t rate Bernardo Silva either, and played him at left-back at Benfica... On the flip side, one thing that stopped him doing even better in his career is his combustible personality (Mourinho on steroids), which tends to grate on players after a while. That shouldn’t be much of a problem with the national side, as he won’t be with them day in, day out. I still have high hopes for him as Portugal’s manager, purely because his tactical acumen is up there with the best in the world. All his teams, from Benfica and Sporting to Flamengo, have played incredibly exciting football. And yes, I was hoping Jesus would be the one with big enough cojones to leave Ronaldo out. Sigh...” Is there a clamour in Portugal to get him gone? In England he’d have been hounded into retirement tiiiiime ago. View image in fullscreen Jorge ‘Jorge’ Jesus Photograph: Joao Gregorio/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Share Updated at 16.04 EDT

54m ago 15.53 EDT “Portugal v Wales, and a painful reminder that one of the greatest month of my life was 10 (TEN!!!) years ago,” says Matt Dony. “The inexorable creep of time. Portugal looked so damn beatable in Euro 2016, but you can’t legislate for Ronaldo scoring that header. Of course he’s not the same player now, but the scars remain. Every time he touches the ball, I expect him to suddenly become the CR7 again. He’ll definitely score. Theres not a doubt in This Sullen Welsh Heart. (Thanks, Nicky Wire).” Well, he’s just made a mess of a diving header for 2-0 but, on the plus side, it gave us a decent look at his yellow highlights. Share Updated at 15.55 EDT

1h ago 15.50 EDT We’re away again in Lisbon and Oslo; Belgrade and Dam soon come. Share

1h ago 15.48 EDT Half-time email: “Not a lot happening in Lisbon,” reports Gareth Rogers. “My personal highlight was the ‘You’re just a shit Gareth Bale!!’ chant from the traveling fans after Ronaldo spurned an easy chance to further pad his goal scoring stats against weak teams, threw his arms dramatically in the air and pointed at the imaginary divot. I will so miss him when he’s gone.” An international level, that song is true of almost everyone. At club level, brilliant though he was, in the company he kept I felt Bale lacked a bit of guile and finesse. But I can’t think of many better international footballers than him. Share

1h ago 15.36 EDT HALF-TIME: Netherlands 0-1 Germany There’s a pleasing tetch to this one and a growing sense of injustice in the Dutch ranks. The second half should be decent. Share Updated at 15.46 EDT

1h ago 15.36 EDT “First half report from Kosovo is that Kosovo are all over Ireland like a duck on a junebug,” says JR in Illinois. “That they’re not up at least 3-0 is bordering on the miraculous.” Share

1h ago 15.35 EDT Ireland are drawing 0-0 in Kosovo at the break. Share

1h ago 15.34 EDT HALF-TIME: Norway 2-1 Denmark Since Denmark halved the deficit, they’ve been the better team – this is another really fun contest. Share

1h ago 15.34 EDT HALF-TIME: Serbia 1-0 Greece Greece has been excellent since going behind, but Serbia had a great chance to make it 2-0 in what is really enjoyable game. Share

1h ago 15.33 EDT HALF-TIME: Portugal 1-0 Wales Portugal are much too good for Wales, but only have a one-goal lead to show for their superiority. Share

1h ago 15.31 EDT Back to Nelson’s email, you don’t really get to develop players in international football – it’s more about picking a team that works. I’d like a bit more pace up front, though I suppose not many teams squeeze high, and I’d definitely like Joao Neves in the team – I’d put Neto up front instead of Ronaldo and work it out that way. Share

1h ago 15.29 EDT Amiri lifts a fine ball over the top for the marauding Brown and, rousting into the box, he might shoot himself, but instead makes sure, squaring for Adeyemi … who somehow shoots over the top! Klopp can only laugh, before applauding the approach-work. That was some miss. Share

1h ago 15.26 EDT “As much as I dislike Jorge Jesus as a person,” writes Nelson Calvinho, “the truth is he’s an elite ‘teacher’ manager, whose attacking, demanding, micromanaging style dramatically raises the tactical awareness and technical quality of his players. He’s absolutely obsessed about details. UK media just don’t rate him highly enough, or completely ignore him, because he’s never managed in one of your so-called big five leagues. But when you think of the players he developed or revitalised into elite footballers (Di Maria, David Luiz, Matic, Ramires, Rafael Leão, Fábio Coentrão, Oblak, Bruno Fernandes, Enzo Perez, Axel Witsel and more, many of whom have publicly called him the best coach they ever had), it’s hard not to dream about what he’ll make of this Portugal side. If we can’t do it with Jorge Jesus, we probably never will.” You never know how international football will work, but as long as he’s picking Ronaldo, I can’t see Portugal winning anything. Share

1h ago 15.24 EDT PSA: earlier today, Eoin Morgan said that Sri Lanka’s total was “in and around par”. It’s such a buzz to see groundbreaking stuff like that. Share

1h ago 15.23 EDT Brobbey is replaced by Mexx Meerdink who, if nothing else, has a tremendous name. Which of us wouldn’t love a dub-X? View image in fullscreen Mexx power. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock Share Updated at 15.37 EDT

1h ago 15.22 EDT GOAL! Netherlands 0-1 Germany (Nmecha 32) With Brobbey down and wanting treatment, having done his hammy running, Germany play on, Kimmich lifts a cross-kick over to the right, Treu crosses low, and though Adeyemi can’t turn in at the near post, Nmecha arrives on the scene to punch in the opener. As youj might imagine, Van Dijk is now even less dignant than previously, and there’s minor argy-bargy before we get going again. View image in fullscreen Felix Nmecha scores for Germany! Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images Share Updated at 15.28 EDT

1h ago 15.19 EDT Back in Belgrade, Jovic has just blasted over from close range – that should’ve been 2-0. And, in Amsterdam, Ebnoutalib hammers a rising shot from a tight angle that Verbruggen has to beat away. Share

2h ago 15.16 EDT Timber accidentally treads on Havertz, who doesn’t enjoy it all; I fear that may be his evening done. On the plus side, I also enjoy Germany’s kit. View image in fullscreen Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock Share
