Sports.title: James Garner keen to live up to ‘mini-Valverde’ tag after late England call
Sports.content:
“It’s a very good comparison,” James Garner says, and he is not kidding. It came from Thomas Tuchel in March after the England manager had watched the Everton midfielder impress on his international debut against Uruguay. He was up against Federico Valverde and Tuchel went big with his praise. Garner was a “mini Valverde”, he said after the 1-1 draw at Wembley.

It was surely too much, despite the prefix that Tuchel attached, yet it was possible to see where he was coming from. Like Valverde, Garner wants to operate in central midfield but he can play at right-back or on the wing. And like Valverde, who they called El Pajarito – or the Little Bird – when he was a kid, Garner can sometimes fly a bit under the radar.

Is Valverde the most underrated player in the game? The more the question is asked, the more the point is lost but there is certainly something there. “You wouldn’t really call him a household name, would you?” Garner says of the Real Madrid player. “But players who have played the game – they know how good he is. I watch a lot of football. I watch all the Champions League games and he always stands out. So yeah, I would go as far as saying that he’s underrated. In my opinion, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world.”

The pros know. And within the game, there is a burgeoning appreciation of Garner, who located such outstanding form at Everton from the turn of the year that he won his first England call-up and was considered unlucky to miss out on the World Cup squad. In the end, Tuchel went with Jordan Henderson and Kobbie Mainoo as the midfield back-ups to Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson. Henderson played six minutes as a substitute during the tournament; Mainoo not at all.

“It was a tough phone call [from Tuchel] because you don’t know whether it’s a yes or a no,” Garner says. “He just said that he could only take a certain amount of players and I’ve missed out this time. I respect his decision and it just makes you hungrier.”

View image in fullscreen James Garner impressed on debut against Uruguay but missed out on the World Cup. Photograph: Alex Davidson/The FA/Getty Images

The 25-year-old is back in the squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures, albeit as a late call-up after the withdrawals of Rice and Mainoo. Henderson was not picked on fitness grounds. Tuchel recalled Alex Scott and Myles Lewis-Skelly in his original selection and continues to overlook Adam Wharton. Anderson stands as the most established midfielder as Tuchel prepares for the visit of Spain to Wembley on Saturday night. Thereafter, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Garner flew to Bodrum in Turkey on Sunday night for a holiday with his partner and he had just put the key in the hotel room door when he got the call from the Football Association. He flew home on Monday before reporting to St George’s Park on Tuesday. “It was a very short holiday,” he says with a smile. “I’m more than happy to be here now.”

Tuchel also gave a late call to Morgan Gibbs-White, who had just got to Dubai for a family holiday. The Nottingham Forest attacking midfielder made a lighthearted TikTok video in which he and his fiancee mimed Gotta Go My Own Way from High School Musical 2 as he packed up and headed back. Was Garner tempted to do something similar? “No. That’s not me,” he replies.

Garner is no-nonsense. He is laidback company but there is a toughness to him on the pitch, a warrior spirit to go with the intelligence of his game, the technique and range of his passing. Growing up in the Manchester United academy, he played as a centre-half until the age of 15 and his boyhood hero feels appropriate.

“I’ve never actually said this but I used to love Nemanja Vidic,” he says. “I used to love the No 15 [which Vidic wore] and things like that. Then you grow up a little bit more, I became a midfielder and I used to love Lampard, Scholes and Gerrard.”

Garner made the move into midfield with United at a junior tournament. “It was the Nike Cup and our midfielder got injured in the first game,” Garner says. “I’ve always been half-decent with the ball at my feet so they thought: ‘We’ll push him into midfield.’ I had a really good tournament and it just went from there. Albeit when I was with England under-16s and under-17s, I played centre-back.”

He is a student of the game. “I watch all matches and also, as mad as it sounds, I played Fifa for so long,” he says. “I’ve been so indulged in football since I was a kid. My brother is five years older than me, he played and I’ve always been around football. I was lucky enough to come through United’s academy, which is one of the best academies in the world, and I learned so much from a lot of good coaches. I’ve just always had that tactical awareness and maybe that helps me playing different positions.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Garner could not see a first-team pathway at United. They loaned him to Watford for six months, then Forest for 18 months. The writing was on the wall for him in the summer of 2022 when United bolstered their midfield with the signings of Casemiro and Christian Eriksen. His move to Everton for a bargain £9m still rankles with a section of the United support.

View image in fullscreen James Garner has no regrets over leaving Manchester United and joining Everton. Photograph: Gary Oakley/Everton FC/Getty Images

“It was the perfect thing for me to do – 1,000%,” Garner says. “I’ve never been shy of going into a more uncomfortable place, changing scenery or anything like that. I went on loan. I moved down to London and Nottingham. It was about playing games and Everton was the perfect choice. I didn’t want to fizzle into the background and just sit on the bench. I wanted to go to a team where I felt like I had a chance to fight for my position.

“Do I have any regrets about leaving United? No, not really. I am a big believer that everything happens for a reason. Had I stayed I wouldn’t have been where I am today so I am more than happy that I left.”

Garner made a statement on the international stage when he starred for the England under-21s in their European Championship triumph of 2023. He was named in the team of the tournament – as a right-back, which was where he played in the final when England beat Spain 1-0. He hopes to make another against the same nation.

“Spain have got the Ballon d’Or winner in their midfield [Rodri] so to play against someone like that is the ultimate test,” Garner says. “You want to go against the best and see how you fare.”

Sports.title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
Sports.content:
The former England forward Andy Carroll has revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.

Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.

The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.

“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.

“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”

Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.

The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”

Sports.title: UK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate
Sports.content:
English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for “bringing Hillsborough into the debate” around drinking in sight of the pitch.

Talk of changing the law to allow fans to drink at their seat or in the stands has resurfaced after Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said the rules were outdated and discriminatory and should be scrapped.

The Football Supporters’ Association (FSA) immediately backed his call but the UKFPU urged caution, stating: “Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster.”

The UKFPU added it would be “incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence”.

“The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.”

The Taylor Report referenced by the UKFPU was commissioned in the wake of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, which resulted in the deaths of 97 Liverpool fans.

The FSA published a thread on its X account setting out its position on drinking in the stands, which began: “Arguably the most important point is that the UK Football Policing Unit’s comments bringing Hillsborough into this debate have to be corrected. The disaster was not caused by alcohol. Full stop.

“Fans were ‘unlawfully killed and a catalogue of failings by police and the ambulance services contributed to their deaths’.”

A spokesperson for the UKFPU said: “It was not our intention to link the issue of alcohol with the Hillsborough tragedy. The laws around alcohol, which we acknowledge were first introduced in 1985, are one of a range of measures in addition to the subsequent Taylor Report recommendations that have contributed to making football much safer for fans in this country.”

Burnham’s comments have sparked social media debate in which differing views have been expressed by match-going fans.

The FSA’s post on Thursday added: “It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We are fundamentally sceptical of any law which is only targeted at football supporters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“That doesn’t mean every club should be forced to serve alcohol to every seat! A club should have the choice to do what is right for its fans. Consultation is critical, some stadiums or stands might not be suitable (eg family areas) whereas it might be popular elsewhere.

“Ultimately, we think clubs, in liaison with their supporters, should be able to determine what is best for themselves, rather than relying on legislation which is decades old and was written through the prism of viewing all football fans as potential hooligans.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales in the top five men’s leagues.

Burnham said on Wednesday: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.

“But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently from others.”

Sports.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
Sports.content:
For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.

There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.

The first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothing false about this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”

As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”

Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez but Atlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”

Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – video

It was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.

“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”

Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo and another at Valencia. Against Racing there was a hat-trick and another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord. Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty Images

Nor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is not even about him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.

Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.

By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. But Lamine Yamal was emerging and, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite the pair that tore up the Euros.

Barcelona failed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirt on social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”

Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelona to the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games. Another title followed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.

His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

That moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”

He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga and Gradient Sports has measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”

Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts and Raphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.

View image in fullscreen Fermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything is anything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.

“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be the pesado [pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”

With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”

View image in fullscreen Raphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Is there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’s the candidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”

Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “The semi-final against Inter [in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético [in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”

Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.

Sports.title: Infantino under pressure to include abandoned World Cup sell-off plan in external Fifa review
Sports.content:
Fifa council members will demand that Gianni Infantino include the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair in his proposed external review of Fifa’s governance.

In a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations on Monday, Infantino said he would ask the council to commission a review of “Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives” at its next meeting, in Zurich on 15 October, but he faces an internal battle over its terms of reference.

The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, wrote to Infantino last week demanding the release of all documents relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme that was abandoned last month, as well as the background to the global governing body’s decision to lift Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, a request that has the support of many fellow council members.

One told the Guardian that without a retrospective analysis of FFE and Balogun, any governance review would lack credibility. Another suggested Infantino was seeking to avoid personal scrutiny by offering to look at Fifa’s governance structures moving forward rather than past controversies.

The council is made up of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents, Infantino and Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström.

In the immediate aftermath of the Balogun affair, when the US striker’s suspension from the World Cup last-32 tie against Belgium was lifted after a phone call to Infantino from Donald Trump, a group of council members attempted to call an extraordinary general meeting but were unable to get the 19 votes required.

The European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations campaigning against Infantino have 21 of the 38 council seats between them, but that includes delegates from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia, who have issued public statements of support for the president.

The German football federation president, Bernd Neuendorf, expressed the European view clearly this week by describing Infantino’s offer of a governance review as cynical electioneering, but any vote on the matter at the council is likely to be tight.

“I regard Gianni Infantino’s letter as a transparent ploy to secure ⁠his re-election next year,” Neuendorf said. “Fundamentally, Fifa now seems to have recognised that changes are essential. However, Gianni Infantino ⁠is definitely not the right person to lead a reform ⁠process.”

Infantino said on Wednesday his letter had been well received. He was speaking while attending the opening night of the Arabian Gulf Cup in Jeddah, from where he will fly to New York for meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I am looking forward to receiving feedback from everyone, following my letter,” he said. “I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other, here in Saudi Arabia, in any one of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

“We have a council meeting next month, so we will continue to have dialogue on these important matters. There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting each other.

“This is not about generating positive headlines, it is about doing what is right for the game. And I have never been more determined and committed in doing that. Fifa is always engaged. I am always engaged and want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Pints and points: the arguments for and against booze at football matches
Sports.content:
THIRSTY WORK

Considering he is a lifelong Everton fan, it’s no surprise that Andy Burnham seems to be in favour of allowing fans to drink Tin at football matches. Bouts of boardroom turmoil, points deductions and assorted relegation battles mean the lot of an Evertonian is not always a happy one. The Prime Minister believes that if he and other fans fancy a sip or two to help ease the pain of watching Thierno Barry head wide of an open goal, then that ought to be their constitutional right as proud Englishmen. Sadly, no such right currently exists, as alcohol consumption within view of the pitch has been outlawed in the top five divisions of English football since the troubled times of the 1980s. Instead, thirsty match-goers are forced to endure an agonising wait of 45 whole minutes before rushing to the bar, joining long queues of fellow fans eager to buy pints of foaming shaft they must subsequently chug back, yard-of-ale style, in enough time to return to their seats for the start of the second half.

In a move some cynical folk have described as populist political grandstanding, Burnham has correctly pointed out that in not being allowed to enjoy a pint during games, football fans are being discriminated against compared to their counterparts in sports such as cricket, rugby and horse racing. “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point,” he told a gaggle of reporters during a flight to New York. “That legislation dates to an era where football was very different and I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done – it could happen on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

While Burnham has a point, reaction to the possibility of booze returning to football match stands has been mixed. While the sanctimonious bleating of “if you can’t last 45 minutes without a drink, then there’s something wrong with you” from the puritan brigade strikes Football Daily as reason enough for an immediate change in legislation and trebles all round, reintroducing alcohol could pose a logistical problem not previously experienced by the current generation of fans. Specifically, them being forced to repeatedly stand up and sit down again in order to make room for an endless procession of people going to and from the bars and toilets. While we’re not proud to admit it, Football Daily has attended enough rugby internationals to know exactly how annoying this can be.

The Football Supporters Association favours Burnham’s suggestion that allowing fans to bring an overpriced, flimsy receptacle of flat lager to their seats would massively enhance the matchday experience and the Premier League is obviously open to any idea that helps its members prise an extra few quid out of customers. The UK Football Policing Unit, however, is understandably less enthused. “Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour,” they harrumphed. “It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.” While alcohol consumption increases the risk of violent disorder, the recent box-park phenomenon of performative and celebratory pint-throwing almost certainly will too. Nobody wants to come home from a football match drenched in beer, even if the only alternatives are to stay at home or start supporting Spurs.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Daniel Harris from 7.45pm BST for hot clockwatch action in the Nations League with Netherlands 1-2 Germany, Portugal 3-1 Wales and more.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Whenever they say they don’t want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go. When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … just look at the numbers, I’m sure you can make some calculations, I’m still doing well. The day they don’t count on me, no problemo, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation. It would be the cherry on the top of the cake to score my 1,000th goal with the national team. It would be the culmination of a beautiful story. I said I wanted to reach that target and I will reach that target. But I don’t have an obsession. If you are obsessed with something, you won’t get it … just enjoy. Carpe diem, enjoy the day.” – Cristiano Ronaldo is completely calm and not at all obsessing over the 21 goals he needs to reach the 1,000 mark ahead of Portugal’s Nations League match against Wales today.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo is 21 goals away from the big 1,000. Photograph: Antonio Pedro Santos/EPA

double quotation mark Like anyone with a sense of football heritage, as soon as I read in yesterday’s Football Daily that Javier Aguirre had joined Valencia, I scrambled to see when they would play Anthony Gordon’s Barcelona. Sadly, it seems we’ll have to wait until the end of January for that particular reunion. Hey, fixture list, beep you” – Jim Hearson.

double quotation mark If Thomas Tuchel believes that 99.9% of supporters he bumps into do not talk to him about his substitutions during the Argentina game (Football Daily Tuesday), has he noticed a significant percentage of fans turning on their heels and walking in the opposite direction muttering furiously to themselves when they spot him? I would estimate that this could encompass approximately 51.8% of England supporters in his orbit. Another cohort, which I would put at around 37.6%, may break down weeping and gnashing their teeth uncontrollably at a missed opportunity to beat a limited and cynical Argentinian team, thereby missing their opportunity to congratulate Thomas effusively on England’s knockout win over Democratic Republic of Congo” – Dexter O’ Riordan.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day prize goes to … Jim Hearson, who wins a copy of Behind the Curtain by Big Website’s Jonathan Wilson. It’s out now and available in The Guardian Bookshop alongside loads of other great football titles. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
Disclaimer: I have made a lot of bad TV programmes. I have done quite a few below-average radio shows. Podcasts, there are millions of them – some might say too many – and I’ve done my fair share that won’t go down in history. In between those, I’ve hopefully done some pretty good ones – it’s not for me to say.

I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. I’ve hosted shows where I’ve had almost complete editorial control, and ones where I could have been replaced by a performing monkey.

I’ve had to host TV shows at every possible height – sitting on a sofa, on a normal chair, on a normal chair behind a desk, on a bar stool in a pub, on a bar stool not in a pub, and standing up when there was somewhere comfortable to sit just out of shot. I complained a lot, but standing did actually work, Murray.

The point being, I have some experience when it comes to reviewing the opening night of the Disney+ coverage of the Women’s Champions League. The Hangout was hosted by Alex Scott with her fellow former England international Lianne Sanderson, the content creators Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess, and quite inexplicably a golden retriever called Barley Boy, who at the time of writing has 82,000 more Instagram followers than I have – I must work on my reels.

The show included a quiz about Italy, including guess the Italian name for football and what pasta the reporter in Milan is cooking. There’s an incredible still image of the panel staring at a load of farfalle on a big screen normally reserved for team lineups or key match incidents.

The immediate reaction was a mix of bewilderment and fury from seasoned lovers of the women’s game. Kathryn Batte wrote an understandable critique for the Telegraph. The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughes posted on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”

Consistent with all the criticism is the truth that the men’s Champions League would never be covered in the same way. It is perhaps interesting to ask how the team arrived at the concept. Why replace former pros with content creators, why replace tactical analysis with asking what’s the biggest city in Italy? Why a dog?

The broadcaster Marva Kreel perfectly articulated one of the issues in her own X post: “I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women’s football broadcasting over analysis and punditry v content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men’s football you can get both – and in different shows. In women’s football you get one show, and so they try to do it all.”

It’s a fair point. I’ve mainly hosted the show before the show – where a dog running around wouldn’t be regarded as a crime against the game. In fact hosting live football is significantly more straightforward than interviewing an indie band about their difficult second album or trying to come up with a three-hour radio show in the middle of the international break. The show Disney tried to make on Wednesday is technically much harder than Super Sunday – but that doesn’t mean it was the right call.

I can understand the thinking. I imagine the bosses told the producers they want to bring in a younger audience. I have been told this before. Exactly how to do that is impossible to work out. Should I stop making references to Jossy’s Giants and Aswad? And Disney could probably argue that most of the criticism didn’t come from young people. It came from people who expect the game to be covered in a certain way.

(From left) Former England international Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and golden retriever Barley Boy. Photograph: Disney+

Disney may be being cynical – people are talking and writing about it. The hardcore will watch anyway. Had they produced more traditional coverage, no one would have said anything. And sometimes you have to try something different. I wouldn’t want to be too critical; Disney may give me a gig one day.

Major broadcasters have less money to make the same amount of stuff – and have had a battle over the past 20 years to work out how to harness social media. I saw it at Sky, where a Facebook livestream filmed on an iPhone in the green room would get as many views as the show itself with the costs of studio/lighting/sound/producers etc.

As a middle-aged man – whose wife accuses him of being a “boomer” – I really dislike the phrase “content creator”; perhaps I’m nervous that eventually they’ll take all my jobs. From what I saw, Bailess and Mills came across as very personable and fun – which was clearly the brief – and you can’t criticise anyone for taking a job. And they bring a following with them – quite how many followers lead to subscriptions is a different question.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

I feel for Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some sort of culture war. You are entitled to regard her as the greatest or worst broadcaster of her generation – or somewhere in between – as you are with me or anyone else. I know many listeners certainly feel the latter about my abilities.

I found the discourse around the end of Football Focus pretty troubling – people suggesting the show went woke and lost its way when she was appointed. It’s much more accurate to accuse me of turning Soccer AM woke, with my clarinet, lefty snowflake opinions and inability to flirt on live television. But then I’m not a woman and I’m white; generally people just accuse me of turning it shit.

But back to the Hangout. I imagine Scott didn’t suggest having a dog in the studio or having guess the pasta. Perhaps she has a lot of editorial control – I genuinely don’t know. But sometimes as a host you have to do what you’re told and do it with conviction.

The reality of live football coverage is that people are watching because they want to watch the game. If people want comedy, they’ll watch Curb Your Enthusiasm. If Liverpool are playing Real Madrid, the fans will watch it – and either enjoy or endure the coverage. But what you can do as a broadcaster is make it as compelling as possible, and there are different ways of being a good host or pundit.

Live football coverage hasn’t changed dramatically in 50 years. Welcome, team news, managers, bit of tactics or player focus, throw to commentators. Half-time: what did you make of that? Full time: what did you make of that?

The dog did not return for the second night of coverage. I know it would have been a strange and difficult day for everyone involved. They made a show, people didn’t like it and they had to go again the next night. Do you double down, screw the haters, or try to subtly move towards a more traditional setup? It seemed on Wednesday they went for the latter.

You can’t magic up an audience, but you can make people feel like you respect the game, you can do it in an entertaining way without introducing animals, and people will come back and watch you again.

Sports.title: I was a former NFL kicker and now coach the next generation, be warned Harry Kane - THIS is the ruthlessly cut-throat world that awaits you if you want to chase a career in Gridiron
Sports.content:
I was a former NFL kicker and now coach the next generation, be warned Harry Kane - THIS is the ruthlessly cut-throat world that awaits you if you want to chase a career in Gridiron

It’s not impossible for Harry Kane to become an NFL kicker one day but I’d still put it at very long odds.

I have seen guys jump from being soccer players to kickers but, even then, they’re usually in their early 20s and only make it to college football. The only real exception is the current kicker Brandon Aubrey, who was drafted by side Toronto before making the switch to NFL.

The big difference is that NFL kickers have focused on one thing for a very, very long time. They probably started specialising in kicking field goals around the age of 13, so by the time they make it to the NFL they have been at it for ten years. Just kicking field goals, nothing else. It would be like a soccer player not practising tackling, passing or even general shooting but just taking free-kicks, non-stop, for a decade.

So, even when you’ve got someone who’s athletic and is a sensational soccer player, like Harry Kane, it’s going to be hard to actually be as good as somebody who just did one thing for many years.

People often compare it to golf but, even then, you have different types of swings, different clubs, different lies. When it comes to kicking, every time you step on the field your goal is the exact same thing you have done since you were 13: hit the ball as far and as straight as possible every single time. Then go back through the video and nitpick every little detail so you can hit it farther and straighter next time and do it over and over and over again. It’s intense and it’s boring, too. This is why it’s dominated by people who have that mental strength to perfect one simple skill.

I’ve coached loads of NFL kickers, including Philadelphia Eagles’ Jake Elliott. These guys aren’t just amazing on game day. They are on it every single day. Their supreme leg strength is probably the least of all the factors to make it. You have to have the skill set and mentality to be almost 100 per cent every single day.

Harry Kane faces a difficult challenge if he wishes to make it as a professional NFL kicker

That’s not to say he can’t do it. It took Aubrey about two years of focused, intense training. If Kane put all of his mind and training into it, he could probably get to that level in a year or two if his body doesn’t give out beforehand due to age or overuse.

Even then, there's so many other kickers that he would be competing with for his job. Ones that are polished and experienced and have the knowledge of kicking in high-pressure situations.

And they have to make them. Kickers have to make above 90 per cent of their attempts to have a job, basically. If you are below 90 per cent, if you miss more than maybe three field goals over the course of a season, they are going to look to replace you.

That's a different pressure to even those experienced by elite soccer players, just from the nature of the game.

To land a spot as an NFL kicker, which is one player per team, you would have to be in the top 32 in the world at what you do. The coach that takes a chance on Harry Kane is putting their job on the line to give him a shot. If it all goes sideways, that same coach might lose their job.

There are some similarities in the technique. They can be launching it more than 60 yards and if you look at the kicks, they’re high and dead straight. There’s zero movement on the ball. In that sense, maybe, it’s more similar to a defender striking it long than a striker.

Brandon Aubrey has warned the England skipper that his job is not as simple as it may seem

There’s lots more body behind the ball because you’re striking a stationary object. You can really get your whole body behind it. In soccer, things are always moving, you’re hitting it off balance, with players around you, from different angles, everything like that. The difference is in being able to maximise getting as much body behind the ball in every strike.

If I had any piece of advice for Kane, it’s this: drills, drills, drills. Do as many as you can. A kicker’s body only has so many full-strength kicks in them in a day or a week, but at half-speed, where you can just dial it in, you can do those from sunrise to sunset. Do it.

Sports.title: Arsenal suffer injury blow as Kai Havertz is forced off in first half of Germany's clash with the Netherlands
Sports.content:
Arsenal suffer injury blow as Kai Havertz is forced off in first half of Germany's clash with the Netherlands

Kai Havertz was forced off during the first half of Germany's Nations League clash against the Netherlands, handing Arsenal an early injury concern during the international break.

Havertz was tasked with leading the line in Jurgen Klopp's first match as Germany's new head coach.

The 27-year-old lasted just 30 minutes of the fixture with the forward having gone down appearing to signal an issue with his hamstring.

Havertz's issue emerged just minutes after he had fallen victim to a poor challenge from Quinten Timber, the brother of Havertz's Arsenal team-mate Jurrien.

Timber had arrived late for a challenge and caught Havertz high on his knee, with the German attacker immediately falling to the pitch.

Havertz appeared fortunate that the late challenge had only seen Timber's boot brush his knee, rather than make significant contact.

Kai Havertz went down with an apparent hamstring injury during Germany's match with the Netherlands

The Arsenal star limped off with the issue after the half hour mark of the Nations League clash

Havertz ultimately left the field with a hamstring issue later in the half, with Younes Ebnoutalib coming on to make his international debut as his replacement.

While Havertz walked off the pitch, the injury will be of concern to Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta.

Havertz has been an ever-present for the Gunners' starting line-up in their first five Premier League matches of the campaign, with Arteta backing him to lead their attack.

The extended international break will give Havertz time to recover before Arsenal's next Premier League match against Leeds on October 10.

There was another injury issue for a Premier League side, with Sunderland forward Brian Brobbey also being forced off with a hamstring problem.

Brobbey, who scored a hat-trick against Man City last weekend, went down for the Netherlands during a Germany attack in the first half.

Despite appeals from the Dutch to kick the ball out, Germany continued to attack and ultimately opened the scoring through Felix Nmecha.

Dutch players clashed with their German opponents after being angered over the nature of the goal, with Brobbey also needing to be replaced due to his injury.

Sports.title: England are BEATEN by Sri Lanka in dramatic ODI: Injury to Jos Buttler derails huge run chase as Harry Brook's side blow chance to win series
Sports.content:
England are BEATEN by Sri Lanka in dramatic ODI: Injury to Jos Buttler derails huge run chase as Harry Brook's side blow chance to win series

England lost in dramatic circumstances at Headingley as Jos Buttler's late injury altered the course of a huge run chase against Sri Lanka.

Buttler was powering his team towards their 322 target, and series victory, it seemed when he pulled his left hamstring running two, but his exit from the field, when unbeaten on 67, transformed the contest and such was his impairment that there were to be no heroics when he returned to the crease with 27 runs required off 14 balls.

England, who had won 13 of 14 internationals since Brendon McCullum was relieved of his Test coaching duties in midsummer, had never knocked off such a score to beat Sri Lanka.

There were just 63 required off the final 10 with five wickets intact, but the Sri Lankans have great memories of Leeds, winning a thrilling Test here a dozen years ago and also dealing England a shock defeat in a group stage fixture during the 2019 World Cup.

Here, they added another chapter to their history, tigerishly defending a total founded on a seventh one-day international hundred from their captain Kusal Mendis with some outstanding reverse swing bowling.

After Gus Atkinson faced 28 boundary-less deliveries and Jamie Overton fell cheaply, an incapacitated Buttler returned to the crease with 27 off 14 required, limping a single to get the set Will Jacks back on strike.

An injury to Jos Buttler proved crucial as England fell short of their target of 322 at Headingley

Jacks blasted the final delivery of Asitha Fernando's excellent spell for a straight six to reach his own half century.

But Jacks holed out in the penultimate over and although Buttler swung from the hip in the last, he too failed to clear the fielder in the deep.

'Losing a player of Jos' ability is always going to have an effect. But there are other reasons why we lost as well,' said England captain Harry Brook.

'I had full confidence in us chasing that total down at the halfway stage. There were plenty of areas where we weren't up to our best.'

England were given an electric start thanks to a career-best 73 off 62 balls from Tom Banton and Ben Duckett, who put his poor sequence in Test cricket behind him with 67 off 63.

Between them they shared an opening stand of 143, before each succumbing to slow left-armer Dunith Wellalage, who threatened to turn the contest on its head with three wickets in as many overs.

When Harry Brook was pinned on the pads by a delivery that was bending its way towards the top of leg stump, England had lost three for 14.

From a position of 157 for three, though, Buttler made a tactical decision to demoralise Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka's best bowler on debut in Chester-le-Street 48 hours earlier, hitting two of his five innings sixes in one over when he was invited to switch to the Kirkstall Lane end.

Kusal Mendis' sparkling knock of 121 propelled the tourists to 321-6 from their 50 overs

Mendis retained his faith in Colombage, however, and was rewarded when Joe Root departed for a rare failure, picking out short extra cover.

Earlier, England found it tough going on a flat pitch four strips along from the one under investigation by pitch consultant Andy Mackay last week following Somerset's County Championship defeat here. Although it is understood Yorkshire will escape censure for that, the contrast between how each played could not have been more striking.

With the ball sliding beautifully onto the bat, there was an onus on Brook's side to take any chances that came their way.

However, after Atkinson's persistent new-ball diligence was rewarded with the leg before dismissal of Pathum Nissanka, following a failed review, they were guilty of a costly miss.

Mendis, on 17, towered Jamie Overton's second delivery from the Football Stand end off the top edge to fine leg with the aid of the afternoon breeze and must have had his heart in his mouth as Gus Atkinson settled underneath it two yards from the rope.

Sri Lanka would have been 68 for two had Atkinson's hands clasped around the ball. Instead, England's attack were flayed around Leeds during a stand of 137 in 120 deliveries between Mendis and his namesake Kamindu Mendis for the second wicket.

At 182 for one in the 30th over, the Sri Lankans were on course to blitz their highest ODI score against England in this country.

They would have been disappointed to fall three runs shy of the 324 for two they hurtled to in completing a 5-0 series whitewash over Andrew Strauss' team here at Headingley 20 years ago, losing momentum once captain Mendis was held on the rope at deep midwicket for 121, attempting a fourth six.

But thanks to a chaotic ending, it proved just enough, setting up a series decider at the Oval on Sunday.

Sports.title: Chaos in the Football League as international call-ups force postponement of matches involving THREE lowest-ranked sides - and key target is missed
Sports.content:
Tighter rules imposed to minimise lower league postponements during international breaks have missed the target with more games off than at this time last year, including those featuring the three lowest ranked teams in the EFL. The League One programme has been ravaged with 16 of the next 24 fixtures off to accommodate national team call-ups. Five games in League Two are also postponed over the next two weekends, including Port Vale against Northampton, who are ranked 90th and 91st. It all seems self-defeating with complaints forever swirling around congested fixture lists and at a time when clubs could feast on greater exposure and bigger crowds without Premier League and Championship action. New criteria were brought in this season enabling clubs to apply for a postponement if they expected at least three players to be on duty for senior, Under-21, Under-20 or Under-19 internationals but only if those players had appeared before the 75th minute in 50 per cent of league games or four of the last five first-team games. This is more stringent than last season, when the limit was also three players but with the qualification rules applied only upon the U21, U20 and U19 – not the seniors – and if players started in 25 per cent of league games or in three of the last five first-team games. The League Two match between Northampton and Port Vale, who lie 22nd and 23rd in the table, is one of several postponed in the EFL due to international call-ups There is a slightly different protocol for goalkeepers, with clubs allowed to request a postponement if both the first and second choice goalkeepers are called up. League One leaders Bradford City are without two goalkeepers with regular number one Jon McCracken in the Scotland squad and Zac Hadi called up by Iraq U23s but Cameron Dawson, McCracken's deputy, is available. Bradford have confirmed their game at Reading will go ahead on Saturday, October 3 but the home game against Barnsley on Saturday has been called off by the visitors, who have Patrick Kelly with Northern Ireland, Tyrese Noslin with Curacao, Jonathan Bland with Wales U21s and Makenzie Kirk with Northern Ireland U21s. Reading's opponents Wycombe will also be without their number one 'keeper Conor Hazard, who is with Northern Ireland. The prospect of two games against teams with deputies in goal may explain some of the thinking behind Reading boss Leam Richardson's decision to play on despite three call-ups from his own squad - Charlie Savage for Wales, Andy Rinomhota for Zimbabwe and Jeriel Dorsett for Montserrat. 'Football is a squad game, and we have confidence in the players available to us, while keeping the fixture in place also helps us avoid adding another game to an already busy schedule,' said Richardson. 'It's better for the supporters too. Saturday afternoon is the ideal time to play football whenever circumstances allow, so we were pleased to keep this one in place.' It is not one dimensional. Some clubs want to play on for their own reasons and like the idea of a break for different reasons. Reading will play on despite having international call-ups and could take advantage of their next two opponents missing their first choice goalkeepers With seven on international duty, five of them first team regulars, it is difficult to see how Luton could be expected to play. This season's changes were made with an eye towards the congested schedules and in the hope of keeping more EFL fixtures on where possible. On a financial level, few clubs in the third tier like to lose Saturday afternoon games which are generally better attended and more lucrative than rearranged evening dates in midweek. But there is an inevitable balance to strike with all managers under pressure to win and reluctant to take the risk with some of their better players unavailable and possibly making selections and substitution decisions with the qualification rules in mind. Crawley Town, rock bottom of League Two, are not playing because of call-ups for winger Dion Pereira with Antigua and Barbuda, left-back Jonny Russell with Northern Ireland Under-21s and goalkeeper Nicholas Michalski with England U20s. Michalski, 19, on loan from Blackburn has been first choice for Crawley since veteran former Arsenal keeper Vito Mannone, 38, was injured in August. In last year's September international break eight of the 12 League One fixtures went ahead with a full set in League Two. In the October break last year there were seven of 12 League One games on and only one game off in League Two. There are different reasons in play. Former Premier League clubs Leicester City and Sheffield Wednesday are in League One this season, with bigger academies and appeal for talented youngsters on loan from the top-flight looking for experience. There is an increase in lower-league players searching out international football via ancestral links. And, for the first time, this year's international break is extended to cover two weekends featuring more games and bigger squads.

Sports.title: James Garner claims he may NEVER have played for England had he stayed at Man United as Three Lions star hails 'perfect' move to Everton
Sports.content:
England midfielder James Garner believes he may never have played for England had he stayed at Manchester United.

United academy graduate Garner is pushing for a spot as Elliot Anderson’s midfield partner against Spain in the Nations League on Saturday after Arsenal’s Declan Rice withdrew from Thomas Tuchel’s squad.

He caught Tuchel’s eye with a series of performances for Everton last season and narrowly missed out on World Cup selection after being man of the match on his debut against Uruguay in March.

Back in the squad as a late replacement, Garner believes leaving his boyhood club was the decision that set him on the right path.

‘I think it was the perfect thing for me to do,’ he said.

‘I am a big believer that everything happens for a reason. When I left they signed three or four midfielders, world class ones. Had I stayed I wouldn’t have been where I am today so I am more than happy that I did.

James Garner has lauded his 'perfect' Everton move after earning a spot in the England camp

Garner, who came through United's academy, says he may not have made the Three Lions squad had he not left Old Trafford

‘I've never been shy of going into a more uncomfortable place.

‘I went on loan three times. I went to Watford and then twice to Nottingham.

‘So I wasn't worried about moving at all, changing scenery or anything that.

‘For me, it was just about playing games and Everton was the perfect choice at that point.

‘I didn’t just want to fizzle into the background and just sit on the bench and stuff like that. I wanted to go into a team where I felt like I had a chance to fight for my position and that's what I have done in the past three or four years.’

Garner, 25, describes the United academy as ‘the best in the world’. He joined when he was 8 and didn’t move to Everton until he was 21. Garner made two Premier League appearances and also played for United in the Europa League.

Now a fixture in David Moyes’ Everton team, a midfielder who started out as a central defender and worshipped United’s Nemanja Vidic is hoping he can nail down a place in Tuchel’s squad for good.

He had just checked in to a hotel in Turkey on holiday at the weekend when he received a call telling him he was being called up as a replacement.

Garner is looking to make an impact after earning a late call up to Thomas Tuchel's squad

‘It was a very short holiday,’ he laughed.

‘I had literally just got into my hotel room and I got the call. That’s not an over exaggeration either.

‘I came back the day after. I slept, had the morning in the sun and left.

‘I’m trying to work on a little thing on the hotel so that I’m not losing all my money!

‘So I can at least go back and have the holiday that I paid for. We’ll see what happens…’

Dubbed the ‘mini Valverde’ by Tuchel after the Real Madrid midfielder Federico, Garner has played left-back for Everton but sees his future in the centre of the field.

‘Yeah, it’s a good comparison to have because in my opinion he’s one of the best midfielders in the world,’ Garner said.

‘There’s probably a little bit of similarity in terms of he plays in different positions too.’

Sports.title: 'Xabi appears not to love him': Inside Estevao's uncertain future at Chelsea, why Brazilian is struggling for minutes under new boss Alonso and the compromise he may be forced to accept
Sports.content:
'Xabi appears not to love him': Inside Estevao's uncertain future at Chelsea, why Brazilian is struggling for minutes under new boss Alonso and the compromise he may be forced to accept

Brazil’s games this international break are in Australia and India, and yet Estevao may not mind travelling to the other side of the world. He knows, at least, that he stands a chance of receiving more minutes for his country than he has for his club so far this season.

Estevao has received a grand total of 23 minutes from Xabi Alonso for Chelsea in the Premier League, a figure that does not include stoppage time.

In their five league fixtures, his contribution can be summarised thusly: 83rd-minute substitute, unused substitute, 81st-minute substitute, 86th-minute substitute, 87th-minute substitute with his team already trailing by two goals to Brentford.

That has led to talk back in his homeland of Estevao feeling frustrated, which would be understandable. Reports in Brazil have even hinted he is considering his future at the club and there would be no shortage of suitors for the 19-year-old, despite Chelsea insisting he is a prospect who very much features in their long-term plans.

Some sources close to the player shot down talk of him being disillusioned to Daily Mail Sport, insisting the season is long and there is confidence he will have fairer opportunities to impress.

Others, however, have said there is surprise at how he has been restricted from finding any rhythm under Alonso. One contact in Brazil said simply: ‘Xabi appears not to love him.’

Estevao has been limited to just 23 minutes of Premier League action by new manager Xabi Alonso so far this season

Reports in Brazil have even hinted Estevao is considering his future at the club - there would be no shortage of suitors for the 19-year-old

Estevao himself showed some understanding when speaking while away with Brazil this week, saying: ‘We have quality players at Chelsea, so what I do is focus on what I can control. I try to give my best in training. When I get an opportunity, I try to give my best. It goes day after day.’

Estevao has recovered from the hamstring tear suffered in April which brought a premature end to last season and saw his World Cup dream dashed. That was a tough blow for the teenager to take.

Any hopes of going on a run with Chelsea have been restricted with Cole Palmer and new signing Morgan Rogers forming a formidable front three with Joao Pedro. Pedro Neto has largely impressed as a right wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 set-up, a position where Estevao may also have to share some of the responsibility himself.

Away at Arsenal, the Brazilian came close to scoring a late equaliser after coming on while Chelsea trailed 2-1, denied brilliantly by David Raya.

It won him a starting place in their Carabao Cup clash with Leeds a few days later. However, he struggled and was hooked at half-time alongside three others as Chelsea came back from 1-0 down at the break to win 6-3.

A lack of European football means impressing in cup competitions is crucial if Estevao wants to play more in the Premier League. Yet he is not alone in his predicament. Indeed, he may not be the only winger concerned by his lack of opportunities under Alonso at Chelsea.

Jamie Gittens – a £52million signing from Borussia Dortmund in 2025 – has been an unused substitute in all five of Chelsea’s Premier League games this season. He too started against Leeds in the Carabao Cup, and he too was hooked at half-time.

Roma were interested in Gittens in the summer. Chelsea insisted he was not for sale because he was an important part of their own plans. We have not seen the evidence to back up those words as of yet.

Estevao's minutes have been limited by the arrival of Morgan Rogers, who has formed a formidable front three with Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer

The international breaks offers an opportunity for Estevao - who missed the World Cup through injury - to stake a claim for more chances back at Chelsea

Geovany Quenda – a £44m arrival from Sporting this summer – has likewise had limited opportunities. He has not started in any competition this season, appearing just twice as a substitute.

When players return from injury – Joao Pedro, Moises Caicedo, Reece James and Marco Palestra all missed Chelsea’s last trip to Brentford – some of these wide men may miss out on Alonso’s match-day squad altogether.

They would then risk falling out of sight and out of mind, much like Emmanuel Emegha and Aaron Anselmino, both of whom have only made one matchday squad all season, each acting as unused substitutes in the Carabao Cup against Luton Town. Anselmino was missing when the Chelsea squad posed for their picture, released last week.

Yet Estevao has attracted more attention than most because his potential is so obvious. Signed for a total package worth £51m from Brazilian club Palmeiras on a pre-agreement for when he turned 18, he showed his worth at times in Enzo Maresca’s 4-2-3-1.

Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 is leaving little room for his inclusion, but this international break could be good for him, as a way to try to take the opportunities that Carlo Ancelotti will allow him.

Sports.title: Inside Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele's 'frosty' relationship: Insiders in French camp reveal 'growing' tension between the stars - and the Ballon d'Or is to blame!
Sports.content:
Inside Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele's 'frosty' relationship: Insiders in French camp reveal 'growing' tension between the stars - and the Ballon d'Or is to blame!

French stars Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele’s relationship has reportedly grown ‘frosty’ amid a dispute over this year’s Ballon d’Or award.

The attacking duo have previously enjoyed a close relationship to the benefit of the French national team, but concerns have been said to have been raised over the distance between them during Zinedine Zidane’s first camp as head coach.

According to RMC Sport, the tension between the pair has stemmed from Mbappe’s comments in the build-up to this year’s Ballon d’Or award ceremony.

When it was put to Mbappe that ten years ago few would have expected Dembele to win the honour ahead of him – having claimed the prize last year – the Real Madrid star responded: ‘But he has always been seen as a talented player. I, on the other hand, have always been seen as the chosen one.

‘I was at the top right away, from a very young age. He had a different journey, with injuries, but he has caught up really well.’

Dembele appeared to reference Mbappe’s ‘chosen one’ remark in a subsequent interview, stating: ‘I've always been like that, you know, at the back of the class, working hard.’

Concerns have reportedly between raised over the relationship between French stars Ousmane Dembele and Kylian Mbappe

The pair are claimed to have grown distant over Mbappe's comments ahead of this year's Ballon d'Or, an honour Dembele claimed last year

Mbappe and Dembele have previously had a close relationship but the former's vocal views that he should win the Ballon d'Or are claimed to have created an issue

‘Throughout my career, I haven't said a word, I've just worked, incredibly hard. Like I said, I've never been chosen, but I've worked incredibly hard.

‘Last year, I was rewarded for a fantastic year with PSG. This year, we'll see. No pressure, relaxed.’

While Mbappe has been open about his view that he should win the Ballon d’Or this year, Dembele put forward his PSG team-mate Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, suggesting his performances have been ‘burned into the retina’.

His remark mirrored previous language used by Mbappe when players have been in contention for the Ballon d’Or.

Despite Mbappe insisting there is no rift with Dembele, RMC reported people who know them around the French set-up have identified a clear difference in their relationship on previous training camps to this one.

The pair have been seen sitting next to each other and talking, but it is claimed there is a ‘chill between them’ and that their relationship is ‘not the same as before’.

According to the report, the French national team do not consider the situation a cause for concern at this stage, with national team captain Mbappe and vice-captain Dembele both acting and delivering professionally at this stage.

Mbappe has suggested he was billed as the 'chosen one' when it was suggested that few would have thought Dembele would have won the award before him

It is claimed the relationship between the two stars will be monitored to ensure there is no impact on the dynamics in the national team.

The tension could prove an early test for Zidane, who will take charge of his first match as France head coach on Friday when they face Turkey in the Nations League.

Zidane succeeded Didier Deschamps following France's fourth-placed finish in the World Cup this summer.

Deschamps had served as France head coach for 14 years and guided them to World Cup glory in 2018.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney reveals his Jewish roots after discovering his grandmother's Polish heritage and taking his sons to Auschwitz
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has revealed he has Polish-Jewish heritage in his new documentary.

The former England captain, 40, is starring in a new £10million fly-on-the-wall show, The Real Rooneys, which was filmed last year for Disney+.

'I’ve recently found out that my mum’s mum, so my nan’s, family were Polish Jews,' he says.

'I’m Catholic, but then I’ve always asked questions like why aren’t we Jewish?'

Asked whether he might investigate further and do a spin-off show, he quips: 'Roo the Jew?'

The Rooneys take a trip to Auschwitz in the documentary and Wayne tells his taxi driver: 'I've watched a lot of documentaries on it and you just wouldn't think human beings could do that to other human beings. It's crazy.

Wayne Rooney pays a trip to Auschwitz with his family in his new Disney+ documentary

Rooney reveals that he has Polish-Jewish heritage via his maternal grandmother

Rooney Pictured with his wife Coleen at the premiere for their 10-part documentary on Tuesday

'Having knowledge of what happened before our time and what people did for us to be able to enjoy the privileges we have now, we forget that sometimes.'

In a poignant scene outside the camp, his son Kit asks about the guard towers, where Rooney and their guide explain how the Nazis presented their prisoners from escaping.

He also visited with his England team-mates in 2012 during the European Championship in Poland and Ukraine.

'I’m a parent and it’s tough to see what happened there,' he said at the time.

'You’ve seen the amount of children who died. You see the children’s clothes and shoes, it’s really sad. You have to see it first hand.'

The Rooneys also take a trip to Krakow with third and fourth sons Kit, 10, and Cass, eight, due to the latter taking an interest in the Second World War from his studies.

Coleen, 40, notes that Wayne has 'a real bug for learning about different places in the world, culture, people, values'.

The Manchester United legend has opened up more about his spiritual side recently, explaining on a recent episode of Stick to United how he would like to visit the site of Jesus' baptism, the River Jordan.

'That’s where John the Baptist baptised Jesus, it would be really interesting to go.'

He used to wear a cross at training and revealed that he used to pray for his family before matches.

'I pray to God, of course. I believe in God,' he said in 2012.

'I pray in the physio room. I go in after my warm-up. I basically spend a few minutes in there on my own.

'I don’t pray to help me score goals. I pray for the health of me and everyone on the pitch.

'It is something I have always done. I pray at night. I pray for my family and friends and for the health of everyone I love.'

The new documentary is an intimate look into the life of the family, which also includes Kai, 16, and 13-year-old Klay, who both play for Manchester United's academy.

At the premiere for the show on Tuesday night, Rooney appeared to have turned back the clock as he displayed his new nose job, slimmer physique and smooth skin.

He looked smart in a crisp blue suit worn over a light-coloured shirt as he posed on the red carpet at the event, which was held at the Picturehouse in central London.

The 10-episode documentary is out today, covering a pivotal year in the Rooney household, after Wayne was sacked as Plymouth Argyle manager, swapping the touchline for school runs.

Rooney first shared the results of his nose job back in August after revealing he’d had an operation to fix it after breaking it twice during his football career.

The former forward first revealed he'd had the operation on his new podcast Stick to United, which he presents with football influencer Mark Goldbridge, a week after having surgery.

He revealed that he was feeling 'a little bit uncomfortable' following the surgery.

Coleen Rooney revealed she considered 'separating' from 'careless' husband Wayne following a series of explosive rows

It seems it's not always happy families in the Rooney household as the former England footballer and the I'm A Celebrity star admitted they can go days without talking to each other

He said: 'It's actually really lucky I've got no black eyes, but I've still got two plastic tubes up my nose, which are coming out very soon. I can't wait for them to come out.

'So, they've cut here [under my nostrils]... So, that's all stitched – a little bit uncomfortable.'

Wayne said the first time he broke his nose was during an FA Cup game against Preston North End in 2015 while playing for United.

He added that he remembered the game for 'a bit of a dive' he made to win a penalty.

Wayne continued: 'And then when I went to DC, I broke my nose again. That was a bad one then.

'So I needed surgery, but I've never had it. Put it off. And then this summer I thought get the World Cup out the way and I'll get it done. So had it done last week. Went well, but these tubes were horrible.'

The sportsman later recalled that during the same 3-1 victory against Preston at Deepdale, his former team-mate Marouane Fellaini also broke his nose.

'But he missed the next couple of games. I didn't miss any games,' he added.
