World.title: Liberia Beats Back Solway Claim to Nimba Licence, Mittal’s Hold Secured
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Government of Liberia has defeated the heart of Solway Mining’s claim over the disputed Blei and Detton iron ore area in Nimba County. An international arbitration tribunal ruled that Solway had no right to compensation for the exploration licence that later went to ArcelorMittal, according to a copy of the award obtained by FrontPageAfrica.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The award, dated September 23, 2026, was handed down under the Permanent Court of Arbitration in PCA Case No. 2024-22. Three Solway companies, two Swiss and one Liberian, brought the case against the Republic of Liberia. The tribunal did find that the government broke its own Investment Act when it seized Solway’s physical assets. It ordered Liberia to pay US$314,619.47 for them, a fraction of the more than US$200 million Solway had claimed.

Justice Minister Betty Lamin Blamo confirmed the ruling when contacted by FrontPageAfrica. “We can disclose the existence of the award but technically not its content,” she said.

Cllr. Blamo confirmed that Solway was awarded US$314,619.47, against its claim of more than US$200 million.

Two of the three arbitrators found that Liberia expropriated Solway Mining’s physical assets in breach of Section 7 of the Investment Act of 2010, and set their value at US$314,619.47. Interest runs from August 31, 2023 at SOFR plus two percent, compounded quarterly, until the debt is settled. The same majority dismissed all of Solway’s other claims, including its claim for the licence itself.

On one point the tribunal was unanimous, and it may prove the most consequential. Liberia had argued that it never agreed to international arbitration and that the dispute belonged in Liberian courts. The panel disagreed and held that it could hear claims under the Investment Act. It declined, however, to hear claims Solway brought under an investment treaty.

Each side will pay its own lawyers and split the tribunal’s costs equally. Liberia must also refund Solway US$38,898.24, because the company put up more than its share of the deposit.

A sharp dissent

Professor John Y. Gotanda, one of the three arbitrators, broke with his colleagues on the central question. The panel was chaired by Cavinder Bull SC and also included Judith Levine.

In his view, the government’s own paperwork told the story. He pointed to the June 2023 Deed of Settlement with ArcelorMittal and the July 2023 Release and Settlement Agreement with Solway. He also cited ArcelorMittal’s September 5, 2023 letter acknowledging that Solway’s licence had been terminated on August 16. All three documents, he wrote, show that Liberia treated Solway as holding real and valuable rights that had to be formally cancelled before they could be handed to ArcelorMittal.

He also rejected the majority’s reasoning that Solway had nothing to be compensated for because it was never guaranteed a Mineral Development Agreement. “The uncertainty surrounding the ultimate development of the project affects the valuation of those rights, not their existence,” he wrote. He would have found that Liberia unlawfully took Solway’s entire investment.

Six years of conflict

The trouble began in 2019, when the Ministry of Mines and Energy awarded Solway an exploration licence for Mt. Detton and Mt. Blei. ArcelorMittal protested that the land was already its own. In a June 26, 2020 letter, it accused Solway of illegally exploring inside the concession granted under its 2005 Mineral Development Agreement.

The standoff soon reached the Executive Mansion. Then-President George Weah said he had pressed both companies to sit down and resolve their differences, and told ArcelorMittal that “Liberians would not be spectators in their own country.”

By mid-2023, the government had chosen a side. Solway’s licence was terminated, and on September 4, 2023, ArcelorMittal received its own exploration licence over the same ground. Anger spilled over in Nimba. On October 28, 2023, traditional “country devils” moved onto the site, drove workers away and took control of the area.

What Mittal gains

ArcelorMittal was not a party to the arbitration and walks away without a scratch. The majority found Solway held no compensable rights to the licence, so no one is paying for what ArcelorMittal received. The company’s hold on Blei and Detton, granted by the government in September 2023, comes out of the ruling unchallenged.

That certainty comes at a crucial moment. In January 2026, the Legislature ratified an amended agreement extending ArcelorMittal’s mining rights to 2050, with an option to renew for another 25 years. The company paid the government $200 million for the extension and reserved rail access, bringing its total investment in Liberia to $3.5 billion. It is ramping up shipments from about five million tonnes a year to 20 million tonnes in 2026, and is studying further expansion.

With the Solway case closed, ArcelorMittal can plan that growth in northern Nimba without a court fight hanging over the ground.

What Liberia gains

For the government, the ruling is an embarrassment it can afford. Solway came to the tribunal seeking more than US$200 million; it leaves with less than two cents on every dollar it claimed. The tribunal has recorded that the state broke its own investment law when it took Solway’s property. But by refusing to value the licence itself, the majority kept the bill to a little over $314,000 plus interest. Had the dissent carried the day, Liberia would have faced a claim for the full market value of an iron ore exploration licence, a far heavier burden on the treasury.

The ruling also removes a cloud over the country’s biggest foreign investment. ArcelorMittal expects that quadrupling its output will lift Liberia’s GDP and increase royalties and tax revenue over the next 25 years. Liberia’s Mines Minister has said the country could produce around 30 million tons of iron ore this year, up from about 10 million last year. Settling the Solway dispute clears one more obstacle to that boom.

The price of the lesson

Neither side should read the ruling as a clean win. The unanimous finding on jurisdiction means foreign investors can take Liberia before an international tribunal under the 2010 Investment Act, with or without a signed arbitration clause. And Professor Gotanda’s dissent shows that the government’s own settlement papers came close to costing it far more.

For a government courting new mining money, the message is plain. Licences must be granted carefully and taken away lawfully, or the next bill may not be so small.

World.title: Liberia: Experts Raise an Alarm as Aid Cuts and Price Rise Lead to Acute Childhood Malnutrition Tripling as More Babies Die
World.content:
Eight-month-old Helen is showing signs of acute malnutrition because her mother does not have food to feed her.

Summary

Aid cuts and rises in the costs of food and health care have contributed to a tripling of childhood malnutrition prompting an outcry from government officials and aid groups.

A recently released national survey found that most Liberian families do not have enough money to buy the food they need. Nearly one in four children are dangerously malnourished, and more than one in four are stunted—causing lifelong mental and physical impacts.

In a new essay a government official warns it is a crisis that will impact the country for generations and rob it of the human capital it needs to grow jobs and build the economy

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

GBAA-GAYE TOWN, Grand Bassa County – Eight-month-old Helen does not play the way babies usually do. She lies against her mother’s chest, as they sit under a palaver hut in this remote village surrounded by forest and accessible by one hand-cut road. Helen’s legs are as thin as reeds, her belly is swollen, her hair yellowing, and her eyes are too large for her face.

Helen cries weakly until her mother, Naomi, lifts a breast to her mouth. Helen should be eating solid food now. But her mother doesn’t have money for her food.

“That food we can get is food for ourselves to eat, but the one for the baby to eat, we don’t get that,” Naomi said grudgingly through an interpreter.

Naomi and her husband – who make charcoal and cut palm for as little as LD$7500 (US$40) a month – have six other living children. Naomi, 35, shows a reporter the mud hut where she shares a single mattress with five children. There’s no mosquito net. Helen was born on this bed and has never been to a clinic since, including for vaccinations.

Naomi knows Helen needs to go to the clinic – a two-hour walk away on muddy paths through the forest. But program manager Alfred Kekula, here with the Irish nonprofit Concern, doubts she will. Just talking appears to come with a psychological weight for Naomi. Kekula says she shows clear signs of post-partum depression.

“She does not value the life of the child,” he says. “Maybe she does not want the child to survive.”

Naomi with Helen inside the mud hut they share with five other children

Kekula and his team are seeing a growing number of mothers and babies in this state across Grand Bassa County. Once upon a time, the nearest clinic would have given a baby like Helen antibiotics and several months’ supply of Plumpy’Nut – the nutrient-dense, prepackaged food that has brought babies here back from the brink of death for decades.

But since the Trump administration closed USAID in 2025, Plumpy’Nut is long gone. In 2025, the government announced that services that were once free at health clinics now cost fees, a deterrent to the extremely poor like Naomi. Concern staff says babies in a critical state would be served free, but that information has not reached Naomi. Advocates here say they are seeing something they have not seen in years – babies dying.

Health advocates are now raising an alarm. A recently released Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey, done last year, found the number of children under five suffering acute malnutrition had nearly tripled to 8.5 percent, up from 3 percent in the 2020 Demographic and Health Survey . Most families do not have enough money to buy the food they need; nearly one in four children under five are dangerously malnourished, and more than one in four are stunted—too short for their age because they have not eaten well for years. (The survey has not been published online.)

And that likely got worse this year. Hunger changes with the seasons. When crops fail, or before the harvest, when roads flood in the rainy season and food cannot move, hunger gets worse. An analysis called the Cadre Harmonisé—used by aid organizations across West Africa to predict hunger—estimated that there would be a jump of nearly 100,000 people to 506,000 or 9 per cent in acute food crisis during this rainy season, when family food stores run empty and the next harvest has not yet come in.

Outside Naomi’s dwelling

The situation prompted Sayba Yawai Tamba, director of food security at the Ministry of Agriculture, to publish a searing essay this month warning that the country’s future is on the line.

“Malnutrition today becomes poverty tomorrow,” Tamba warns. When children do not eat well in their early years, their bodies and brains do not develop properly. They fall behind in school and face lifelong challenges: lower earnings, worse health, and less opportunity for success. According to UNICEF, stunted children carry this damage into adulthood, “reinforcing cycles of poverty across generations. For Liberia, where improving human development remains central to achieving inclusive economic growth, addressing malnutrition is an essential investment in the country’s human capital.”

The damage spreads beyond individual families. When hunger is widespread, communities become fragile. People are sick more often, miss work and school, and cannot earn enough to survive. This strains government services, removes workers from the economy, and slows growth. A country cannot build prosperity if its people are hungry and sick, Tamba says. Liberia needs a healthy, educated, and productive population to compete and create jobs. Without enough nutritious food, that future becomes impossible.

“Babies are dying”

Today’s crisis is compounding decades-old problems here that have never been properly addressed.

Most women here were teenagers when they had their first child. They have access to family planning in the form of injections given free at the clinic, but many women gave it up because of the cost of getting there and family pressure to keep having children. There’s no reproductive health education in schools here, if a girl like Naomi went at all. Parents say it is not their place to teach it. By 13 young girls here are usually out of school, unclear how pregnancy happens, and vulnerable to the attention of boys and older men.

Concern’s Kekula flags commercial bike riders as a problem. They come through towns, find short term girlfriends and disappear when she becomes pregnant.

At a ministry of health training on malnutrition in Gbaa-Gaye Town not one mother is in the audience. It is made up of men and a few grandmothers.

The young girls don’t know how to raise a baby, and misinformation abounds. Babies cannot absorb nutrients from food and water in the first six months of life. Water and food introduce germs that their bodies are unable to handle. Only breast milk is safe. But health workers here concede that few mothers follow the rules, if they ever hear them at all. Most babies are given rice and unsafe water from their earliest days.

Some mothers believe prolonged breastfeeding drains their bodies of nutrients. Others worry it will flatten their breasts and make them unattractive. Others believe babies need water and solid food to thrive. One grandmother told a reporter here recently that her own children were given water and family foods, from a young age, and none died or needed hospital care.

“People can hear plenty funny things in the city,” she said. “But in the bush, you will not hear it, don’t give the baby this one, give the baby that one.”

Another baby showing signs of acute malnutrition in Gbaa-Gaye Town

That leaves babies malnourished and vulnerable to malaria, infections, and other illnesses. The damage to their development then leads to the cycle beginning again. Women can be grandmothers here at 26; great-grandmothers before they reach 40. Another factor: many families don’t invest resources into children until they are five years old, believing only those who survive are strong enough to justify the cost.

Before, the closure of USAID supplemental formula for those under six months, and Plumpy’Nut for those older, was providing a lifesaving stopgap measure when it made it to mothers like Naomi. (Much of it did not. Stories of truckloads of supplies disappearing and reappearing for sale in markets here are common.)

But now that stopgap is gone.

“No Plumpy’Nut, the baby will obviously die,” Kekula says frankly. “Babies die and will continue to die in the absence of Plumpy’Nut.”

Clinics powerless to help

At the clinic in nearby Bokay Town, officer-in-charge J. Alaska O. Madeh says staff here are facing heartbreak daily. Plumpy’Nut supplies dwindled in 2025; by the start of this year it was gone.

Without therapeutic food, health workers are left providing only counselling and advice. Few think it will be followed when they leave. “Even if we even treat them, most of them will lose their life,” Madeh says.

J. Alaska O. Madeh, head of the nearby Bokay Town clinic, measures a child’s arm width, one of the determinants of malnutrition

Naomi is in an area covered by Concern, which supports the clinics here to ensure at-risk babies are identified and brought to the clinic. In another area of the county, there is no such help.

Babies are already dying

In Tepenneh Town, a two-hour bike ride on a heavily damaged road from the closest clinic at Compound 2, in District 2 of Grand Bassa County, babies are already dying. At a recent gathering of the community here, Concern’s Alfred Kekula identified several children with clear signs of malnutrition.

Climate change has devastated farmers here who live on what they grow. That once would have got them through the full year with money for medical costs and school. But now they run out of food early. Rice and vegetables will not be ready for several months. Cassava, which grows year-round, is not yielding enough to sustain them.

“Now at this present moment we are buying food,” says Tepenneh’s women’s leader, Naomi Vorgar, through an interpreter.

Diets consist of rice and cassava – not enough variety to provide nutrients needed for growing children. Chicken, eggs, milk and other nutrient-rich foods are out of reach.

A measles outbreak ran through this area in June this year. Mamie’s two-year-old son was already malnourished. Babies are usually given their first vaccines after birth, if they are born in a health facility. But they need to come back to complete the series. Measles vaccines are given at nine months.

A toddler recovering from malnutrition. She was one of the last babies here to receive Plumpy’Nut.

All mothers interviewed here never went back for vaccines. The cost they believed they had to pay at the clinic and the cost of the motorcycle to get there were barriers that were just too big. Though a 2022 study claimed half the households in the country have treated mosquito nets, no one here has seen one in use.

When Mamie’s son became sick with measles, she had no money to take him to the clinic. He soon died.

Another mother named Hannah sits with her malnourished seven-month-old son in her lap. In June he was a twin. The second baby became sick, and so that’s when Hannah took him to the clinic for the vaccine, she says. Like most mothers interviewed here, Hannah thought the vaccine was a treatment, not a preventative. It will not cure a child who is sick. The boy soon died.

Several mothers told us they had never heard that babies could only have breast milk for six months or that they need more food after that period. Malnutrition would have made the children more vulnerable to infection.

“When breast milk is lacking, and at the same time food is lacking, definitely it worsens the condition,” says Kekula.

In her essay, Tamba lauds the Boakai administration’s National Agricultural Development plan, which seeks to transform Liberia’s agriculture sector by increasing productivity, strengthening food systems, improving market access, promoting private sector participation, and building resilience to climate change. But she warns that food security and nutrition cannot be achieved by increasing food production alone. The country must pursue an integrated approach, with every part of society contributing: individuals and families through diversified household food production and improved infant and young child feeding practices; local governments through strengthening community health services and water and sanitation infrastructure; the national government through continued investment in agriculture, nutrition, maternal and child health, climate adaptation, rural infrastructure, and social protection; and development partners through long-term investments that strengthen national capacity and help the country become more self-reliant.

“Success will be measured not only by reductions in malnutrition rates, but by the changes people experience in their daily lives,” writes Tamba. “This means children growing up healthy and ready to learn, families having reliable access to affordable and nutritious foods, farmers earning better incomes from productive and resilient farms, and communities being better prepared for future shocks. It means a Liberia where every child has the opportunity to reach their full potential and where nutrition becomes a foundation for stronger families, healthier communities, and sustainable national development.”

For Helen and other babies born into extreme hunger in Liberia, this overhaul needs to get moving fast. For now, the number of babies dying and being harmed for life looks set to get worse.

This story was produced in collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Gov’t Says Ex-VP Howard-Taylor Broke House Arrest; Another Official Calls The Raid Routine; Her Lawyer Calls It Humiliation
World.content:
MONROVIA — The sheriff’s deputies came on Tuesday evening. By the time they left the former Vice President’s residence, the house had gone quiet in a new way. There was no desktop computer and no internet modem. Even the phones of the officers guarding the house were gone.

By Rodney D Sieh

The interim order behind the raid is dated September 22, 2026. It is signed by Clerk of Court Amos Gbowah on the directive of His Honor Ousman F. Feika, Assigned Circuit Judge of Criminal Court “C.” It instructed the sheriff to go “immediately” into the residence where Madam Howard-Taylor is being detained. Deputies were to inspect the property, seize every telephone, mobile phone, and communication device on the premises or in her possession, make an inventory, and hold everything at the courthouse “until you are otherwise advised.” A handwritten note shows the order was received by one of her defense lawyers at 6:27 p.m.

The inventory reads like the contents of any Liberian family home:

1. A complete desktop computer, with keyboard, printer and accessories

2. Two orange modems serving two televisions

3. Two personal laptops that belonged to her late son

4. Under a returned order, every cell phone belonging to her personal attendant and to the Bureau of Corrections officers on duty that night.

A son’s laptops

The third item on that list is the hardest to read. Her only son, Charles Neilson Philip Taylor IV, known as Philip, died at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center on January 20, 2026, at the age of 42. Reports said he first suffered a respiratory arrest while being treated at GIMS Hospital in Paynesville. He held a master’s degree in Shipping and Port Administration from the Regional Maritime University in Accra, and he left behind five children.

At his funeral, the woman who had survived elections, defeats and national reckonings described his death as the worst moment of her life as a human being. President Joseph Boakai himself visited her Congo Town home to console her the day after he died. Eight months later, the state has returned to that home and carried his laptops away.

Nothing in the public record ties Philip Taylor to the drug investigation. The court has not said what it hopes to find on his computers.

How she got here

She served as Vice President from 2018 to 2024 under President George Weah. Before that she was First Lady and Senator for Bong County. On August 19, state security stopped her from leaving the country at Roberts International Airport. Investigators have tied her arrest to the July seizure of nearly four metric tons of cocaine in Duazon, which authorities valued at about US$317 million.

Justice Minister Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh listed charges including unlicensed importation and sale of controlled substances, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy and money laundering. Three foreign nationals, two Croatians and a Ukrainian, were charged in the same case in absentia. She has denied the allegations and rejected any connection to the network.

Her health quickly became part of the case. Her lawyers told the court she suffers from asthma. She was hospitalized after her blood pressure reportedly rose while she was in custody.

On September 4, Judge Feika released her from Monrovia Central Prison on compassionate medical grounds and placed her under house arrest with a travel ban. The conditions were strict. The state was ordered to guard the residence around the clock and keep a full log of every visitor, including their phone numbers and addresses. One caregiver, preferably a relative, was allowed to live with her. The judge warned that any breach would send her straight back to prison.

The questions the order leaves open

The order explains what the sheriff must do. It does not explain why. That leaves the public with several questions:

What changed? The court order itself says nothing about a breach. It cites an ongoing investigation by National Joint Security authorities. Was the raid about gathering evidence, keeping her safe, or punishing a violation?

Why take the guards’ phones? Seizing phones from Bureau of Corrections officers assigned by the state suggests someone suspects messages were passing through her own security detail. If so, who is under suspicion: the detainee or her keepers?

Why the dead man’s laptops? Are investigators treating Philip Taylor’s devices as evidence, or simply as devices that happened to be in the house?

Why now? On September 17, her lawyers asked the court to grant her bail and lift the home detention. On September 21, Lenn Eugene Nagbe, chief of staff to former President Weah, noted that about 33 days had passed since her arrest without an indictment. The raid came the next evening.

Was the defense heard? The order appears to have been issued without a hearing and delivered to her lawyers at dusk. Was that proper?

The government’s answer

An official at the Ministry of Justice, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told this paper the search and seizure was routine. The official said corrections officers carry out such checks in prisons from time to time, and that house arrest is an extension of that system. “The former vice president is no exception,” the official said. According to the official, the aim is simply to make sure nothing harmful is kept around her.

Other government officials have since offered a sharper account. They told FrontPageAfrica that the former vice president had violated the terms of her house arrest and was found with at least six different phones. Some family members say several of those phones were theirs. Officials say that claim has not been proven.

Attorney Kowou pushed back. He noted that house arrest is relatively new in Liberia’s courts and that everyone is still learning how it is meant to work. But he said Judge Feika’s September 4 ruling “did not expressly state that our client should be denied access to her personal communication devices.” The defense, he added, is still trying to learn whether the search was requested by the State or ordered by the court on its own initiative.

The two explanations do not sit easily together. One calls the raid a routine safety check. The other describes a breach of court conditions. If it was a breach, the judge’s own ruling warned that the penalty is a return to prison, and no such move has been announced. Neither account explains why the sheriff also took two television modems and the laptops of a man who died in January.

A presumption still standing

The government itself has said the allegations must be tested in court and that she remains presumed innocent. Judge Feika wrote that her medical release was not a dismissal, acquittal or pardon. That cuts both ways: house arrest is not freedom, and it is not a verdict either.

Those defending her see something darker in the raid. “I honestly do not understand why they would go this far,” said Attorney Gbawou Kowou, a lawyer, security expert and university lecturer who is part of her defense team. House arrest, he acknowledged, can come with prison-like restrictions. “But what is being done in her case, in my view, goes far beyond what is reasonably necessary.”

“At this point, it is difficult for me to see this as anything other than a calculated attempt by the government to further humiliate and break her spirit,” Kowou said. “There is a point at which the exercise of governmental authority ceases to be about legitimate restrictions and begins to look like deliberate punishment and humiliation.”

He insisted she would not break.

“You cannot easily break a person who has a good heart, a strong spirit, and faith in the truth,” he said. “She has endured a great deal already, and I remain firmly convinced that she will come through all of this. In the end, I believe the tears she sheds will not be tears of defeat, but tears of joy, relief, and victory.”

Whatever the reason for the raid, a 63-year-old woman who was once one heartbeat from the presidency now waits in a house with no line to the outside world. Her son’s laptops sit on a sheriff’s inventory, and her questions, like the public’s, remain unanswered.

World.title: Liberia: Cummings Cautions Against Budget Spending That Fails to Benefit Ordinary Citizens
World.content:
ANC Political Leader Welcomes US$1 Billion Revenue Milestone, Calls for Greater Accountability and Improved Public Welfare

MONROVIA – The Political Leader of the Alternative National Congress (ANC), Alexander B. Cummings, has welcomed Liberia’s achievement of surpassing US$1 billion in domestic revenue collection but cautioned that the milestone would mean little if the government’s spending priorities fail to improve the lives of ordinary Liberians.

By Augustus D.R. Bortue

Cummings said the achievement was encouraging, particularly as the government moves toward its ambitious US$1.2 billion national budget. However, he stressed that the impact of the increased revenue would depend on how the government allocates and spends the funds.

He warned that if the government continues allocating resources in the same manner as in previous years, ordinary Liberians may not experience meaningful improvements in their living conditions.

The ANC leader made the remarks in an interview with journalists on Tuesday, September 22, at the Don Bosco Youth Center in New Matadi, Monrovia.

“When the US$1.2 billion national budget was presented, there were doubts about whether such an ambitious target could be realized. Today, surpassing US$1 billion in domestic revenue collection has shown that the target was not merely an aspiration. It was achievable,” Cummings said.

Reflecting on his earlier advocacy for a billion-dollar national budget, Cummings recalled that he faced skepticism when he made the proposal during a presidential debate in 2017.

“I think it is a good thing. You know, in 2017, I said at a debate at the time that Liberia should have a billion dollars, and people were laughing and said it was not possible. It should have been a billion-dollar budget years ago, and I say now it should be two, three billion dollars,” he stated.

Cummings argued that Liberia’s budget remains comparatively small when measured against those of neighboring countries, suggesting that the country has the potential to mobilize more resources to finance development.

“If you look at our neighboring countries and where their budgets are, and you compare them with our budget, ours is still behind,” he said.

Despite welcoming the revenue milestone, Cummings emphasized that the government must ensure that increased public resources translate into tangible benefits for citizens rather than simply expanding the size of the national budget.

Calls for Accountability

Asked what message he had for Liberians, Cummings said the country could achieve more and urged citizens to remain resilient while demanding accountability from the government.

“My message to all Liberians is that Liberia deserves better. We can do better than what we have. We should not give up; we should be resilient,” he said.

He called on citizens to continue demanding results from the government, which he said bears responsibility for the welfare of the country.

Cummings also cited persistent corruption concerns and unresolved questions surrounding the Foya Project and developments at the Guinean border as issues requiring greater public scrutiny.

“We are still talking about the corruption of the country. We wrote a letter on the Foya Project, and we are not giving up on this. We still do not know what is happening at the Guinean border,” he said.

“There are a lot of challenges. We should be demanding until we get results.”

ANC Open to Opposition Unity

On the prospects of opposition political unity, Cummings described collaboration among opposition parties as important and said the ANC remains open to discussions with other political groups.

However, he cautioned that any renewed effort must take into account the lessons learned from the collapse of the Collaborating Political Parties (CPP), a former alliance of opposition parties.

“We have learned from the mistakes of the past of the Collaborating Political Parties. We will not repeat those mistakes. So, we will see where things go. We are open to conversation and making sure that this time it is in our interest,” Cummings said.

The CPP was established by the Alternative National Congress, Unity Party, Liberty Party and All Liberian Party to consolidate opposition support. The alliance, which was certified by the National Elections Commission in 2020, experienced internal divisions and the withdrawal of member parties before its eventual dissolution in April 2024.

Cummings Commends Youth Initiative

Cummings made the remarks while attending an awards ceremony organized by Montserrado County District #9 Representative Frank Saah Foko Jr. to recognize outstanding young people and professionals for excellence and community service.

The initiative celebrates individual achievements while encouraging academic advancement, professional growth and youth empowerment in the district.

Cummings praised Rep. Foko for sustaining and building upon the legacy of the late former District #9 Representative Munah Pelham-Youngblood, who initiated the program.

He described the awards ceremony as a wonderful initiative and said he was inspired by what he witnessed at the event.

Cummings also commended the young people and other participants for their contributions to the district, thanking Foko for continuing the legacy of his predecessor.

For his part, Rep. Foko thanked Cummings and other dignitaries who attended the ceremony, reaffirming his commitment to sustaining the initiative in honor of the late lawmaker.

World.title: Liberia, U.S. Hold High-Level Maritime Security Talks Amid Push for Economic Cooperation
World.content:
NEW YORK — The Republic of Liberia and the United States of America on Sunday, held a high-level closed-door maritime roundtable in New York, convening senior foreign policy, national security, and maritime officials from both governments for strategic discussions on maritime security, economic cooperation, and the growing importance of secure sea lanes to global trade and supply chains.

According to a release, the roundtable was co-chaired by Madam Sara Beysolow Nyanti, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Liberia, and Ambassador Michael G. Waltz, Permanent Representative of the United States to the United Nations and former National Security Advisor to President Donald J. Trump.

Commissioner Neto Lighe and National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods led the technical presentations from the Liberian side. Discussions focused on maritime security, fisheries and the blue economy, and economic development opportunities of mutual interest to both nations.

Participation by the private sector and representatives from maritime nations, including Argentina and Panama, reflected broad international interest in the economic diplomacy framework guiding the engagement.

For Liberia, the roundtable underscored the country’s expanding role in global maritime affairs and its commitment to leveraging its strategic maritime position to advance national economic interests, deepen security cooperation, and attract investment. The engagement also reinforced the longstanding partnership between Liberia and the United States, with both sides affirming practical cooperation around shared economic and security priorities.

The Liberian delegation was led by Foreign Minister Nyanti and included National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods; Commissioner and CEO of the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA), Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe, Sr.; and Liberia’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Lewis G. Brown II.

The United States delegation was led by Ambassador Waltz and included Frank Garcia, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs; Wesley R. Brooks, Assistant Secretary of State for Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs; and former Illinois Governor Bruce Rauner, among other senior officials.

The seniority and breadth of both delegations, spanning African affairs, oceans and environmental policy, national security, and maritime administration, reflected the strategic scope of the discussions and the importance both governments place on deepening cooperation in the maritime domain.

The meeting was held on the margins of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, where Liberia is engaged in a series of high-level diplomatic meetings.

Liberia is currently serving a two-year term on the United Nations Security Council for 2026 to 2027 and will assume the Presidency of the Council in December 2026, further elevating the country’s voice in international discussions on peace, security, and multilateral cooperation.

World.title: Liberia: NOCAL Finance Chief Azango Held In Contempt, Entity Faces Shutdown, as Government Struggles With Decade-Old US$764,762 Liability
World.content:
Monrovia — National Oil Company of Liberia Vice President Finance and Chief Financial Officer of NOCAL Emmanuel Azango on Wednesday, September 23, found himself at the center of a growing financial and judicial crisis after the Commercial Court held him in contempt and kept him on the court’s bench for more than two hours, as the Government of Liberia faces enforcement over a decade-old debt dispute that has reportedly ballooned into a US$764,762 court award.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

The dramatic development unfolded Wednesday, when Chief Judge Eva Mappy Morgan ordered the immediate closure and sealing of the National Oil Company of Liberia, NOCAL, and the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, directing the Commercial Court sheriff to seal the institutions’ entrances and remove occupants.

The order grows out of an Action of Debt brought by former NOCAL officials Vida A. Mensah and Cllr. Idella Cooper-Shannon against NOCAL and its corporate officers.

The dispute, according to publicly available reporting, began with claims of approximately US$85,000 each arising from NOCAL’s controversial 2015 restructuring and severance arrangements.

After nearly a decade of litigation, accumulated interest and penalties reportedly pushed the combined court award to US$764,762.

That old dispute has now returned with renewed force, this time placing Azango, NOCAL’s financial leadership and the Ministry of Finance directly in the path of a Commercial Court enforcement action.

Azango at the Center

When confronted by FrontPage Africa about why the debt allegedly remained unpaid and what responsibility he bore as NOCAL’s Vice President for Finance and Investment, Azango pointed away from NOCAL’s current financial management and toward the Government of Liberia.

Azango said the matter was before the Government and that the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning was supposed to take charge of the payment.

He also maintained that the debt was an old obligation. But the Commercial Court’s September 23 order makes no distinction between an old debt and a new one in directing enforcement. It names NOCAL and the Ministry of Finance and orders their premises closed.

Azango further told FrontPage Africa that he was kept on the court bench for hours and that the court demanded payment of 25 percent of the obligation. He referred FrontPage Africa to the court documents, emphasizing that the debt dates back years.

The immediate question now is whether NOCAL’s financial leadership did everything required to ensure compliance with the court’s directives, or whether responsibility was allowed to move between NOCAL and the Ministry of Finance until the dispute reached the extraordinary point of a court-ordered institutional shutdown.

The US$764,762 Liability

The latest confrontation cannot be understood without looking back at the history of the underlying case. Public reporting in May 2026 said the Commercial Court had awarded nearly US$800,000 to former NOCAL executives Vida Mensah and Cllr. Idella Cooper-Shannon.

The combined figure reported was US$764,762. The claims reportedly began at approximately US$85,000 each, before years of litigation, interest and penalties substantially increased the amount.

The case traces back to the period when NOCAL was experiencing severe financial distress and undergoing re-structuring. In August 2015, Liberia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ daily media summary reported that Mensah, then NOCAL’s Vice President of Administration, had resigned as the company moved toward an interim management arrangement amid a financial crisis.

According to the May 2026 reporting, Mensah and Cooper-Shannon were among the former executives who did not accept the reduced severance arrangement offered during the restructuring and instead pursued litigation.

That litigation has now produced a liability hundreds of thousands of dollars larger than the original claims.

FROM US$170,000 TO US$764,762

The evolution of the debt is one of the most consequential elements of the case. What reportedly began as approximately, Vida Mensah, US$85,000, Idella Cooper-Shannon, approximately US$85,000, has grown, according to published reporting, into US$764,762 in combined court awards after years of litigation, penalties and interest.

That means the Government of Liberia is now confronting a liability more than four times the original combined principal reported in connection with the claims. And the financial consequences are no longer confined to the two former executives and NOCAL. The dispute has reached the Government’s central financial institution.

The Commercial Court commands Acting Sheriff Emmanuel Morris, or his deputy, to have NOCAL and the Ministry of Finance “closed with immediate effect.” The sheriff is ordered to seal the entrances and remove occupants.

He is also commanded to make an official return to the court detailing the manner in which the order was served and executed. The order is signed by Randolph B. Sneh, Clerk of the Commercial Court, and bears the official seal of the court.

This means the case has moved well beyond a dispute over whether money is owed. It has become a question of judicial enforcement against the Government of Liberia and one of its most important public institutions.

Who Is Supposed To Pay?

If the debt belongs to NOCAL, why should the Ministry of Finance be expected to pay it and if the Government of Liberia is responsible for satisfying the judgment, why has the dispute been allowed to reach the point where NOCAL’s financial leadership is facing contempt and the Ministry of Finance itself is under a closure order?

Azango answers that the matter is before the Government and that the Ministry of Finance should take responsibility. But the court’s action suggests that the distinction has not resolved the issue; instead, both institutions now face enforcement.

NOCAL’s Old Financial Problems

The underlying dispute emerged during one of the most difficult periods in NOCAL’s history. By 2015, the state-owned oil company was experiencing a serious financial crisis. Government records from that period show that NOCAL was undergoing restructuring and replacing its leadership with an interim management arrangement.

Mensah resigned as Vice President of Administration during that period. The company’s historical finances have also been subjected to scrutiny by the General Auditing Commission. An earlier GAC report identifies Idella Cooper-Shannon as a former NOCAL board member.

The company’s past financial affairs have also been scrutinized in relation to executive bonuses and payments associated with the 2013 Block 13 transaction. A 2018 FrontPageAfrica report on the Special Presidential Committee investigating the Global Witness allegations reported that Cooper-Shannon was among former NOCAL board members identified in connection with proposed restitution of payments.

The report said the committee recommended restitution from officials in connection with bonuses and honoraria. Those matters are separate from the present Action of Debt and should not be conflated with the current judgment.

The 2015 Breakdown

The history is important because it explains why an apparently old employment-related dispute is now creating a new financial crisis. NOCAL was already facing financial difficulties when the restructuring took place. Mensah was among the senior executives leaving the corporation in 2015, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ contemporaneous media summary. The severance dispute subsequently became a legal battle.

According to reporting published in May 2026, the litigation continued for approximately a decade before the Commercial Court’s ruling produced the US$764,762 award.

Why Azango’s Role Matters

Azango was not a member of NOCAL’s management at the time the original severance dispute arose. That fact is important. The present NOCAL financial leadership should not automatically be blamed for creating a liability that originated under previous management.

But once a judgment exists, current officials have a responsibility to explain what actions were taken to address it. That is where Azango’s role becomes relevant. As NOCAL’s Vice President for Finance and Investment, he occupies a senior position within the corporation’s financial management structure.

His explanation that the Ministry of Finance should take responsibility raises another concern about what formal steps did NOCAL took to secure payment from the Government, and when those steps were taken.

The 25-Percent Question

Azango says the court required 25 percent of the debt to be paid. But the September 23 closure order supplied to FrontPageAfrica does not state the exact monetary amount represented by that 25 percent. Nor does the document itself establish whether the payment was made.

That leaves several questions unanswered, as to what exact amount of twenty-five per cent was actually made and if the US$764,762 award was the amount against which the 25 percent was calculated?

A US$764,762 Case Now Threatens Government Operations

An employment or severance dispute that reportedly began at approximately US$170,000 in combined claims has evolved into a court award of US$764,762 and is now threatening the physical operations of two government institutions.

The Commercial Court’s action means that a dispute originating from NOCAL’s troubled 2015 period is now confronting the Boakai administration more than a decade later. And Azango, who was not part of the NOCAL leadership involved in the original dispute, is now one of the officials being called upon to explain how the corporation responded to the judgment.

The Bigger Accountability Issue

The case exposes a recurring problem in Liberia’s public sectorororor, where old liabilities can survive changes in government, management and policy, but eventually return with financial and legal consequences.

The present controversy is therefore not simply about Azango, it is about how NOCAL and the Government of Liberia manage inherited liabilities and whether court judgments against public corporations are promptly incorporated into government financial planning.

For now, the Commercial Court has taken the strongest possible step. NOCAL have been ordered closed, Azango has been held in contempt, a 25-percent payment has reportedly been demanded and a debt dispute that began roughly a decade ago, reportedly at approximately US$85,000 for each of two former NOCAL executives, has grown into a reported US$764,762 court award.

Whether Liberia’s public financial system will resolve the liability, or whether the old NOCAL dispute will continue generating new costs, new contempt proceedings and new answers for the country’s debts, remains a concern.

World.title: Digitalisation key in achieving Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
The Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, has highlighted the crucial role of digitalisation in achieving effective public service delivery to support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Kangwa says digitalisation and human capital development are vital components of service delivery.

He emphasised that fully embracing technology and innovation in the public service will enhance service provision to the people and advance the Grow Zambia vision.

Speaking during the Eighth Senior Public Service Management meeting in Lusaka, Mr Kangwa further called on all Permanent Secretaries to take ownership of the Grow Zambia Agenda and work collaboratively to ensure nationwide growth.

Mr Kangwa also noted the need for tangible service delivery and a functional public service through institutional reforms as assured by President Hakainde Hichilema.

He reaffirmed the President’s call to pursue a further ambitious reform agenda aimed at delivering positive results at all levels to improve the welfare of the Zambian people.

Mr Kangwa reaffirmed the government’s commitment to fighting corruption, urging Permanent Secretaries to ensure that public resources are used for their intended purposes.

He echoed President Hichilema’s remarks during his inauguration, urging citizens to prioritise national interests over personal interests.

Mr Kangwa further said peace, unity and reconciliation remain the cornerstones of public service and emphasised that Zambia must continue to uphold the “One Zambia, One Nation” motto.

He added that the public service will continue to evolve to ensure effectiveness, emphasising that this is vital in attaining the Grow Zambia agenda.

Mr Kangwa stated that public-private partnerships will continue to drive national growth at all levels.

He encouraged the private sector to seize opportunities in Zambia, particularly in mining and other sectors.

World.title: Over 7, 000 retirees access NAPSA interest-free advance facility
World.content:
Over 7,000 retirees have so far accessed more than K90 million under the National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) interest-free advance facility.

NAPSA Chief Executive Officer, Muyangwa Muyangwa, revealed that out of 34,000 retirees on the NAPSA payroll, over 7,000 have already claimed the advance, with the demand increasing daily.

Speaking at a media workshop in Siavonga, Mr Muyangwa explained that most retirees had challenges accessing the facility initially because it is claimed online through the eNAPSA portal, but the Authority has since provided support.

“You don’t need to come to NAPSA, you just need to log into eNAPSA and you will find it shows that you can push a button and claim your advance,” he explained.

Mr Muyangwa said the interest-free advance has been introduced to address long standing complaints that monthly pension payouts are insufficient to meet retiree’s needs.

He disclosed that every NAPSA member has a funeral grant, which currently stands at about K22,000 and is adjusted upwards every year and the grant is however, only paid after death.

“So we said instead of keeping that money for post-life, can people start accessing that money, so that this the advance they are getting. They are actually getting it against the funeral grant, but there is no interest,” he explained.

He said retirees are entitled to 75 percent of the funeral grant as an advance, which is recovered through a small monthly deduction from their pension, ensuring they continue to receive a monthly income.

“It is an easier way of providing interest free money instead of them going to do Kaloba, we don’t allow them to borrow the whole amount so that they can still have their monthly cheque,” he said.

Mr Muyangwa said once the advance is fully recovered after 18 months or when the funeral grant is adjusted upwards in the new year, retirees can access it again.

He has urged all retirees to take advantage of the facility.

“Whatever we can do to make sure there is dignity in retirement, we shall work on it as NAPSA,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Muyangwa disclosed that NAPSA has so far paid out over K11 billion to more than 600,000 members under the 20 percent pre-retirement partial withdrawal benefit.

Mr Muyangwa attributed delays and rejections in processing some claims to accounts that are not clean, citing missing contributions, double contributions and cases of members sharing NRCs.

He said NAPSA has set up a unit of 165 staff to clean members’ accounts from the year 2000 to 2025 so that accounts operate like bank accounts.

“We want that when you go to the ATM it pays. There is nothing like we go first and check which company you worked for,” he said.

He also added that the team is actively engaging members and employers to obtain missing returns so that their accounts can be updated.

World.title: Zambia calls for stronger coordination in global commitments
World.content:
Zambia has called for accelerated action and stronger institutional coordination to ensure global commitments turn into affordable financing, jobs and improved services for ordinary families.

Representing President Hakainde Hichilema at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81) in New York, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe noted that joint efforts are needed to turn global commitments into tangible results.

Mr Haimbe was speaking during the high-level event titled “Keeping the Momentum: Implementing the Seville Commitment.

Meanwhile, Mr Haimbe who attended another high-level side event on Climate Action and Just Transition, which was held alongside the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, reaffirmed Zambia’s commitment to building climate resilience and diversifying energy sources under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Haimbe stressed that Zambia is also focusing on strengthening agricultural adaptation and advancing a just transition as part of its climate action priorities.

Zambia is actively engaging in bilateral meetings as the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81) continues in New York, to advance its national interests while participating in high level events that provide an opportunity to contribute to global discussions and shape international dialogue.

World.title: Zambia selected for UN Country support mechanism
World.content:
Zambia has been selected as one of six countries to participate in the United Nations (UN) Country Support Mechanism on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, designed to help resource-rich countries move up the global value chain.

This is in a press statement made available to the media in Lusaka today by First Secretary Press and Public Relations to the United Nations in New York, Namata Njekwa.

Ms Njekwa stated that UN Secretary-General, António Guterres announced the first six countries during the Climate Summit 2026, held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

She added that the other countries selected are Guinea, Indonesia, Madagascar, Nigeria and Zimbabwe.

ZANIS reports that Ms Njekwa explained that the programme is part of the UN Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, which is jointly led by the United Nations Development Programme, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development and the United Nations Environment Programme and aims to ensure that mineral resources help improve people’s lives and support development as the world increases its use of clean energy.

Meanwhile, Ms Njekwa revealed that, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe, who is representing President Hakainde Hichilema at the UN General Assembly, said Zambia wants to benefit more from its mineral resources.

She said Mr Haimbe also noted that Zambia has been producing Copper for many years and now wants the growing demand for critical minerals to bring more investment, industries and jobs to the country.

She however said Mr Haimbe observed that Zambia wants its citizens to take part in the growing clean energy and technology industries, while good management, investment and partnerships help develop the mining sector.

World.title: Government appeals for investment in disaster preparedness
World.content:
Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, has appealed for investment in last-mile early warning services that will improve preparedness for disasters like the anticipated El Nino.

Dr Siame has noted that the experience and capacity of countries like Britain in this area could help strengthen Zambia’s resilience to climate shocks.

He has acknowledged that while Zambia has systems in place, they often fail to reach households and businesses directly thereby stressing the need for advanced technology in early warning systems.

The Minister said this when the British High Commissioner to Zambia, Rebecca Terzeon called on him at his office in Lusaka today.

Dr Siame called for greater participation of the British private sector in Zambia’s carbon markets, stressing that the country holds vast opportunities in this emerging space.

He observed that despite carbon markets being a presidential directive and a national priority, Zambia has not secured a significant share of global investment in the area.

The Minister stressed that tapping into British private sector expertise and capital can therefore help unlock financing for government and citizen-driven priorities.

“By tapping into the British private sector space, this is an area we can work around and prioritise, so that we have more participation in the carbon credit markets, innovative in nature, to open up capital finance that can speak to the investment priorities of government and of the citizens,” Dr Siame stated.

And in a separate courtesy call by Chinese Ambassador to Zambia, Han Jing, Dr Siame called for investment in renewable energy, noting that this would contribute to the achievement of the 10 000 megawatts electricity generation target and ultimately economic growth.

The Minister further appealed to China for environmentally friendly investment that will ensure no pollution, stressing that his Ministry wants to balance economic growth with environmental sustainability.

He also called for investment in the Forestry sector, especially along the TAZARA line of rail, adding that this will not only create jobs but also protect the environment.

And Chinese Ambassador to Zambia, Han Jing expressed China’s readiness to introduce its artificial intelligence-driven climate pre-warning system to Zambia, as both nations grapple with the severe impacts of climate change and the looming El Niño.

Mr Han disclosed that discussions had already commenced, with officials from Zambia’s Meteorological Department under the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment.

“This system allows us to make pre-warnings tailored to the realities of different nations, and we would like to introduce such systems into Zambia”, Mr Han said.

Meanwhile, British High Commissioner to Zambia, Rebecca Terzeon reaffirmed her country’s commitment to supporting Zambia’s green growth and clean energy transition, highlighting critical minerals as central to the global shift towards renewable energy.

Ms Terzeon said the UK–Zambia Green Growth Compact, signed between the two countries, continues to frame bilateral cooperation.

She noted that the compact includes key agreements such as a climate finance memorandum of understanding, under which the Climate Finance Unit was established.

Ms Terzeon noted that such initiatives are clear examples of responsible, long-term investments that deliver social and developmental benefits while boosting investor confidence in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“We have a very strong and clear agenda to support the Zambian government and the Zambian people to achieve the Grow Zambia agenda sustainably and in a climate smart way,” said Ms Terzeon.

World.title: Kawana stresses timely Human Resource case processing
World.content:
The Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary, Thabo Kawana has acknowledged the crucial role in ensuring the smooth and timely processing of human resource cases within government institutions emphasising that it’s a duty that directly impacts the efficiency of public service.

Speaking during the official swearing in ceremony of the Human Resource Management Committee (HRMC), a vital body established under the Service Commissions Act of 2016.

The Ministry of Information and Media, Human Resource and Administration Director, Lazarus Mulenda and Internal Auditor Christine Kabwe were sworn in as Chairperson and member of the HRMC respectively.

Mr Kawana further emphasised the importance of their roles, noting that a professional and motivated civil service, coupled with prompt handling of personal matters such as staff confirmations, promotions, and separations are key components of President Hakainde Hichilema’s “Grow Zambia” agenda.

The Permanent Secretary further reminded the newly sworn in members that their work is vital not only for internal operations but also for motivating staff and ensuring the government’s policies reached the public effectively.

He explained that, according to the law, such appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission, but the swearing-in ceremony was delegated to responsible officers.

He also assured that the ceremony symbolised their official assumption of duty and the trust placed in them to serve with integrity and confidentiality.

World.title: Court declares Mwewa winner of Lusaka of Mayoral seat
World.content:
The Local Government and Elections Tribunal Chaired by Dominic Makalicha has withdrawn the Lusaka Mayoral election petition where Gabriel Kibombwe has petitioned the election and declaration of Chitambala Mwewa as Mayor of Lusaka.

Makalicha has since withdrawn the petition of Gabriel Kibombwe and has declared Chitambala Mwewa as duly elected Mayor of Lusaka.

Earlier, the Tribunal ordered the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to produce all the documents relating to the August 2026 mayoral elections and a witness from the ECZ to testify on the documents.

The Petitioner, Gabriel Kibombwe, Chitambala Mwewa and their lawyers jointly agreed that the petition be withdrawn.

Later during the hearing after an adjournment, the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) Lawyer, Eric Kamwi, told the tribunal that the parties consented to withdraw the petition by mutual consent.

“You ordered ECZ to produce before the tribunal today, the bundle of documents and to avail the witness to speak to the said bundle, while complying with these orders of the tribunal, the ECZ received considerations from the other parties to the case, that is the Petitioner, Mwewa and their advocates, It was jointly agreed by consent of all the parties that this petition be withdrawn by mutual consent of all the parties,” said Kamwi.

Kamwi further said that the parties therefore jointly filed their notice to withdraw the petition pursuant to Rule 28 of the Local Government Election Tribunal Rules, SI number 32 of 2026.

He added that the said proposed consent has since been filed before the tribunal stating that with the information given, the advocates sought further direction from the court to consider the mutually consented, consent judgment.

Mwewa’s lawyer, Mambwe Lungu also indicated that the Tribunal is vested with the jurisdiction to grant the parties to the matter the requisite lead of the Tribunal to withdraw the matter.

Lungu based the submission on the fact that the application for leave itself is part and parcel of the Joint notice of intention to withdraw the matter in accordance with Rule 28 of the Local Government Tribunal Rules of 2026.

In response, the Tribunal Chairperson, Dominic Makalicha granted leave of application and also acknowledged receipt of the application to withdraw the petition and other documents.

Makalicha has since withdrawn the petition for Kibombwe from the Tribunal and that Mwewa remains duly elected Mayor of Lusaka district.

“It is therefore clear that law has been followed for this petition to be withdrawn and is in conformity of the law and Local Government Tribunal rules, having found that the parties were in conformity with the Law, the Tribunal has therefore granted the application to withdraw the Petition,” Makalicha said.

World.title: Mpunga Community in Zambezi West receives new classroom blocks
World.content:
Government has officially handed over two newly constructed 1×3 classroom blocks to the Mpungu community in Zambezi West Constituency, Zambezi District, North-Western Province.

The two educational infrastructure projects were constructed at a total cost of over K1.8 million using the 2025 Constituency Development Fund (CDF) allocation to improve learning conditions and expand access to quality education in the area.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, Zambezi West Member of Parliament, Vumango Musumali reaffirmed the government’s commitment to developing underserved rural areas and bringing essential public services closer to the people.

Mr Musumali highlighted that the continued utilisation of CDF funds demonstrates the government’s dedication to decentralisation and direct community empowerment.

Speaking at the same event, Zambezi District Commissioner, Simeon Machayi assured the people of Mpungu of continued government-led development in the district.

Mr Machayi further said President Hakainde Hichilema has demonstrated good leadership and called on residents to maintain their support for him and his administration’s development agenda.

And newly elected Zambezi Town Council Chairperson, George Njolomba expressed gratitude to the Mpungu community for overwhelmingly voting for President Hichilema and himself during the August 13, 2026 General Elections.

Mr Njolomba pledged that the local authority and UPND district leadership will work tirelessly to deliver on their developmental campaign promises.

He further warned parents against marrying off school-going children, emphasising that education is free under the government’s policy and that every child belongs in the classroom.

Meanwhile, District Education Board Secretary (DEBS) representative, Alexander Simoonga noted that the new facilities will significantly reduce the long distances pupils previously walked to access school.

Mr Simoonga urged the community and parents to guard the new infrastructure against vandalism to benefit future generations.

And Mpungu Primary School Headteacher, Brighton Kufwainda expressed profound gratitude to the government, describing the new classroom blocks as a timely response to the community’s long-standing infrastructure challenges.
