World.title: Breaking up Troy Aikman and Joe Buck would be a big mistake for ESPN | Bobby Burack
World.content:
ESPN will broadcast its first Super Bowl this February, with Joe Buck and Troy Aikman on the call. It will mark the duo’s seventh Super Bowl broadcast together — and perhaps its last.

Buck recently agreed to a new six-year, $108 million contract extension with ESPN. However, sources confirm to OutKick that Aikman and the network remain far apart in contract negotiations. Aikman’s current deal expires after the Super Bowl.

Aikman, who turns 60 in November, has not received a long-term offer from ESPN. It remains unclear why the network is hesitant to make such a commitment.

ESPN finally found an NFL analyst who meets the standard required for its most prominent broadcast booth. For years, the network cycled through analysts such as Jason Witten, Booger McFarland, Brian Griese and Louis Riddick. They each struggled.

Meanwhile, Aikman is widely regarded as the best color commentator in sports. He has worked with Buck since 2002, when the two began calling games together at Fox. This season marks their 25th year as a broadcast team. They joined ESPN together in 2022.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

ESPN could view Greg Olsen, whose contract with Fox also expires after this season, as a younger and cheaper alternative. Olsen is good in the booth. Still, he may not have the same chemistry with Buck as Aikman does — at least not initially.

Chemistry is difficult to project. It is even harder to manufacture.

Unless Aikman is seeking Tom Brady money — reportedly $37.5 million annually — it would be difficult to view losing him as anything other than a mistake.

The two sides should be able to reach a financial agreement if they want to. ESPN has demonstrated that it will spend more than $100 million on talent it considers to be in the upper echelon, including Buck, Stephen A. Smith, and Pat McAfee. Aikman is in that tier.

AS EXPECTED, MEDIA MOCKS JAXSON DART INJURY BECAUSE HE DARED TO INTRODUCE TRUMP ON STAGE

The small details separate Aikman from his peers. He criticizes coaches, players, and officials when warranted. He explains the game with great clarity and precision.

However, ESPN may have reasons beyond quality to move on.

For one, ESPN is back in the diversity business following unfounded accusations of racism from former employees Ryan Clark and Dan Le Batard. Despite the baseless nature of those accusations, management appears determined to prove, yet again, that it is "not racist."

What better way to prove that than by breaking up one of the most accomplished white broadcast teams in sports and replacing Aikman with an analyst of color?

The network could return to a three-person booth featuring Buck, a white analyst, and a black analyst.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In that scenario, Jason McCourty would be a name to watch. McCourty is part of ESPN’s NFL coverage and has joined the network’s Monday Night Countdown team. ESPN is high on the former NFL cornerback, sources say.

If ESPN doesn't re-sign Aikman, he should have options elsewhere.

Kirk Herbstreit’s contracts with ESPN and Amazon also expire after this season, potentially creating an opening on Amazon’s Thursday Night Football team.

CBS is high on JJ Watt as a full-time replacement for Tony Romo. But with CBS set to broadcast its first Super Bowl under Paramount Skydance ownership in 2028, the Ellison-backed conglomerate may view Aikman as an upgrade.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Netflix is another possibility as it continues expanding its NFL portfolio. Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria suggested last week that the streamer would be interested in acquiring more of the league’s international schedule. Netflix has not established a permanent game booth.



YouTube is also a wild card and could factor into NFL rights negotiations in 2029. Aikman could be an option there, too.

Aikman is one of the few talents ESPN could not easily replace. It would be a mistake to break Buck and Aikman up.

World.title: Madison Beer gets new skin while Justin Herbert sinks to 0-2, Aaron Rodgers' ex lashes out & NFL or college?
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Over the hump and safely onto the other side of the week. Our long, 72-hour nightmare without football is over. Thank goodness.

Thursday night football tonight. College games tonight, tomorrow and Saturday. NFL back at it on Sunday.

We've also got the Presidents Cup starting today, although nobody really cares about this one, and the final weekend of MLB regular season baseball. That's right.

TEAM USA GOLFERS WELCOME TRUMP’S EXPECTED PRESIDENTS CUP VISIT, SHARE PRIDE IN REPRESENTING AMERICA

The MLB playoffs start in less than a week. Red Sox-Yankees in the Bronx for a 3-game Wild Card series? How lucky are we?

Best time of year, folks. Let's dig in.

Welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Justin Herbert's fiancee, Madison Beer, gets some new skin while Justin tries to figure out how to beat the Bills in Buffalo on Sunday.

You'll see.

AARON RODGERS’ FAMOUS EXES FROM SHAILENE WOODLEY TO THE ROMANCE THAT SENT HIM INTO A 'TAILSPIN'

What else? I've got another one of Aaron Rodgers' ex-girlfriends stuffing him in a locker, some old reader mail from last weekend that I need to clear out, and I fear the new John Madden movie may just be the worst movie of all time.

The trailer dropped today, and folks — it's a humdinger. I thought it was fake.

It was not.

OK, grab you a controller and some pizza rolls, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

Madison Beer has her new Fortnite skin

Look, it's slow out there today. It's weird, given the time of year we're in, but it's just a slow news day. So, we're gonna keep this class short and to the point, because A) there's football on in a few hours, and B) I have a new water pump to install so I can use the toilet without dumping a gallon of water in the back each time.

Yep. I woke up this morning to the absolute worst noise of all time ... silence.

I went to take my morning pee, flushed, started to walk away, and then stopped. I didn't hear anything. No refilling. No noise from the back. No slow leak that's been annoying me for a year now.

Just silence.

I went to fill up the coffee maker ... and nothing came out. The worst feeling in the world. I went outside, checked on the water tanks, and the silence was equally deafening. The pump, which started to fade back in May, had finally breathed its last breathe.

So, our house has been water-less all day. I've got a new one en route as we speak. Until then, if it's yellow, let it mellow!

OK, let's use some virtual water and cleanse ourselves with Madison Beer becoming a new video game character while Justin Herbert tries to simply get a win:

What are our thoughts on the new Madden movie?

Just a tough scene here for Justin Herbert. The Chargers have been horrendous through two games this season, and that's coming from a miserable Dolphins fan.

Herbert has been awful. Mike McDaniel's offense has been awful. And now, they get to go to Buffalo and face the best team in the NFL.

Meanwhile, Herbert's new fiancee is out there modeling her tail off, and getting featured in a video game.

Yes, for those who don't know (all of you, I assume), a Fortnite "skin" is basically just what your character can look like in the game. So, essentially, gamers can shoot people as a bikini-clad Madison Beer for the next few weeks ... if you're into that sort of thing.

Different worlds.

OK, let's keep this train rolling and check in on this new John Madden movie. The final trailer dropped today ahead of the release in a few weeks, and I've gotta say ...

I think this one is in big trouble:

Aaron's ex, reader mail & is the NFL serious here?

It's just bad, right? This has nothing to do with Nicholas Cage, by the way. I love Nick. I think he's great. The two National Treasure movies are my childhood. PEAK cinema.

But the Madden voice is horrible. Truly horrible. And what is Shane Gillis doing here? Why is he in this? Is it supposed to be a comedy? I was so confused.

Maybe it'll be good. It won't be, but maybe!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big night of football (and hopefully water!). First up? Remember earlier this month when Aaron Rodgers called out most of his exes, including Danica Patrick?

Well, another former lover — Milwaukee Bucks Heiress Mallory Edens — has decided to clap back:

"My ex is currently on a press tour talking about how he never loved anyone he dated after 2017. Unfortunately for him, I am also on a press tour, for a movie inspired by how down bad I was. Really exciting time for competing narratives!!"

Get him, Mal! Rodgers and Eden dated, briefly, back in 2022. It never really evolved into anything serious, but apparently, it left enough of a mark for Mallory to clap back at Aaron four years later.

For those who missed it, here's what Rodgers said earlier this month:

"No one cares what they have to say until they say my name. I dated two women who nobody gives a f--- about unless they drop my name — and they like to say their version of the history of what actually happened."

Rodgers never mentioned Mallory Edens, but he surely name-dropped Danica, calling her "depressed" and saying she had no interest in having sex.

Seems like Mallory got off easy, if you ask me!

Next? Let's empty the mailbox on the way out.

On Monday, I asked a simple question: Which do you prefer? NFL or college? It all stemmed from last weekend's Saturday-Sunday slate, which I thought was clearly dominated by college football.

From Jim A:

"I speak from experience. College over NFL any day, any time.

We had Browns season tickets from 1980-2024, and Buckeyes season tickets from 1987-2009. Over those years, I missed maybe six Ohio State home games and probably 20 Browns games. Both teams had ups and downs (mostly downs for the Browns) but Ohio State was always a much better, and much more fun atmosphere. I can say the same after having been to games at Ann Arbor, South Bend, and East Lansing.

College offers more excitement, more pageantry, more history, more fun, and fewer bitter people (granted, Browns fans have every right to be bitter). I could easily sit on my couch starting at 9A for GameDay, and not leave the house until the west coast games were over after midnight. Sunday? I’d rather blow leaves or go to the grocery store."

And, from Gary B:

"College football is better then the NFL mainly because of the rabid fan base and loud stadiums. It doesn't matter if the game means nothing. Ohio State/ Michigan, Alabama/Auburn the stadium is packed and loud. There are states that don't have an NFL team but they all have college teams. It's football on a more personal level."

Yeah, I think I have to agree with both Jim and Gary here. I don't imagine this weekend's slate of games is gonna change my mind much, either.

Have you SEEN Saturday's slate of SEC football games? Lordy. What a wonderful time of year.

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Good class. I have a water pump to go install.

On the way out, here's another reason the NFL is inferior to college football ...

Absolutely pathetic. What are we doing here?

World.title: Netanyahu defends Iran war, calls Gaza genocide accusations a lie in defiant U.N. address
World.content:
Mamdani released a statement later saying that Netanyahu “used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” the mayor said.

Netanyahu also took swipes at Qatar and Turkey, accusing them of spreading antisemitism and false information about Israel to the world. And he attacked critics of Israel’s actions in Gaza, which have resulted in the death of more than 75,000 people, according to Palestinian health officials.

“Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century,” he said.

The leader also suggested that soaring settler violence in the West Bank, a growing threat to Palestinian communities there, was the work of “a handful of young juvenile delinquents.”

Netanyahu arrived in New York on a whirlwind trip that highlighted the growing isolation of the U.S. ally over its assault on the Gaza Strip.

With only a handful of diplomatic meetings on the sidelines of the assembly and Trump’s focus firmly on his summit with China’s Xi Jinping, the prime minister was expected to return to Israel shortly after his address to be back in time for the major Jewish holiday of Sukkot on Friday evening.

“I am leaving tonight for New York in order to defend, from the U.N. podium, Israel and IDF soldiers,” the prime minister said in a video Wednesday night before he left. “You hear the terrible lies that are being spread there.”

Netanyahu was anticipating that the delegates would, as they have in years before, walk out in protest over the conduct of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip. But that spectacle was also likely to play well with his domestic supporters, for whom he has styled himself as a defiant truth teller standing up for Israel on the global stage.

While much of the world has condemned Israel for the huge loss of civilian life and continuing humanitarian tragedy in Gaza, Netanyahu’s primary domestic challenge comes from an Israeli right wing that accuses him of not being tough enough in the country’s multifront war on Iran and its proxy groups.

“The main reason that brings him to the UN General Assembly this time is the opportunity to talk, using the UN microphone, to his voters in Israel, in his polished English, in a speech that of course will be accompanied by exaggerated descriptions of his great achievements,” Ephraim Ganor, a political and strategic affairs expert, wrote in the right-leaning Israeli newspaper Ma’ariv.

Before he delivered the speech, Netanyahu hinted that he would focus on populist, patriotic causes.

In a video posted to social media on Tuesday, Netanyahu took aim at Mamdani, who had pledged to arrest him for crimes against humanity before later acknowledging that he lacked the jurisdiction to do so.

Appearing to adopt the posture of a professional wrestler and looking straight into the camera, Netanyahu accused the mayor of supporting Hamas — which Mamdani has strenuously denied — and fomenting riots against New York Jews. He added that he would “tell the truth about you” and “tell the truth about our heroic soldiers.”

Netanyahu’s mention of Israeli soldiers appeared to be a reference to “NAZA,” a documentary made by two Israeli filmmakers in which 24 anonymous Israelis, described as military and intelligence officials, talk about the cynical process by which the country’s military evaluated the need for civilian deaths during the Gaza war.

A popular target that has riled Israeli leaders ahead of the elections, “NAZA” has earned plaudits abroad but condemnation at home.

Politicians have stumbled over themselves to publicly condemn the documentary in the harshest terms, with some demanding a criminal investigation into the duo and even that they be stripped of Israeli citizenship.

Netanyahu, who has a history of peppering his General Assembly speeches with props, gags and gimmicks, said his speech would include “surprises.”

For this speech, Netanyahu held up a pager similar to the explosive-laden devices the Israelis used to kill dozens of Hezbollah supporters in 2024.

“Remember the beepers? Remember these things? Remember them?” Netanyahu said. “Well, I can tell you this, Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”

Netanyahu also taunted the Iranian delegates with a Starlink satellite internet device, telling them that “when they inevitably defect, they too will be able to freely tell their story on social media.”

Netanyahu holds up a Starlink device Thursday. Timothy A. Clary / AFP via Getty Images

Last year, he told the audience that his speech was being broadcast into Gaza through massive loudspeakers and streamed to mobile phones so that Israeli hostages trapped in Gaza could hear him speak.

He also wore an oversized QR code on his jacket, encouraging audiences to activate the code to visit a website with a video showing Hamas’ attacks on Israel in October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed.

In the years before that, Netanyahu brandished regional maps to make his points. Two years ago, he displayed two maps that showed the “blessing” of Israel’s influence contrasted with the “curse” of Iran’s expanding power.

And in 2012, more than a decade before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in what they said was an attempt to keep the Islamic Republic from getting a nuclear weapon, Netanyahu held up a cartoon image of an Iranian nuclear weapon with a “red line” for its maximum enrichment level.

Matt Bradley reported from Tel Aviv and Corky Siemaszko reported from New York City.

World.title: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
World.content:
Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil jumped to as high as $108 per barrel.

The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.47%, a level not seen in 22 years.

After posting its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing on Thursday. In early trading it climbed as high as 5.18%. That remains its highest level since 2007.

Due to the influence that the 10-year yield has over consumer borrowing rates, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.37% on Thursday, its highest level since May 2024.

Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress toward ending the seven-month war.

Much of the day’s gains in oil were reversed shortly after midday Eastern time, following a Reuters report that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path out of the war. The path reportedly involves Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters’ multiple unnamed sources.

NBC News has not confirmed the Reuters report.

The reversal was short lived, however, and international Brent crude oil continued rising and closed higher by 3.4% at $106.60. U.S. crude oil ended the day higher by 2.6% at $94.61 per barrel.

Since the start of the year, both Brent and West Texas Intermediary crude are up more than 65%.

Those rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to all-time records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $6.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier, but up 73% since the Iran war began.

Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon.

Stocks fell in early trading, but like oil, sharply reversed course on the Reuters report. The S&P 500 erased a drop of 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite erased a 0.9% slip. Both indexes closed flat.

A global sell-off

Around the world, the bond sell-off is roiling sovereign debt markets.

“The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth.

The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009.

“As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts.

“But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom.

One major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, that found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.”

That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation.

It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said during a speech in London Thursday.

Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it.

Another key official, Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, said Thursday that she too expects “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”

In central banker parlance, tightening refers to raising rates.

Bessent makes a move

The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month.

“I am the house now,” Bessent said on Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.”

Rates have also continued to surge despite a warning from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in early September. Finn Gomez / Getty Images file

At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds.

But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday, the Japanese yen had again weakened to levels on par with it’s exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September.

Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasurys in an effort to keep their yields low.

In response to the department’s initial buyback earlier this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended.

But Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it.

“If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview on Sept. 10.

The second round of Bessent’s buyback plan was conducted Thursday, when the Treasury bought back about $4 billion worth of 20- and 30-year bonds. As with the initial round, yields rose to their highest level of the session on the news — but the jump was far less notable than it had been a month ago.

“Mechanically, today’s operation went more smoothly,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo. But “long-end yields are still being set by inflation, Fed expectations,” and the volume of debt being issued.

“Today’s operation is unlikely to alter the trajectory of long-term interest rates, which we believe will continue to move higher until the market believes inflation is being brought under control,” he added.

“US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” wrote Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, on Thursday morning.

CORRECTION (Sept. 24, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated Thursday’s national average price for diesel. It was $6.51, not $4.51.

World.title: These young quarterbacks were supposed to break out. Now they’re hurt.
World.content:
The New York Giants were one of the NFL’s pleasant surprises in Week 1, beginning the John Harbaugh era with an impressive win over the Dallas Cowboys thanks in large part to the play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

The Giants’ dreams of a turnaround season quickly hit a roadblock on Monday, however, as Dart became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury. And now Dart may miss the rest of the regular season after imaging on Tuesday revealed his knee was hurt worse than the team initially feared, according to multiple reports.

Only two weeks into the NFL season, several of the game’s young stars are seeing their seasons upended due to varying degrees of injuries.

Dart joined the Chicago Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2. That trio joined a list of sidelined quarterbacks that also includes the Minnesota Vikings’ Kyler Murray and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks’ Sam Darnold.

All five of those players are former first-round draft picks — and all are under the age of 30.

Dart left in the first quarter of New York’s 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. On a third-and-8 pass attempt, Dart was sandwiched by multiple players as the pocket collapsed around him, and he took a substantial hit to his left knee from a Rams linebacker.

Dart limped off the field and was taken back to the locker room. After initially being ruled questionable to return, he was ruled out for good in the second half.

“He’s going to be OK,” Giants general manager Joe Schoen told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during the “Monday Night Football” broadcast, adding that Dart would undergo X-rays at the stadium.

Dart’s hard-charging play style raised eyebrows during his rookie season, when he missed time due to a concussion but seemingly refused to tone down his aggressiveness when he returned.

Jaxson Dart lays on the field after being injured during the first quarter of a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on Monday. Logan Bowles / Getty Images

During the preseason, Dart even expressed confusion at why he so often is required to enter the blue medical tent on the sidelines.

“I really respect the rules, and the thought behind, you know, the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things,” Dart said in August after a big hit required he undergo a mandatory medical evaluation. “But at the same time, I’m still puzzled by just feeling like every time that I get hit, you know, I just find my way in there.”

Dart’s injury Monday, though, came on a relatively routine pass play, highlighting how no quarterback is ever truly safe.

The same can be said of the Commanders’ Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow while trying to regain his balance after he was tripped by one of his own lineman in a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, dislocated the same elbow last season, in which he appeared in only seven games due to multiple injuries.

“It sucks for him,” Washington coach Dan Quinn told reporters Monday. “I know how much these guys put into it. So, when there are setbacks like this, you just want to stand by them.”

A little before Daniels’ exit, the Bears’ Williams was carted off the field with a hamstring strain in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. While Williams’ emotional exit from the game quickly became a social media meme, it also cut short what had been an exciting start to the season. Chicago was coming off a Week 1 in which it had scored 59 points.

“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here. We’ll see what that looks like,” Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters Monday.

Johnson added that Williams has an ability to recover quickly, and his injury is considered week-to-week.

While the Bears, Giants and the Commanders all lost after their starters went down, their seasons are far from over.

The Vikings lost Murray in Week 1 but still managed a 2-0 start to the season with Carson Wentz at the helm. And now Murray is expected to start in Week 3 after recovering from a concussion.

The Seahawks are also 2-0 with Drew Lock playing in place of Darnold, and even exploded for 31 points on Sunday. Darnold is expected to return to practice this week, though his starting status is up in the air.

For now, the Bears will turn to Tyler Bagent, the Giants to Jameis Winston, and the Commanders to Marcus Mariota as the three clubs try to keep their seasons afloat without their young leaders.

And Dart, Williams and Daniels — all three of whom have flashed potential to not only be great players but stewards for the league because of their exciting style of play — will have to wait a little longer to cement their star turns.

World.title: Stanford apologizes saying AI-altered photo that changed student’s gender and race  violated policy
World.content:
Stanford University said the use of artificial intelligence to alter the race and appearance of students in a promotional photo violated its policy and was “a serious error in judgment.”

The controversy centers on an image taken of three students posing in front of Star Ginger in the university’s dining hall, according to The Stanford Review, the student-run newspaper that first reported the story.

The original photo shows one female student and two male students holding their plates as they pose for the camera. The altered image shows one of the male students replaced with an AI-generated Black female student. The other two people in the altered image were made to look noticeably slimmer.

The Stanford Review reported that the altered image was used by Stanford Residential & Dining Enterprises in its s. Its editor-in-chief Garret Molloy, said the altered photos were placed on welcome banners around campus.

Billy Ramirez, who is Hispanic, was the student who was removed from the image, according to The New York Times.

“To see me erased like that so easily was kind of very upsetting,” he told the outlet.

Ramirez told The Stanford Review that he initially “found it hilarious” that the school had used AI to change the photo. “But after looking at the comparison, I was also upset because I don’t agree with Stanford making those choices about how we were represented,” he said.

“Seeing my identity changed and being left out of the picture made me feel, in a way, silenced and erased from a representation that was supposed to include me,” he continued.

Ramirez did not immediately respond to an email Thursday seeking comment.

Molloy said he believes the school was “trying to create this kind of artificial perception of diversity.” He noticed on Wednesday that the banners had been taken down.

“In the past, we did that with college photographers going around campus and trying to find a diverse friend group,” he told NBC News in a phone interview on Thursday. “Those college photographers are now being replaced with AI.”

The university said in a statement that the altered image violated its policy on using AI for marketing and communications.

“Not only the fact that the image was altered, but the ways in which it was altered, reflect a serious error in judgment. We have apologized to the students in the photo whose images were altered or erased,” a school spokesperson said. “Quite simply, this was wrong and should never have happened.”

The university said it has launched an investigation to determine what happened and “to put in place protocols to prevent it from happening again.”

World.title: Pittsburgh doctor attacked and killed while he slept, wife also stabbed
World.content:
A physician and medical director from UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh was killed in an overnight stabbing that also left his wife injured in his home in Edgewood Borough.

Dr. Idris Evans, 46, died after he and his wife were violently attacked while they slept in their home along Linden Avenue early Thursday, police said. A suspect has been taken into custody.

According to court paperwork, Evans' wife told police that they awoke to a man attacking them in bed with a kitchen knife. She said he was wearing only underwear and uttered about "being God," the report said.

At some point during the attack she yelled for their children, 8 and 12 years old, to get out of the house and go to a neighbor's.

She told police that her husband called their attacker by the name "Elijah," as if he knew him.

Dr. Idris Evans, a physician from UPMC Children's Hospital in Pittsburgh, was killed in a stabbing in Edgewood Borough. UPMC

The Allegheny County Police Department said they were called to the scene around 12:30 a.m.

Responding officers found a man and woman suffering from stab wounds. Both individuals were taken to the hospital in critical condition, but Evans later died.

Suspect arrested in deadly double stabbing

A man was detained at the scene and in an afternoon update, police identified the man as 32-year-old Elijah Hemingway. He has now been charged in Evans' death.

Investigators said that Hemingway was found behind a nearby home with cuts to his hand and he was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment. KDKA's news crew at the scene witnessed Hemingway in handcuffs, being loaded into the back of an ambulance by first responders.

Hemingway is facing charges of criminal homicide, aggravated assault, burglary and trespassing.

"Dr. Evans was a dedicated caregiver and valued member of our hospital and university communities," a UPMC spokesperson said in a statement. "Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time. We ask that their privacy be respected."

According to his profile with the University of Pittsburgh, Evans was the medical director of the Pediatric Critical Care Transport Team at UPMC Children's Hospital and an assistant professor of critical care medicine at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine.

Neighbor recounts deadly stabbing scene

Sandra Trappen lives in the home next door to where the stabbing took place and said she couldn't believe the number of police that were surrounding her house, only to find out that the suspect was hiding in her backyard.

"He was hiding, there's an area of my garden that's not particularly well manicured like the other parts," Trappen said. "He had found a way to conceal himself, but apparently he was injured and bleeding."

Trappen called the incident "incredibly shocking."

"Small and close-knit community"

Late Thursday morning, Edgewood police spoke out about what they called a tragic event in the community.

"We are a small and close-knit community and we are sure that many of you may be feeling shaken today," police said. "You may be sad, angry, anxious, distracted, or just having a hard time making sense of what happened."

Police asked that people be thoughtful about what they share in regard to the deadly incident, noting that things like rumors, graphic details, speculation and photographs can make an already difficult situation harder for those involved and others in the neighborhood.

World.title: DOJ says it's moving to end more than 50 decades-old school desegregation cases
World.content:
The Justice Department said Thursday it was seeking to end more than 50 long-standing consent decrees dating back decades that sought to curb unlawful racial segregation that was prevalent during the Jim Crow era.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said her office was "ending prolonged federal oversight of these school districts" because the effort "does not reflect the reality of those classrooms today."

The Justice Department did not provide a list of all 50 cases, but cited several examples including consent decrees in Waterbury, Connecticut, as well as Flagler, Florida. Dhillon described the consent decrees as "onerous and outdated."

A federal judge must agree to dismiss a consent decree, and it was not immediately clear how many of the 50 cases that the Justice Department has sought to dismiss have been formally tossed out.

At the end of Reconstruction, many states — particularly in the Deep South — enacted what were known as "Jim Crow" laws that enforced racial segregation at public facilities. These laws were spawned by an 1896 Supreme Court decision known as Plessy v. Ferguson, which created the "separate but equal" doctrine that allowed for racial segregation.

In those states, Black children were forced to attend separate schools that often lacked adequate resources and were not easily accessible by public transportation.

A landmark Supreme Court decision in the 1954 civil rights case of Brown v. Board of Education overturned the "separate but equal" doctrine, making it unlawful for public schools to discriminate on the basis of race.

For decades since that decision, the Educational Opportunities Section of the Civil Rights Division has brought legal actions to protect students from unlawful racial discrimination, often through court-monitored consent decrees with those schools. Some of those consent decrees have remained in effect for decades, dating back to the 1960s and 1970s.

In some cases, the agreements struck by the Justice Department required school districts to change how students are assigned to different schools or modify other policies to prevent students from being segregated by race.

As of May 2022, the Justice Department still represented the federal government in some 140 school desegregation cases, according to an archived press release.

Since last year, the Justice Department has filed court papers seeking to dismiss desegregation cases in several school districts. Federal officials said the districts had achieved "unitary status," meaning they had eliminated the vestiges of Jim Crow-era racial desegregation. In some of those districts — including in Tennessee, Florida and Mississippi — judges have agreed to dismiss the cases.

The Justice Department said on Thursday it is undertaking a "case-by-case review" of all pending desegregation cases that were filed in the 1960s and 1970s.

"After concluding that a school district has achieved unitary status, the Department will seek dismissal of the case," the department said.

Kristen Clarke, the former Assistant Attorney General of the Civil Rights Division who is now the general counsel at the NAACP, told CBS News: "This administration's relentless campaign to dismantle work done to end racial segregation in our nation's public schools displays is a stain on democracy."

"Brown vs. Board of Education stands as the singularly most important decision ever issued by the Supreme Court and it has taken continued partnership between the government and school districts to keep school systems on track. Carefully-negotiated consent decrees provide important protections for children today who face discrimination and barriers," Clarke said. "No doubt, this Justice Department's actions threaten to fuel resegregation and discrimination in public schools, to the peril of all of our children."

Dhillon has largely upended the Civil Rights Division since her arrival last year by dismissing or declining to pursue the types of race-related discrimination cases that had historically been its focus. More than 75% of the division's staff have resigned or retired early, CBS News has previously reported.

Dhillon has hewed closely to President Trump's policy directives. Her division has launched investigations into diversity, equity and inclusion policies at universities, filed lawsuits to prohibit transgender athletes from playing on girls' and women's sports teams, and litigated against dozens of states in an effort to access unredacted copies of their voter registration lists.

World.title: Man wounded during 2024 Trump rally shooting in Butler County dies
World.content:
One of the men who was wounded in the attempted assassination of President Trump at a 2024 campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died.

According to the House Republicans' social media feeds, Jim Copenhaver died two years after sustaining serious injuries.

"We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jim Copenhaver, who was gravely wounded in the horrific shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania," the tweet from the House GOP account read. "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance. We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time."

Copenhaver was one of two rally-goers injured during the shooting on July 13, 2024. David Dutch of New Kensington was also injured and Corey Comperatore was killed.

One bullet hit Copenhaver in the triceps and another was lodged in his body after it took chunks of his colon, leaving him with nerve damage.

About a week after he was hospitalized, Copenhaver was discharged.

Both Copenhaver and Dutch spoke with KDKA-TV nearly a year after the assassination attempt and recalled the terror that broke out during the campaign rally for Mr. Trump.

"I was standing up looking at the Jumbotron behind me, and next thing I know my sleeve has been yanked," Copenhaver said. "I could see a portion of it going by pretty fast, and I heard 'pew.' I heard it, and I didn't realize at the time that I had gotten shot. But I turned around, and that's when I got the second shot."

Copenhaver was 76 years old.

World.title: Sylvester Stallone jokes about one of his wildest jobs before fame
World.content:
Sylvester Stallone said he took a series of odd jobs to make ends meet before the bruised but unbowed Rocky Balboa. One of them involved cleaning out lion cages at New York City's Central Park Zoo.

"Yeah, that's a rough one, because I felt so bad for these magnificent animals. And then I felt bad because I smelled like them, you know, going home. It's pretty pungent," Stallone joked with "CBS Sunday Morning" correspondent Tracy Smith in an interview airing this weekend.

He added that he would jump into the shower afterward with his clothes still on: "I had no choice. I couldn't afford a laundromat."

Stallone moved to New York City in his early 20s to pursue his dreams of becoming a writer and actor. In 1975, he wrote the screenplay for "Rocky," which went on to win three Academy Awards, including Best Picture, and transform his career. Afterward, Stallone co-wrote and starred in another blockbuster hit, "First Blood," as well as its sequel, "Rambo."

After finding early success with two major franchises, his career entered a challenging period marked by a string of underperforming films.

"It was more than a drought. It was about eight years of spiderwebs on the phone," Stallone previously told "CBS Mornings" co-anchor Gayle King. Season 4 of Stallone's hit Paramount+ show "Tulsa King" will return in October. Stallone has also written a new memoir, "The Steps," which will be published next Tuesday.

Watch more of Tracy Smith's conversation with actor Sylvester Stallone on "CBS Sunday Morning" this weekend. Stallone will also join Smith on Monday, Sept. 28, at 6 p.m. for a candid conversation before a live audience as part of "CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY," a new series featuring in-depth conversations with some of the biggest names in the arts, politics and beyond. You can watch the conversation live online at www.92ny.org or later on CBSSundayMorning.com, YouTube and Paramount+.

World.title: Officer thwarted Ontario synagogue shooting despite life-threatening injuries
World.content:
One of the officers who helped prevent a shooting at an Ontario synagogue on Yom Kippur continued fighting off the gunman despite being shot multiple times, officials revealed Thursday. Police also confirmed the shooter was targeting the Jewish community in a "hate-motivated" attack.

Constable Jeff Smith was shot several times, suffering wounds to his head and torso, but continued fending off the attack until a second officer, Constable Mike McCurdy, arrived, Belleville Police Service Chief Murray Rodd said at a Thursday news conference.

Smith was shot almost immediately with a shotgun, Rodd said, before he was even able to get out of his car.

"Despite suffering life-threatening injuries, within moments of encountering the armed suspect, Constable Smith exited his vehicle and engaged the attacker," Rodd said. This went on for almost three minutes before McCurdy arrived.

Rodd said Smith and McCurdy's actions prevented "what would have become an unimaginable tragedy" and that they were the only thing that prevented the gunman from getting into the synagogue.

Spray from buckshot can be seen on the side of a vehicle where a police officer was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Ontario, Canada. Nick Lachance/Toronto Star via Getty Images

Smith remains hospitalized and is set to undergo several surgeries related to "serious head trauma," Rodd said, adding: "While his recovery will be lengthy and challenging, he is making progress every day."

Smith's injuries include bone fractures, and he still has shrapnel inside him, officials said.

The shooting took place Sunday near Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario. The gunman, identified as Sean Ward, 29, from Quinte West, was hospitalized with serious injuries after the shooting and later died, police said earlier this week.

Rodd said Thursday the attempted attack was a "hate-motivated crime."

A police officer walks past the Sons of Jacob Synagogue. Nick Lachance/Toronto Star via Getty Images

"This was a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community during one of the holiest observances of the year," he said.

Rodd also noted the shooter "had the means, the motive, and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue. The loss of life and irreversible damage that could have been rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated."

Rodd said the shooter had several firearms with him, in addition to the shotgun, and enough ammunition to continue a gun battle for a "long period of time," along with containers of gasoline in his car.

World.title: Netanyahu says "shame on you" to Mamdani, claims "Jews no longer feel safe"
World.content:
Washington — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu berated New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday in a contentious address to the United Nations General Assembly that saw many delegates walk out before it even began.

Netanyahu accused Mamdani, a longtime critic of Israel and supporter of Palestinian independence, of being antisemitic. The mayor has insisted in the past that he opposes "hate or bigotry of any kind."

"Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of the city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," Netanyahu said in his U.N. address. "They talk to me. They tell me, 'This is not the city we remember.'"

"Shame on you," Netanyahu said. "Shame on you for distorting the facts, shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor, shame on you for spitting in the face of truth."

During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani vowed to carry out an international arrest warrant against the Israeli leader on his next visit to the city, declaring him a war criminal in response to Israel's actions in Gaza. But Mamdani conceded in July that New York officials did not have the legal authority to arrest Netanyahu.

Netanyahu's address to the U.N. marks the first time he has visited New York since Mamdani took office in January.

Netanyahu, who denies accusations of genocide in Gaza, also addressed Mamdani's criticism of his government.

"You falsely, repeatedly accuse Israel of genocide," Netanyahu said. "You try to stop me from coming here. You try to silence me. Well, you can't silence me. You can't silence the truth. Here's a simple truth: Israel didn't commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide."

In a statement after the address, Mamdani said: "As he has done time and again, Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians. Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity."

Shortly before Netanyahu took the stage, Mamdani shared a video about planting an olive tree at Gracie Mansion with Palestinian families from Gaza.

"May peace be our future," he said.

World.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of $7B St. Thomas, Ont., battery plant to 2029
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Volkswagen subsidiary building an electric vehicle (EV) battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.

PowerCo Canada made the announcement in a news release about hiring Mississauga, Ont.-based EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for construction of the factory.

"St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve," said a news release.

PowerCo declined to make a spokesperson available for an interview with CBC News about the delay.

Originally scheduled for a 2027 opening, the $7-billion factory — with a promise of up to $13 billion in subsidies from the federal government — was first announced in 2023. It was estimated it would result in the creation of 3,000 direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect jobs in the region.

To prepare for the arrival of the plant, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government have undertaken infrastructure projects to increase sewer and road capacity for the population boom that was expected in 2027.

Before the plant was announced, the province allowed St. Thomas to annex land from the neighbouring municipality of Central Elgin to make room for the development.

In August 2025, PowerCo Canada announced it had awarded two major construction contracts for the project. Construction began in October 2025, with work starting on the foundations for the facility.

St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who has championed the factory as a major driver of economic growth for his city, told CBC News he's unfazed by the two-year delay.

PowerCo has set up a temporary office in downtown St. Thomas. (Andrew Lupton/CBC News)

"They've picked a great local Canadian general contractor and in doing so, they had to adjust the [opening] date," said Preston.

PowerCo has been hiring workers in the St. Thomas area since August 2025. Preston estimates roughly 500 people are currently employed by the company in the surrounding area.

He also cited "the number of employees they already have working and living in the city of St. Thomas, the amount of construction that's going on in that site each and every day" as reasons for maintaining confidence in the project.

Preston also pointed to Yarmouth Yards, a large industrial park developed by St. Thomas, which is being populated by industries that are complementary to battery production.

Provincial officials also welcomed EllisDon's selection as general contractor.

In a written statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade said the contract "represents a major milestone as they work towards the start of production that will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs across the supply chain."

The ministry's statement didn't address the two-year delay.

"We look forward to continuing to work with PowerCo as they progress on their $7-billion gigafactory in St. Thomas that will position Ontario at the forefront of innovative battery and automotive production for decades to come," it said.

Area MP raises concerns

Andrew Lawton, the Conservative MP representing Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, called news of the delay disappointing and questioned Volkswagen's commitment to the plant.

“I realize that Volkswagen is saying it's just about pace and not about the overall commitment. But ultimately, it is about the commitment because we were expecting this to be moving forward at a speed that we're just not seeing,” Lawton said.

Lawton also said he wants to know what the federal government is doing to move things along and ensure Volkswagen remains committed.

"We saw $13 billion worth of federal subsidies put forward to this and the promise — the expectation — was 3,000 well-paid local jobs, not to mention the construction jobs. All of this has been thrown into jeopardy right now."

EV market shifts affect Ontario auto plans

The market conditions cited by PowerCo come as automakers across Ontario have adjusted plans for electric vehicle production amid changes in EV demand.

In April 2025, General Motors cited lower-than-expected demand when it announced plans to halt production of the Chevrolet BrightDrop electric delivery van at its CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll. Hundreds of workers were laid off.

Honda also delayed plans for a $15-billion EV plant in Alliston in 2025 before ultimately cancelling the project. The company said it would continue to assess the EV market.

At the same time, Canadian EV sales have shown signs of growth.

Statistics Canada data released in June showed the number of new EVs purchased by Canadians had increased by more than 20 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier.

Canadians bought 8,672 new EVs in January, 12,547 in February and 21,574 in March before sales fell to 17,795 in April.

World.title: CEO who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax is no longer CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Michigan tourist who recently went viral over a Facebook photo where she and three family members appeared to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts has parted ways with her employer.

Jane Smith, the former CEO of Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, is no longer employed there, according to a statement posted on Wednesday to the company's website.

"We are reaching out to inform you that Jane Smith is no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately," reads the statement addressed to "Family First Credit Union Members and Community" and signed by the chair of the board of directors.

The statement continues to say that chief operations officer Jason Acosta is now serving as interim CEO. It does not provide any further information about why Smith is no longer employed, or whether the decision to leave the company was hers.

CBC News has reached out to Smith, Acosta and the credit union's marketing team, and not yet heard back. But the company apologized in a statement posted to the Family First Credit Union Facebook page on Wednesday.

"We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community," the post reads.

"We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first."

A screen grab of an Instagram post by Breaking News Canada from Sept. 13 shows the since-deleted Facebook post by Jane Smith that went viral. (@breakingnews.ca/Instagram)

'Like our sweatshirts?'

The news comes in the wake of the backlash over a photo Smith had posted to Facebook on her way to Halifax, in which she and three family members pose wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts that Smith later said were AI-generated.

"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Smith, and later shared by her sister, followed by "lol lol."

Judging by the reaction online, just weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.

In a previous interview with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.

WATCH | Republican mayor rejects Lake Ontario name change: Republican mayor rejects Trump's Lake Ontario name change | Duration closed caption 5:09 Robert Corradino is the Republican mayor of Oswego, N.Y., a city on the southeastern shore of Lake Ontario. He says the body of water is central to his community's identity and the city's decision not to follow U.S. President Donald Trump's directive to rename the lake 'Lake America' is one his constituents 'overwhelmingly' support.

"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.

"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that, you know, one of the Great Lakes's names were getting changed."

She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.

When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who reposted it publicly, added the comment and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.

"We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."

There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name-change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always." In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."

World.title: N.S. teacher charged with sexually assaulting student at school
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Nova Scotia teacher is facing a slew of charges, including sexual assault involving a student at the school where he taught, and RCMP say they have identified other victims in similar alleged incidents.

Matthew Donahoe, 53, of Bible Hill, N.S., has been charged with sexual assault, sexual interference, assault with a weapon, two counts of assault by choking, four counts of assault, and administering a noxious substance.

RCMP said the charges relate to multiple victims, but would not say how many.

Police also would not share information about the age or gender of the victims, what grade Donahoe taught or whether the affected students were in his class.

Donahoe is a teacher at Dr. W.A. MacLeod Consolidated School in Riverton, N.S. The school serves students in pre-primary to Grade 8.

RCMP said they received an initial report of an assault on Sept. 10, just five days into the school year. During their investigation, they identified other victims of similar alleged assaults.

All the alleged assaults occurred within the 2026-27 school year and took place inside the school, during the school day, RCMP said.

According to police, the Chignecto Central Regional Centre for Education removed Donahoe's access to the school and students at the time of the initial allegation of an assault.

In a statement, the regional education centre said the charges are "deeply troubling" and it takes the matter "very seriously."

The centre had supports available at the school on Thursday and will continue to do so into next week. The school has notified families that Donahoe has been placed on leave, the statement said.

RCMP said there may be more victims, and said investigators will use a supportive and trauma-informed approach to investigating.

"Investigators understand that coming forward may be difficult," Cpl. Carlie McCann told CBC News.

"We want you to understand that we can go at the pace and use the process that is going to work for you or your loved ones or the people you care for and we understand that this maybe a difficult thing for people to bring forward."

McCann said victims can come forward to police without deciding immediately if they want to be involved in the full investigation or court process. She said resources are available to help.

Donahoe was arrested Wednesday.

He appeared in Pictou provincial court on Thursday afternoon with a white beard and collared shirt. Families of students also attended court.

Some of Donahoe's release order conditions include:

No contact with persons under age 18.

He's not allowed to attend places youths frequent.

He has to abide by a curfew.

He must reside with a surety in Dartmouth, N.S.

Attending court when directed.

Remaining in Nova Scotia.

Not being within 500 metres of any home, school or workplace of 10 named individuals.

Not possessing any weapons.

Not attending any public park, school ground, daycare centre, swimming pool, playground, skating rink, community centre, recreation centre or anywhere persons under the age of 18 are present or might reasonable be expected to be present.

Donahue is due back at court on Oct. 19.

World.title: Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations in Gaza after mass walkout at his UN speech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza are not only false but "the biggest lie of the century," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told world leaders Thursday in a defiant speech that asserted his nation's right to wage war against Iran — and was not heard by scores of delegates who trooped out before he started speaking.

Netanyahu, his voice rising in emphasis, said attacking Iran "was one of the easiest decisions [he's] ever had to make" and denounced as "moral cowards" a mass of delegates who walked out of the UN General Assembly when he took the podium to speak.

"In defending itself, Israel is also also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall," Netanyahu said. "In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes."

When Netanyahu walked to the rostrum, a mix of cheers, boos and mass walkouts erupted. Scores of delegates marched out and most of the visible seats sat empty afterward.

"If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now," Netanyahu said.

The Palestinian Mission to the UN had said in a message to many of the 193 UN member nations to bring as many staff as possible to the assembly hall and "collectively walk out of the assembly" once the Israeli prime minister is announced.

"This will send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end," the message said.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly via pre-recorded video in New York City on Thursday, hours before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took the stage to address world leaders in person. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

His remarks — which at times sounded like a stump speech as Israel gears up for elections — came after a week filled with speeches by world leaders accusing Israel of genocide and war crimes in Gaza.'

Israel rejects allegations that it committed genocide and war crimes and that it is illegally occupying Palestinian territory. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government insists they are legal.

Netanyahu, who is prone to using visual aids during his General Assembly speeches, at one point held up a pager while reminding the audience of Sept. 17, 2024, when Israel remotely detonated thousands of pagers that had been distributed to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. The pager attack wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children.

He reminded the assembly of the scale of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people, according to Israeli tallies. "This is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours," he said, or 16 times the death count on the 9/11 attacks that left nearly 3,000 people dead in New York.

Netanyahu thanked U.S. President Donald Trump for taking decisive action against Iran, and he insisted Israel would prevail: "We will continue to win because we have no other choice."

Abbas denied visa

Earlier Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the world leaders in a pre-recorded video from his office in Ramallah after the U.S. denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.

"The Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times in its history," Abbas said, citing long-term military occupation in the West Bank and the war in Gaza. Israel, he said, "has targeted all of the basic necessities of life."

As Abbas spoke, the Israeli delegation's seats in the General Assembly hall sat vacant.

In his speech, Abbas once again implored the international community to take more vigorous action and speak out more loudly against Israel.

"How much longer will some states continue to remain silent against Israel or supply it with the weapons it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the tremendous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank," Abbas said. "What is the international community waiting for in order to protect the Palestinian people?"

Though negotiations have not taken place for years, Abbas urged the international community to push for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Netanyahu has said no Palestinian state will be established while he is Israel's leader and has argued that the Palestinian Authority is not a partner for peace.

WATCH | A plan to remove Palestinians: Israel set to oust Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. signs off, defence minister says | Duration closed caption 2:06 Israel's Defence Minister says his country is ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza if the U.S. approves, a plan described as ethnic cleansing. Israel Katz said 'there is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration.'

The international community has backed Trump's plan for a group of apolitical administrators to govern Gaza under the Board of Peace. But Abbas said the territory could not remain politically separate from the West Bank and East Jerusalem for the long term.

He said the Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem and the West Bank needed to be governed by "one state, one government, one law and one legitimate entity authorized to bear arms."

Abbas recorded the video on Wednesday.

Since 2005, the now-90-year-old Abbas has led the Palestinian Authority, which is the internationally recognized representative of the Palestinian people. But his support among Palestinians has withered during years of corruption and the sometimes-violent advance of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Under Abbas, Palestine has been recognized as a country by a majority of UN member states. But on the ground in the West Bank, the mostly symbolic moves have not affected Israel's decades-long military occupation. Throughout the war in Gaza, Abbas and the authority have been largely sidelined from negotiations over its future in favour of a transition process shepherded by the U.S.-backed Board of Peace.

The Palestinian Authority was created under a series of peace agreements with Israel in the 1990s and administers semi-autonomous areas of the West Bank, while relying heavily on foreign aid.

It was ousted from Gaza after Hamas won parliamentary elections in 2006 and violently seized control. Abbas was elected to what was supposed to be a four-year term in 2005. The authority has not held presidential or legislative elections since 2006.

Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The Palestinians and much of the international community view the settlements as illegal and as an obstacle to creating a viable, contiguous Palestinian state.

World.title: RCMP says no sign of interrupted investigations following FBI's outcry over CBC
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of the RCMP says there's no evidence to suggest investigations were impacted following a report that FBI Director Kash Patel temporarily halted co-operation with the Mounties in retaliation for an internal CBC memo.

According to a New York Times story published last week, an irate Patel sought to punish the Canadian national law enforcement agency in the wake of a leaked internal memo from the public broadcaster instructing reporters to not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks ahead of the 25th anniversary. The policy was amended following international outcry.

RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said he received no formal notification that the FBI would stop co-operation.

"My concern was the perception of the Canadian public with regards to 'did this really happen?'" he told reporters after appearing before a parliamentary committee on Thursday.

FBI Director Kash Patel said any Canadian agency that did not 'publicly reject' the CBC memo would 'no longer have friend in this FBI.' (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

"So we did do a little bit of research throughout the country and there's nothing that was reported that any of our investigations have stopped."

Following the memo from CBC — which is editorially independent from the RCMP and the government at large — Patel put out a statement on X that "any agency in Canada that doesn't publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in U.S. history will no longer have friend in this FBI."

According to the New York Times's sources, Patel sought to punish Canada and FBI officials cancelled meetings with their Canadian counterparts — telling them they would be out of touch for some time.

Duheme said he also heard Patel "told people not to go into the embassy those certain days, but there's no way for me to prove it," while stressing the RCMP's relationship with the FBI "remains very strong. "

U.S. intelligence-sharing to continue

Any kind of meaningful falling out with the FBI could be devastating for Canada. It's largely a net importer of intelligence and leans heavily on partnerships like the Fives Eyes — which includes the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand — to pass on information.

The RCMP and FBI have a longstanding partnership and collaborate on a range of issues from the shared border to terrorism and cybersecurity.

Still, the two countries' intelligence and security alliance has been called into question since the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump who has repeatedly goaded Canada with annexation rhetoric and started a trade war with his northern neighbour.

From the RCMP's perspective, Duheme said there's no thought to reduce co-operation.

"How would it be perceived if you're withholding information and an incident actually happened?" he said.

"We're all aware of the political environment we're operating in," Duheme said. But he said the agencies share a common purpose: "Protecting the Americans, protecting Canadians, working together. And I think that's what people would expect."

The FBI has declined to comment on the New York Times report.

Asked about the report, a spokesperson for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) said last week that it maintains "longstanding and mutually beneficial relationships with numerous agencies in the U.S. intelligence community.

"When it comes to security and intelligence, the FBI remains an important partner, and it is in our shared interest to continue working together."

CBC has a longstanding policy to generally avoid labelling specific acts as terrorism without attribution.

Following the outcry, Basem Boshra, CBC's senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, issued a clarification on Aug. 28 saying "direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism."

When reached for comment, CBC spokesperson Chuck Thompson said "it's not our place to comment on matters between the FBI and the RCMP."

World.title: Actors Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder among detained protestors outside Netanyahu's UN speech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among the protestors detained in New York City on Thursday as Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a speech to the United Nations General Assembly.

Photos showed Sarandon, 79, and Einbinder, 31, in handcuffs with members of the New York Police Department, with the former wearing a shirt that said "fund people not bombs."

CBC News has contacted both actors' representatives for comment.

Several hundred anti-Israel protesters gathered near the United Nations before Netanyahu's speech, with dozens blocking traffic and chanting: "Stop arming Israel, let Gaza live" and "Stop arming Israel, let Iran live."

Dozens of delegates stood up and walked out of the UN hall when Netanyahu began his speech to the meeting of world leaders. His supporters in the gallery chanted in Hebrew: "The people of Israel live."

WATCH | Sarandon detained by NYPD: Susan Sarandon detained at NYC protest demanding end to arms for Israel | Duration closed caption 0:27 Actor Susan Sarandon was detained by police in New York on Thursday during a protest demanding an end to U.S. arms support for Israel. Officers detained Sarandon near the U.N. headquarters, along with another demonstrator whose wrists were secured with zip ties.

Describing those members as "moral cowards," Netanyahu asked anyone else who felt the same way to leave the room before he started to speak.

Netanyahu faces an election next month widely seen as a referendum on his responsibility for the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023 and his ability to defend Israel's reputation on the world stage.

Day after day this week, as other heads of state have stepped to the UN podium, many have harshly criticized Israel's actions, particularly in Gaza.

Actors Hannah Einbinder, right, and Sarah Sherman take part in protest ahead of Netanyahu's UN address on Thursday. (Eric Cox/Reuters)

Ahead of his visit, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the U.S. should honour a warrant for Netanyahu's arrest issued by the International Criminal Court. The prime minister is wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed in Gaza, though the U.S. is not a member of the court and New York City lacks the authority to make an arrest.

Earlier on Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the assembly through pre-recorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.

"The Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times in its history," Abbas said, citing long-term military occupation in the West Bank and the war in Gaza.

Israel, he said, "has targeted all of the basic necessities of life."

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.
