We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”
World.content:
UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:59 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

The United Kingdom has asked for a written statement to be placed in the official record of the UN General Assembly in response to Argentine President Javier Milei's address, saying Buenos Aires' conduct over the Falklands “is wholly incompatible with the principles established in the United Nations Charter and is not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”.

The text, released by the British mission to the organisation, was submitted under agenda item eight of the 81st session, after Milei referred on Wednesday to sovereignty over the archipelago and over South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. It is the same procedure London used in 2012 to reply to then president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

The document states that the United Kingdom “has no doubt” about its sovereignty over both territories and their surrounding maritime areas, and that it remains steadfast in supporting the islanders' right of self-determination, set out in the UN Charter and Article 1 of the two international human rights covenants. It says Argentina “continues to deny that this fundamental human right applies” to those inhabitants and actively seeks opportunities in international fora to assert its sovereignty claim.

The United Kingdom has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.



Our statement in response to the Argentine General Assembly Statement regarding the Falklands: pic.twitter.com/eWw8aS2MDI — UK at the UN (@UKUN_NewYork) September 23, 2026

The statement rebuts point by point the legal argument Milei set out. It says General Assembly Resolution 2065 “does not prohibit economic development or displace the Islanders' right of self-determination”, and that Resolution 31/49 “likewise does not limit or remove the rights of the Islanders to freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development”. It adds that calls for negotiations “do not modify or dilute the obligation of nations to respect the legally binding right of self-determination”. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

On the ongoing dispute over oil companies, the text says efforts to obstruct and harass international companies involved in the archipelago's hydrocarbons, and other local industries, “are a wholly unacceptable attempt to exercise extra-territorial jurisdiction, and have no justification whatsoever in international law”, describing them as obstructive to global business and inconsistent with free trade. It further states that hydrocarbon development is a legitimate commercial venture regulated by the legislation of the archipelago's government in strict accordance with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that Argentine domestic law does not apply there.

The document includes a detail about the 2013 referendum that London does not usually highlight: alongside the 99.8% vote to maintain the current status, on a 92% turnout, the vote was supervised by independent observers from Canada, the United States, New Zealand and three South American countries: Uruguay, Chile and Brazil.

The statement closes a forty-eight-hour sequence. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham included the archipelago among the challenges to the rule of law in his address; that same night, Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno exercised the right of reply before the plenary and said “the illegal British occupation of the islands dates back to January 1833”, when the authorities and the established Argentine population were expelled. Milei spoke on Wednesday, and the British text followed hours later.

Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors. None of the allegations has been proven.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date
World.content:
Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:47 UTC Full article

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, announced on Wednesday before the United Nations General Assembly that her country will hold elections, without specifying when, and thanked US President Donald Trump for “his willingness to return to the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation”.

“Democracy is not measured by the existence of elections. Democracy is measured by the quality of the competition that precedes those elections. An election should be a solution, not a generator of irreconcilable conflicts,” she said before the announcement. She added: “I want to say it very clearly in this General Assembly: in Venezuela there will be elections and, in that direction, we have begun a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition,” under “equal conditions for all”. On timing, she said “the Venezuelan people, with their ancestral wisdom, will determine the right moment”.

Rodríguez said Venezuela has begun an “orderly, institutional and verifiable” transition to democracy, citing among its pillars a reform of the justice system and the “responsible exercise” of politics. She said the country had endured “two great and painful trials” this year: the “strangulation of its internal political life and the sharpened confrontation with the United States”, and the double earthquake of June 24, which left more than 6,500 dead. “Venezuela is being reborn,” she concluded, in a speech lasting under twenty minutes.

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke. The tone contrasted with Rodríguez's own remarks in the same forum in 2019, when as vice president she said she came “in the name of the Venezuela that does not kneel before any imperial power”, conveyed Maduro's greetings and denounced Trump's “supremacist hatred” and “imperial claws”.

She did not mention Maduro at any point. Her predecessor remains in US custody alongside his wife Cilia Flores, awaiting trial on drug trafficking and related charges, which he rejects. Before her address, videos circulated in which Rodríguez declined to say whether she would visit Maduro at the Brooklyn detention centre where he is held.

The acting president also praised the agreement granting the United States access to more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, a share the US government puts at around a quarter of the country's total. Trump had referred to the deal the previous day, from the same podium, with the phrase “to the victor belong the spoils”.

According to Axios, citing White House sources, Trump pressed Rodríguez during Tuesday's meeting to call elections: “In the end, you're going to have to call elections,” he reportedly said. Neither participant confirmed that account. Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed it differently on Wednesday, saying the ultimate goal is “free and fair elections” but that an economic collapse must first be avoided. “If there is a social collapse or an economic crisis in Venezuela, not only are the elections in jeopardy, but also the survival of democracy in the country,” he said.

Rodríguez took office in an acting capacity on January 5, two days after Maduro's capture in a US military operation in Caracas, and faces questions over her legitimacy for not having been elected. Separately, the circle around opposition leader María Corina Machado said this week that three attempts to return to the country from Panama had been thwarted, bringing the total to seven in recent weeks.

World.title: Machado's team says three attempts to return to Venezuela failed in 24 hours
World.content:
Machado's team says three attempts to return to Venezuela failed in 24 hours

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 18:11 UTC Full article

Asked about the matter, Trump denied having told her not to return, saying he had said nothing to her about it

The circle around Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado said this week that three attempts to return to Venezuela from Panama, by sea and by air, were thwarted within roughly 24 hours. One was recorded in a flight manifest placing her among the passengers of an aircraft that never took off; the document does not establish why.

“In recent hours there have been three attempts, by sea and air, from Panama, without success. That makes seven attempts — yes, seven — in recent weeks. They will not let her return to her own country,” her international relations adviser, Pedro Urruchurtu, wrote on X. The reasons given for the cancellations come from the account of journalist Idania Chirinos, of NTN24, who is accompanying Machado in Panama: on Monday, a sea crossing was suspended when the vessel's owner cited mechanical faults that Chirinos called “strange”, even though Machado's passport had already been stamped by immigration; on Tuesday morning, a flight to Aruba did not take off; and in the afternoon the attempt via Curaçao fell through. “The Nobel Peace Prize winner is a prisoner in Panama,” Chirinos said. Her daughter, Ana Corina Sosa, confirmed to the same channel that she remains in that country.

The manifest for the third attempt, obtained by the outlet UHN Plus, details a flight scheduled for Tuesday, September 22, aboard a Beechcraft BE-90F, registration HP-4DMB, from Marcos A. Gelabert airport in Panama City to Hato airport in Curaçao. Alongside Machado it lists four others: Monique Herrera, Rafael Alfonzo, Esteban Fraga and Ferdelin Bonilla, whose name appears with different spellings depending on the source. According to El País, Alfonzo is the opposition leader's lobbyist in Washington and Bonilla an adviser to Panama's foreign minister and a director of a state electricity company; those details were not independently verified.

The document also records that Machado would travel on a Panamanian passport, serial PD2000017. The outlet that obtained the manifest describes it as diplomatic; El País says it would be a special travel document Panama grants on humanitarian grounds to foreigners with a documented public record, and that it does not entail acquiring a new nationality. Her Venezuelan passport expired years ago and the authorities have not renewed it. Panama's government has not commented.

There are two hypotheses about the source of the obstruction, and neither is established. El País attributes the blocking to Washington, citing Axios reporting that Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau had approved an earlier trip while Assistant Secretary of State for Latin America Mike Kozak conveyed that US policy is not to facilitate Machado's return. Machado herself, however, said on June 29 that it was the Venezuelan government that had closed commercial airspace to prevent her from entering.

Leopoldo López's party, Voluntad Popular, recalled that Venezuela's constitution recognises citizens' right to enter national territory and called on the interim authorities to guarantee Machado's return and her political participation without restrictions.

Asked about the matter, Trump denied having told her not to return, saying he had said nothing to her about it. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said days earlier that Machado can return to her country “whenever she wants”; asked this week about the failed attempts, he avoided a direct answer and noted he had spent the day at the UN.

Machado, founder of Vente Venezuela and the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, left Venezuela in early December that year to receive the award in Oslo, after more than a year and a half in hiding. The attempts coincided with the presence in New York of acting president Delcy Rodríguez, who is attending the General Assembly and met Trump on Tuesday.

World.title: Milei at the UN: “The Malvinas are a national cause for us”
World.content:
Milei at the UN: “The Malvinas are a national cause for us”

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:54 UTC Full article

It was his third speech as president to the body and the eighth of the day's speakers, running 19 minutes

Argentine President Javier Milei called on the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday to act over what he described as unilateral British actions in the Falklands, and accused the organisation of having “decided to look the other way” on the dispute. “The Malvinas are a national cause for us,” he said, repeating the phrase twice at the start of his address.

It was his third speech as president to the body and the eighth of the day's speakers, running 19 minutes. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, Economy Minister Luis Caputo and UN Ambassador Francisco Tropepi listened from the floor.

Milei focused his criticism on non-compliance with Resolution 31/49, adopted in December 1976, which urges Argentina and the United Kingdom to refrain from introducing unilateral modifications while the dispute continues. “Fifty years later the situation has not changed, but the unilateral modifications continue,” he said, adding: “What use is a resolution if for decades the other party can act against it and that resolution remains intact in the archives but powerless before reality? There is no shortage of words or resolutions; what is missing is that they carry consequences.”

On the archipelago's population, he argued that the principle of self-determination does not apply “since this is a population implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”, and said the Assembly itself has determined as much in numerous resolutions. That is Argentina's reading of those texts. The United Kingdom holds the opposite position: in his address on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country would stand firm against those who “threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands”. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters in the archipelago chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

Milei listed the measures taken: “We presented warning notices, we turned to the available legal tools, we sanctioned the companies involved and their suppliers, and we sent Congress a National Sovereignty Defence Bill.” According to official figures released so far, the foreign ministry has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied, three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors, and around 180 warning notices sent to individuals and companies in 30 countries. None of the allegations has been proven. He repeated the call on London to “resume negotiations to find a peaceful solution” and to exchange views on the exploitation of natural resources.

“Malvinas”:

Por el reclamo de Javier Milei en la Asamblea General de la ONU pic.twitter.com/LX5iwTsBBB — ¿Por qué es tendencia? (@porquetendencia) September 23, 2026

Argentina had already responded to Burnham before the presidential address. Quirno exercised the right of reply before the plenary on Tuesday night, speaking for nearly three minutes alongside Tropepi: he reiterated Argentina's “full willingness” to resume bilateral negotiations and said the islands are “illegally occupied by the United Kingdom”. Asked whether the premier's remarks would require changes to Milei's speech, he said they would not, because “we already made the reply ourselves”. That same day, the foreign ministry delivered a formal protest note at the British embassy over the five-year extension of offshore oil licences, which it called an “unlawful act”.

Elsewhere in the speech, Milei described pandemic lockdown policies promoted by UN-affiliated bodies as “genocide”, saying they “cost the lives of millions of people who died alone”. It is an extreme and contested characterisation, made by the Argentine president.

On artificial intelligence, he announced that Argentina will not regulate pre-emptively and will offer “a cutting-edge legal framework”, with limited liability for companies and tax benefits, aligning with Donald Trump, who in Tuesday's address rejected any “globalist scheme” of regulation. Burnham, from the same podium on the same day, had called for the opposite: “a single set of global principles and standards”.

World.title: Chilean Defense Committee meets in Punta Arenas to address pretensions over Magellan sovereignty
World.content:
Chilean Defense Committee meets in Punta Arenas to address pretensions over Magellan sovereignty

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:48 UTC Full article

Chilean Vice-president Claudio Alvarado arrives at Punta Arenas for the Magellan Strait ceremony

The five Senators from the Defense Committee who also participated in reaffirming Chilean full sovereignty over the Strait

Chilean Vice-president Claudio Alvarado praised the Defense Committee from the House of Deputies which is planning to hold a formal meeting next Friday at the Austral Naval Command in Punta Arenas, to address the Defense budget, Armed Forces capability and austral sovereignty particularly the Magellan Strait.

The minister of Defense Fernando Barros, members of Congress linked to foreign relations, the commanders of the armed forces branches, heads of regional units and from the Austral Command will also be present at the meeting.

The motive for the gathering has been the 183rd anniversary of the Chilean whole undisputable possession of the Magellan Strait, following a resurgence of certain Argentine claims.

The official session will be strictly reserved given the sensitivity and strategic defense issues to be addressed, naval procurement and austral sovereignty, according to lower House sources.

Vice-president and Home Secretary Alvarado recalled the feat of the schooner ‘Ancud’ which left the island of Chiloe and four months later, on September 21st 1843 arrived at the Magellan Strait and raised the Chilean flag taking possession of the strategic maritime passage. This is the 183 anniversary of such a feat that also meant the final establishment of the Chilean state in its territory at the end of the South American continent.

Precisely last Monday (21st September), a delegation of Senators from the different political blocks in the House also joined the vice president in the commemoration of the event and reaffirmation of complete Chilean sovereignty over the total Magellan Strait.

“The Defense Committee represents popular sovereignty and this is why it is so important that all branches of government are present and concerned about the reality of our austral territory and waters. We must remember the brave men 183 years ago when, ‘…faced with difficulties, never gave in’”.

Alvarado recalled that the crew and officers of ‘Ancud’ when they landed at St. Ana flew Chilean colors and they founded Fort Bulnes, in honor of Chilean president at the time, but later had to move northwards and in December 1848, started Punta Arenas.

Independent deputy and member of the Committee Daniel Valenzuela said that “the defense of the nation demands responsibility and reserve, The Republic of Chile must be respected and we are not going to allow any nation to try and move a millimeter of our territory, or come to tell us how we must defend our sovereignty. Chile has professional armed forces, well prepared and capable of defending our territory”.

Valenzuela also underlined that the strategic scenario of the region must be analyzed very seriously, particularly “the Argentine growing military expenditure, and addressed to Patagonia, plus the defense acquisitions of Peru, and with our GDP percentage we must focus on security and national defense”.

“We can’t expect things to happen, prevention is also defense”. Chile’s sovereignty and defense policies, belong to the Chileans, no foreign power or neighboring country is going to tell us the lead.”

Finally when Alvarado met the press and was asked if Argentina had effectively derogated the decree questioning sovereignty over the Strait, the vice-president bluntly replied, “the Magellan Strait is indisputably Chilean, therefore the existing Treatises, 1881 and 1984, must be respected no matter whatever is said about them. The Treaties were signed by both countries and the sovereignty over Magallanes Strait is entirely exercised by Chile”.

Alvarado also promised that on his return to Santiago he would talk with President Antonio Kast to have the 21st September nominated as a regional holiday in Magallanes, a long standing ambition of the locals.

World.title: Chilean Senate reaffirms Magellan Strait sovereignty and support for Punta Arenas to trade with the world
World.content:
Chilean Senate reaffirms Magellan Strait sovereignty and support for Punta Arenas to trade with the world

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 13:58 UTC Full article

The transversal delegation of five Senators that reaffirmed exclusive, complete sovereignty of the Magellan Strait

A delegation from the Chilean Senate was in Punta Arenas to subscribe a declaration reaffirming Chilean exclusive sovereignty over the Magellan Strait and committing extra funds for its maintenance and reinforcement of strategic capacities when discussing the 2027 national budget. Likewise they supported the right of the people from the Magallanes Region to freely trade with whoever they decide in the world.

”The visit this week was in the framework of the 183rd anniversary of Chile’s possession of the Magellan Strait (21 September 1843) and the transversal delegation (members from the main political parties’ blocks), included, the President of the Chilean Senate Paulina Nu;ez, and her peers Rodolfo Carter, Ximena Ordenes, Gaston Saavedra and Karim Bianchi, underlining the compliance of the international treaties in force.

“…the Magellan Strait is part of the national territory and is under Chile’s control and exclusive sovereignty,” and Chile’s management and protection is in the framework of its international obligations.

The document also points out that the navigation and trade regime is established by the valid enforced treaties such as the 1881 Boundary Treaty between Argentina and Chile and the Peace and Friendship Treaty from 1984. Likewise in this context the document defends the right of the people from Punta Arenas and the Magallanes Region to develop their commercial activities freely and expeditiously.

The president of the Senate, Paulina Nu;ez reaffirmed the transversal character of the declaration, and added it was a clear signal of unity from the State institutions emphasizing that as president of the Senate together with colleagues “we have come to ratify not only the control and exclusive sovereignty of Chile over the Magellan Strait but also to recall that the inhabitants of Punta Arenas and the austral zone have the right to trade freely with the world”, She added “this right does not admit interpretations which denaturalize the established regime in the Treaties, or delays in their compliance”.

“International treaties are above any declaration or media release. As members of the State our responsibility is to recall and ratify the treaties we have with Argentina, sovereignty is not only a declaration it must be protected every day with decisions, political signals and an effective presence of the State”.

The Chilean Senators recalled that the 1881 Boundaries Treaty established the ‘neutralization’ of the Magellan Strait and the free navigation for the flags of all world nations. And the Peace and Friendship Treaty from 1984 confirmed such a regime and established specific obligations as to the maritime transit.

Regarding the Treaties, the Senators said they constitute an essential condition for the rule of the law and legal certainty and the good relation between Chile and Argentina, and in particular reaffirmed their intention of reinforcing cooperation and good neighborhood on the basis of the compliance of the commitments agreed by both countries.

Finally Senators anticipated that when the discussion of the National Budget 2027 they will promote a greater attention to the needs of the austral zone including the reinforcement of the necessary capacities for the vigilance and protection of sovereign spaces, security and freedom of navigation, national connectivity and the normal development of maritime trade.

World.title: Burnham at the UN: “the rights of British territories to remain British”
World.content:
Burnham at the UN: “the rights of British territories to remain British”

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 09:49 UTC Full article

“We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law,” he said

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham placed the Falklands among the challenges to the rule of law in his first address to the United Nations General Assembly, delivered on Tuesday evening in New York, setting them in the same sentence as Russia.

“We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law,” he said. “Not just from Russia, but also from others, including where they threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands.” He did not mention Argentina at any point in the speech.

The wording goes further than his September 9 statement to the House of Commons, when he said his government would be “relentless” in defending the islanders' right to choose to be British. Hours before the speech, after his first meeting with US President Donald Trump, the prime minister said he had raised the issue: “I felt I owed it to the people, obviously in the Falklands and back at home, to make the position very clear and that's what I've done today.”

The same day left the Chagos Islands agreement in doubt. The deal transfers sovereignty over that British territory to Mauritius, with a subsequent lease of the Diego Garcia base. Trump called it “terrible” and “ridiculous” and said Burnham was “going to be looking at it”; the prime minister replied “yep”. Asked later by the BBC whether the deal was dead, he did not deny it, saying he had inherited it and that “we need a resolution” safeguarding the base's future. The cost is measured three ways: the government cites £3.4 billion in net present value, around £101 million a year over 99 years; the Conservative opposition uses the £34.7 billion nominal cash total; a third measure puts it at about £10 billion.

Most of the speech was devoted to what Burnham called an “industrial-scale assault” by hostile actors on Britain's information environment. According to the prime minister, Russian agencies used bots, fake websites and falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations including universities and the BBC, amplified far-right narratives, and there is evidence they tried to interfere in the 2019 general election. He put Kremlin spending on information manipulation at around £1.3 billion a year. These are British government assertions, presented without accompanying public documentation. He announced he had tasked security chiefs with beginning work on a National Centre for Information Defence and offered to share British experience with other countries, following support given to Moldova.

On artificial intelligence, Burnham called for “a single set of global principles and standards” and said he would put the issue at the heart of Britain's G20 presidency next year, alongside a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect critical national infrastructure. Trump, in his own address, rejected any “globalist scheme” of regulation.

The prime minister also backed Ukraine, criticised Russian strikes on civilian energy infrastructure and, on the Middle East, said the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and the West Bank are not justified, after condemning the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023. He listed measures taken with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband: banning trade with illegal settlements, recognising the occupation as unlawful and sanctioning those involved in settlement construction.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies, and last week sent Congress a sovereignty bill. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez calls her meeting with Trump "historic" and thanks him for his support
World.content:
Delcy Rodríguez calls her meeting with Trump “historic” and thanks him for his support

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 08:55 UTC Full article

Hours earlier, in his address to the General Assembly, Trump had called Maduro an “outlaw dictator” and said hundreds of political prisoners had been freed since his capture in January

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, described her first meeting with US President Donald Trump as “historic”. The encounter took place on Tuesday evening in New York behind closed doors and with no press access. Her post on the social network X is the only available account of what was discussed: the White House confirmed the meeting and those present but released no agenda or outcomes.

“We held a historic meeting with the President of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote, posting a photograph alongside the president and thanking his administration for its support.

It was an informal encounter on the margins of the official agenda, scheduled for 7:40 p.m. at the Lotte New York Palace hotel in Manhattan, during a reception Trump hosted for foreign leaders for the General Assembly's high-level week. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller took part. Unlike other meetings Trump held in New York this week, such as his bilateral with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, this one was closed to reporters.

It is the first meeting between a US president and a Venezuelan leader in more than eleven years, since the brief encounter between Barack Obama and Nicolás Maduro at the 2015 Summit of the Americas in Panama. Maduro remains in US custody a few kilometres from the hotel where the meeting took place, awaiting trial and with the presumption of innocence.

Hours earlier, in his address to the General Assembly, Trump had called Maduro an “outlaw dictator” and said hundreds of political prisoners had been freed since his capture in January. On the oil agreement signed with Caracas last month, which gives the United States access to more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, he said: “To the victor belong the spoils,” describing it as “perhaps the biggest deal ever made.” He said he expected some US$100 billion in investment to flow into Venezuela's oil industry. He also presented January's military operation as evidence that the United States would use its “unmatched military might” to protect its interests in the Western Hemisphere.

Rodríguez arrived in New York on Monday and had earlier met UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the heads of the International Monetary Fund, Kristalina Georgieva; the World Bank, Ajay Banga; and the Inter-American Development Bank, Ilan Goldfajn. According to the UN, her talks with Guterres covered ongoing economic reforms, debt restructuring, dialogue initiatives and cooperation on human rights, as well as “the path towards full democracy”. State channel VTV described the meetings with the financial institutions as reflecting a “progressive normalisation of relations”.

Venezuela's diplomatic reintegration is not limited to Washington: on September 19, Caracas signed the restoration of relations with Paraguay at the Miraflores palace. Rodríguez addresses the General Assembly on Thursday.

World.title: Mexico pushes to raise regional content in electronics exports as US trade talks continue
World.content:
Mexico is working with the United States and Canada to develop a plan aimed at replacing manufacturing inputs from Asia and other parts of the world with regional content, a high-ranking Mexican official said Wednesday.

Speaking in Mexico City at the American Society of Mexico’s 5th Mexico–United States Binational Convention, Deputy Economy Minister for Foreign Trade Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said that the goal is to increase regional value added in manufactured products, including electronic goods.

Mexico’s export revenue has increased significantly in 2026, in large part due to a sharp increase in the shipment to the United States of AI servers and other computer and electronic equipment. However, much of the content in such products is sourced from Asia, particularly Taiwan.

Gutiérrez said that Mexican value added in electronics sector exports to the United States is around 7% to 8% on average. That figure is well below the 44% of Mexican value added across all “Made in Mexico” exported products, per 2024 data.

According to a report by the news agency EFE, Gutiérrez said that the goal is to increase the Mexican — or at least regional — value added in electronic goods to “20, 30 or 40%, hand in hand with the United States and Canada.”

Gutiérrez said that Mexico, the United States and Canada are seeking to identify what additional inputs — for the electronics industry and other sectors — can viably be produced in North America.

“We’re working with the United States to develop a plan for a gradual transition,” he said.

According to EFE, Gutiérrez framed the initiative as part of Plan México, and said that the goal of reducing the reliance on imports from outside North America was being discussed in ongoing trade talks between Mexico and the United States.

Among the goals of Plan México, an ambitious economic development and industrial policy strategy unveiled by the federal government in early 2025, is to increase the use of domestically made content in products made by the Mexican automotive, aerospace, electronics, semiconductor, pharmaceuticals and chemicals industries.

As part of efforts to protect Mexican industry and ensure its ongoing viability, on Jan. 1 Mexico imposed new and higher tariffs on a wide range of goods from countries with which it doesn’t have free trade agreements. The tariffs apply to goods from China and Taiwan, among other countries, and have led to a reduction in imports across almost 1,500 product categories.

However, there are suspicions that some imports from Vietnam — which more than doubled in the first six months of 2026 — are in fact Chinese goods.

Gutiérrez: Fourth round of Mexico-US trade talks have been postponed

After the American Society of Mexico event on Wednesday, Gutiérrez told reporters that a fourth round of trade talks between Mexico and the United States won’t take place next week as planned. The talks could instead be held in October, he said.

Gutiérrez attributed the postponement to scheduling conflicts related to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States and the upcoming G20 Summit, which will be held in Miami in December.

“We agreed with the United States that in the coming weeks we’ll announce when the fourth round [of talks] will be,” he said.

“… We’re working practically every day with the Office of the United States Trade Representative [and] with the Commerce Secretary [Howard Lutnick],” Gutiérrez added.

He said that Mexico is conducting the talks with the U.S. with a “cool head,” as advocated by President Claudia Sheinbaum.

“Our priority is ​reducing Section ​232 tariffs ⁠on steel, aluminum and automobiles,” Gutiérrez said.

The United States imposed duties on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles last year. Nevertheless, a large majority of Mexico’s exports continue to enter the United States tariff-free under the USMCA free trade pact.

The ongoing trade-focused dialogue between Mexico and the United States is taking place after the Trump administration announced on July 1 that it had declined to renew the USMCA in its “current form.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said at the time that the United States would “continue to engage with Mexico and Canada to address the Agreement’s shortcomings and our trade deficits with these countries.”

Despite the U.S. government’s decision not to renew the USMCA for an additional 16 years, the trade pact remains in effect.

Reuters reported that the current Mexico-U.S. “negotiations are seeking an interim bilateral bargain ‌under ⁠which Mexico could win relief from some U.S. tariffs while addressing U.S. demands on areas including automotive content and Chinese investment.”

“… The negotiation agenda has expanded from 54 issues to nearly 90, which ⁠Gutiérrez ​described as the natural evolution ​of complex topics such as digital platform regulation,” the news agency reported.

With reports from EFE, Reuters and La Jornada

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Ghosts, zombies, Xolos and Día de Muertos
World.content:
From spine-chilling ghost stories to costumed zombies, mythical dogs and candlelit concerts, Mexico City comes alive with the spirit of the season each fall.

This year, the capital offers no shortage of ways to celebrate Halloween and Día de Muertos, whether you’re looking for an immersive journey into the city’s darker legends, a playful parade of the undead, a celebration of the legendary Xoloitzcuintle, or a more atmospheric evening of music.

Here are four events to put on your calendar this October and early November.

Mexico City’s Turibus turns terrifying

By day, Mexico City’s Turibus is a cheerful crash course in the capital’s most iconic landmarks, neighborhoods and sprawling geography. But once the sun goes down, the familiar red bus will take a decidedly darker turn.

Every Saturday and Sunday evening throughout October — plus Nov. 1 and 2 — Turibus Terror invites brave passengers aboard for a journey into Mexico City’s darkest legends, haunted histories and otherworldly mysteries. From 7 p.m. to 11 p.m., the city becomes a backdrop for an evening of eerie encounters and immersive storytelling.

The circuit weaves together some of the capital’s most chilling lore with guided visits to Posada del Sol, Casa Negra, Fidel Mansion and the Land of the Goblins House. Along the way, live actors and immersive experiences blur the line between sightseeing and something more sinister.

As Turibus puts it: “The best legends are the ones that make you feel part of the story.”

Dates: 7 p.m. — 11 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday in October, plus Nov. 1 and 2.

Location: Tours depart from the Turibus stop at the Ángel de la Independencia.

Cost: 799 pesos, including the tour and a hamburger and French fries dinner. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit Turibus’ website.

Join the 19th annual CDMX Zombie March

If Turibus Terror doesn’t sound immersive enough, perhaps Mexico City’s 19th annual Zombie March is more up your fog-filled alley.

Beginning at 10 a.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18, the city’s undead — and those willing to join them — will descend on the Monumento a la Revolución. Expect a spectacle of playfully gruesome costumes, from classic zombies and fungus monsters to creature-feature icons, half-dead sports stars and whatever else emerges from the city’s macabre imagination.

The festivities will build throughout the day with activities including Monstrous Aura Battles and a Horror Runway show, before the main event: at 4 p.m., the horde will stagger, shuffle and lurch its way toward the Zócalo in the Historic Center, roughly a 30-minute march through the city.

This year’s edition comes with an international twist. According to organizers, Marcha Zombie México is launching a new partnership with Spain’s Zombie Walk, presented by the Galician Freaky Film Festival — giving Mexico City’s undead a chance to join forces with their European counterparts.

Date: Sunday, Oct. 18. Gathering begins at 10 a.m.; the march kicks off at 4 p.m.

Location: Monumento a la Revolución (Pl. de la República s/n, Tabacalera, Cuauhtémoc, 06030 Ciudad de México, CDMX)

Cost: The event is free, but participants are encouraged to bring a 1-kilo donation of rice, beans, or non-perishable food for Alimento Para Todos. For more information, visit the official Marcha Zombie México Facebook page.

A dog’s Day of the Dead

Some of us would rather spend the afterlife with dogs than humans. Enter Mexico City’s first annual Xoloitzcuintle Dog Festival, a nearly week-long celebration of one of Mexico’s most distinctive and mythologically fascinating animals.

Organized by the capital’s Secretariat for Indigenous Peoples, Neighborhoods and Resident Indigenous Communities (SEPI), with support from local institutions and museums, the festival will take over Mexico City’s Historic Center and feature a program exploring the “Xolo” through history, science, music and art. The full lineup is still under wraps, but the theme is already hard to resist.

The Xoloitzcuintle — or Xolo, for short — is Mexico’s iconic hairless dog, a breed whose history stretches back centuries. In pre-Hispanic Mexico, Xolos were revered as companions and guides for the dead, believed to accompany their human counterparts on the journey into the afterlife.

The connection is more than legend. According to Raúl Valadez Azúa, a researcher at UNAM’s Paleozoology Laboratory, the earliest references to xolos date to the 7th century AD, when they were associated with funerary contexts and served as guardians of sacred spaces.

Simply put, if you’re looking for the perfect Día de Muertos companion, this particular dog has been preparing for the job for a very, very long time.

Dates: Oct. 26 — Nov. 1, with an inaugural event at 5 p.m. on Oct. 27

Location: Mexico City’s Historic Center

Cost: Additional details will be released via SEPI’s official Instagram and Facebook accounts.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Lego to invest US $400M in Nuevo León: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🧱 Lego to invest US $400 million in Nuevo León: Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard announced that Lego will invest $400 million in Nuevo León between now and 2029, creating 1,300 “new, well-paid jobs.” Lego’s head of manufacturing in the Americas, Nancy Sánchez Moya, said the money will fund a new packing facility and an automated warehouse, calling it “the next chapter” of the company’s growth story in the state.

⛽ Sheinbaum pressed on Guanajuato fuel seizure: A reporter asked whether the 59 million liters of fuel seized at a Guanajuato storage terminal last week was in fact huachicol (stolen or contraband fuel) amid speculation that it was not. Sheinbaum said the Attorney General’s Office is still reviewing the case and will report back in due course.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The announcement of a significant investment by Lego in the northern border state of Nuevo León gave added weight to President Sheinbaum’s Thursday morning press conference.

The Danish toy manufacturer has operated a plant in Monterrey for almost 20 years, investing heavily in the facility over that period. Today’s announcement reaffirmed the company’s strong commitment to Nuevo León, an industrial powerhouse.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to speculation that a huge quantity of fuel seized by authorities at a storage facility in Guanajuato last week was not in fact stolen or illegally brought into the country.

Citing sources in the Federal Attorney General’s Office, La Jornada newspaper reported on Wednesday that the fuel seized is not “huachicol fiscal.“

Huachicol fiscal refers to fuel that was passed off as a different product when brought into the country in order to avoid the IEPS excise tax on fuel.

Lego to invest US $400 million in Nuevo León

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard announced that Lego will invest US $400 million in Nuevo León, a state where the Danish company has its largest plant in the world.

He said that the investment, to be made between this year and 2029, will generate 1,300 “new, well-paid jobs.”

Ebrard also said that Lego’s investment “will allow the revival, the expansion, of the toy industry in Mexico and also of the petrochemical industry that is linked to all this.”

“… In order to make Lego, polymers, solvents and pigments are needed, [as well as] sometimes silicon, adhesives and many kinds of plastic,” he said.

Nancy Sánchez Moya, Lego’s head of manufacturing in the Americas, said that the $400 million investment will be used to fund a new packing facility and an “automated, high-capacity warehouse.”

She said that the investment will allow Lego to “strengthen” its production and logistics chains, “supporting the growth we have in our business.”

Sánchez spoke positively about Lego’s experience in Nuevo León, where the company has operated since 2008.

Over a period of almost two decades, Lego has “found qualified talent, solid logistics infrastructure and a world-class manufacturing ecosystem” in Nuevo León, she said.

Sánchez also said that “what we’re announcing today is not an isolated project.”

“It’s the next chapter of a story of growth for Lego Group that we’ve built in Nuevo León,” she said.

“It reaffirms the confidence we have in Mexico and in Nuevo León, but especially in the talent we’ve found [here] to continue growing every day,” Sánchez said.

Was the fuel seized in Guanajuato last week actually stolen?

A reporter put it to the president that it “now appears” that the 59 million liters of fuel seized at a storage terminal in Guanajuato last week was not in fact huachicol. The reporter noted that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) delegate in Guanajuato was dismissed after the seizure of the fuel.

The Reforma newspaper reported on Thursday that “the false, ‘historic’ confiscation of huachicol in San José de Iturbide” had claimed its “first victim” — FGR delegate Juan Francisco Vera. Reforma also reported that the “illegality” of the seized fuel has not been confirmed.

In a separate report on Thursday, the news outlet Debate wrote that the fuel seizure in Guanajuato was “initially presented as a historic blow to huachicol,” but added that the bust was soon questioned due to a lack of evidence about the alleged illegality of the “confiscated product.”

According to La Jornada newspaper, the original search warrant was for the facilities of Gas del Noreste, an unregistered company. However, the search was carried out at the facilities of Gas Natural del Noroeste, a national gas distributor owned by Grupo Simsa.

For its part, the company Gas Natural del Noroeste said last week that “the operation of the storage terminal is entirely lawful and verifiable.”

The aforesaid reporter asked the president what the federal Security Cabinet had told her about the “alleged huachicol” that was seized in Guanajuato.

“I understand they’re still working on the permits that this company had or has,” Sheinbaum said, referring to Gas Natural del Noroeste and an FGR investigation into the operation of the storage terminal.

“The Attorney General’s Office will have to report in due course,” she said.

“I asked the attorney general [about the case] and she told me they’re still reviewing the permits and that they’ll report in due course,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that it can’t be determined whether the seized fuel was huachicol or not until the FGR completes its investigation.

World.title: From jungle to oak forest: Hiking above Lake Chapala
World.content:
Nature lovers who live on the shores of Lake Chapala are lucky indeed. All they have to do is step outside their door and start walking uphill. Within minutes, they will enter a network of around 100 kilometers (62 miles) of trails leading to scenic ridges and peaks. They truly live in a hiker’s paradise!

For an introduction to these trails, I recommend connecting with one of the already established hiking groups in the area. You can easily find them by contacting the Lake Chapala Society.

The Caracol Trail: From Africa to Canada?

One of the most fascinating lakeside hikes is to La Mesa del Ocote, the Mesa of the Old Pine Tree. The trail leading up to it is called Sendero El Caracol, the Snail Trail, because it includes a stretch of tight, continuous switchbacks that mimic the spiral of a snail’s shell, resulting in an altitude gain of 625 meters (2,050 feet).

The trailhead is located 3.3 kilometers (2 miles) north of the Chapala campus of the Tecnológico Superior de Jalisco.

The hike begins in a kind of jungle that practically swallows the narrow path you are following. On all sides, you hear birdsong as you brush past wild sage and maidenhair ferns. The trees above are thick with lichens, and the rocks below are carpeted with bright green moss.

‘Cuidado, hombre, you are still in Mexico’

After 3 kilometers (1.8 miles), the Caracol switchbacks begin, and the jungle slowly gives way to rocky outcrops, which then, amazingly, transform into a forest of slender, straight oaks. Underneath them is a seemingly endless carpet of golden leaves, upon which no underbrush is growing. I’ve never seen woods like this elsewhere in Mexico: You are in a forest, but you can see forever in any direction. It’s as if you climbed out of Africa straight into Canada and then, when you are good and confused, you top a ridge and here’s a humongous agave 2 meters (6.5 feet) tall, which says, “Cuidado, hombre, you are still in Mexico.”

At last, you come to El Picacho, the peak, at an altitude of 2,447 meters (8,028 feet), where there is an antenna. From here, you have what some consider the very best view of Lake Chapala and the towns along its northern shore.

It could take you as little as 90 minutes to reach the top, but this timeframe can easily expand to four hours if you stop to take pictures.

The Indigenous Ceremonial Grounds via El Tepalo

This 5-kilometer (3-mile) hike begins at the north end of Hermenegildo Galeana Street in Ajijic and heads for a so-called waterfall called El Tepalo, where I keep hoping to glimpse water someday.

Along this trail, you will come upon “tourist trees” (Bursera simaruba), which appear red and peeling like many a tourist. These are commonly called papelillos in Spanish, so named for their smooth, thin, paper-like bark, which peels off in small curly strips.

Here you can also see an amate tree (strangler fig) sitting on a big rock. Amates often start as tiny seeds deposited on a tree branch. Amazingly, they are capable of sending a thin root all the way to the ground. Slowly, they grow around their host, eventually strangling it.

Once you are above the waterfall, check out the great view of the lake below you. And, by the way, don’t be surprised if you end up sharing one of these trails with a herd of cows.

La Danza del Sol

Next, you cross a saddle locally known as El Pandito.

And, a mere 1.3 kilometers (0.8 miles) west of El Tepalo, as the blue mockingbird flies, you come to Danza del Sol. One minute you’re on a narrow trail beneath a canopy of creeping vines, and suddenly you step into a wide, flat, grassy meadow that takes your breath away. In the middle of it, there’s a lone tree festooned with long red, white, blue, green and yellow strips of cloth. The tree is surrounded by a very large circle of stones, and nearby, there are two buildings that serve to shelter and feed the many Indigenous people who come here from far and wide. Just outside the circle are two igloo-shaped frameworks made of thin branches. With the help of blankets, these are transformed into temazcales, or sweat lodges.

Here, for many years, Indigenous groups would gather for a piercing ritual known as La Danza del Sol, immortalized in the 1970 movie “A Man Called Horse.”

From the Ceremonial Grounds, you have a great view of the lake, and then a short, steep trail takes you back to Ajijic.

Trail guide in English

25 great hikes like these are described in the 140-page trail guide published in 2021 by Senderos de México in both Spanish and English versions. The guide has 100 color photos, as well as 26 maps featuring contour lines, estimates of hiking time and levels of difficulty.

Hanging bridge and Spanish moss

Curious about what lies south of Lake Chapala? How about a 350-meter-long (1,150-foot-long) hanging bridge over a deep gorge — or a river full of Montezuma cypresses festooned with more Spanish moss than a Louisiana bayou? You’ll find these and 98 more nearby sites for hiking and camping in the “Outdoors in Western Mexico” books, out of print but still available digitally. Happy trails!

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: Mexico posts second-best Q2 growth among G20 nations
World.content:
Mexico recorded the second highest quarter-over-quarter economic growth among G20 countries in the second quarter of 2026, an achievement highlighted by President Claudia Sheinbaum this week.

Mexico’s economy grew 1.4% on a quarter-over-quarter basis between April and June, recovering from a 0.6% sequential contraction in the first quarter of the year.

The only G20 country that recorded higher sequential growth in the second quarter was India, whose economy expanded 1.8%. Indonesia and Turkey were the only other G20 countries that recorded sequential economic growth above 1% in Q2.

Mexico’s quarter-over-quarter growth rate was double the G20 average of 0.7%. The U.S. economy grew 0.4% in the second quarter compared to the previous three months, while Canada’s economy expanded 0.8%.

At her Monday morning press conference, Sheinbaum noted that Mexico outperformed most other G20 countries in economic growth in the second quarter.

“Mexico, 1.4%, second place in economic growth in the second quarter of 2026,” she said.

“And we’re going to do better in the third quarter and the fourth quarter,” Sheinbaum said.

Mexico’s economy grew 1.9% annually in the second quarter of 2026 and 1.2% in the first six months of the year.

Annual growth in 2025 was 0.8%.

OECD lifts its Mexico growth forecast

The Organization of Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) increased its 2026 economic growth forecast for Mexico to 1.5% from a prediction of 0.8% in June. The updated projection is included in the OECD Economic Outlook Interim Report, published on Wednesday.

The OECD said that growth in Mexico is “expected to recover to be 1.5% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, helped by the continued strength of tech-related production and the lagged impact of lower policy rates.”

Mexico has recorded strong growth in export revenue this year, in large part due to a sharp increase in the shipment to the United States of AI servers and other computer and electronic equipment. Imports of tech inputs from Taiwan have also surged.

On Wednesday, the OECD also raised its 2026 growth forecasts for the global economy and the U.S. economy. The organization anticipates economic growth of 2.9% for the world as a whole and 2.2% for the United States. The OECD lowered its 2026 growth forecast for Canada’s economy to 0.9% from a previous prediction of 1.2%.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: A bad day for the peso: It depreciates over 1%, passing 17.5 to the dollar
World.content:
The Mexican peso depreciated by more than 1% against the dollar on Wednesday as the market adjusted its expectations in light of stricter U.S. Federal Reserve policies and the Bank of Mexico’s impending monetary policy decision.

The spot exchange rate reached 17.50 to the dollar Wednesday, a loss of nearly 20 centavos for the Mexican currency, extending a streak of weakness over recent sessions.

The exchange rate stood at 17.50 to the dollar at 3:20 p.m.Wednesday, Mexico City time.

Pressure on the peso comes from the likelihood of further interest rate hikes in the United States, with the market assigning a probability of approximately 54% to another rate increase in October.

The Fed recently raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points, bringing it to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. Markets have interpreted comments from Fed officials as a signal that the fight against inflation will continue to require tight financial conditions.

“Following last week’s interest rate hike, Fed officials have maintained a hawkish tone, reinforcing expectations of up to three additional 25-basis-point hikes through mid-2027,” Felipe Barragán, a market analyst at Pepperstone, told El Economista.

The exchange rate adjustment takes place ahead of the Bank of Mexico’s (Banxico’s) monetary policy decision on Thursday at 4:00 p.m. local time. Traders expect Banxico to keep its key rate unchanged at 6.50%, signaling what is anticipated to be a considerable period of stability.

With Banxico at 6.50% and the Fed at a high of 4.00%, the spread is now around 250 basis points. Another U.S. rate hike, with Mexico remaining unchanged, would once again narrow the interest rate differential between the two countries, making peso-denominated investment less attractive.

Meanwhile, the U.S. currency is also strengthening globally, with the dollar index rising toward 100.7 points, its highest level in approximately eight weeks. A weakened dollar was a major reason for the peso’s earlier strengthening, but those days appear to have ended for now.

The recent drop in oil prices may help alleviate some global inflationary concerns, but so far, it has not been enough to reverse the strengthening of the dollar.

With reports from XTB

World.title: The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 1: Health and healthcare
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND MEXICO WELL-BEING SERIES

A data-driven look at well-being in Mexico

MND Intelligence · Part I: Health and healthcare

Since the second quarter of 2026, Mexico News Daily has published the MND Sheinbaum Index™ and the MND Economy Index™ on a monthly basis.

The former examines what is happening in Mexico on President Sheinbaum’s watch by assessing the country’s performance across eight key pillars, including security, employment and economic growth.

As its name suggests, the MND Economy Index™ focuses specifically on Mexico’s economic performance across 10 pillars, including inflation, manufacturing health, the investment climate, economic growth and productivity.

In our inaugural MND Sheinbaum Index™ article, we noted that two pillars conspicuously absent from the index were education and healthcare — not because they are unimportant, but because official data for those areas is not published monthly, or even quarterly.

To fill that gap, Mexico News Daily is launching the MND Mexico Well-being Series, which will examine how Mexico is performing across key areas that directly affect people’s lives, including education, healthcare, poverty, happiness and gender equality. We will publish a total of six articles — five that examine a range of data points and a final report that holistically considers how Mexico is doing in the different areas assessed.

In these articles, we will present data that is directly relevant to Mexicans’ well-being and compare Mexico with other countries. We will draw on the most recent internationally comparable data, as well as data from the past decade, to assess what has changed in Mexico during the eight years that the ruling Morena party has been in office.

Improving the well-being of Mexico’s most disadvantaged people is a stated priority of both Morena and President Sheinbaum.

We launch the MND Mexico Well-being series today with an article focused on health and healthcare in Mexico. There are hundreds of relevant indicators, but for this article, we selected eight that we believe are among the most important.

We compare Mexico with other countries that belong to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) as well as OECD partner and accession countries included in the organization’s internationally comparable datasets. We recognize that many OECD members are wealthier than Mexico and can therefore spend more on healthcare.

However, it is important to note that Mexico is one of the world’s 15 largest economies and is aiming to become the 10th biggest by 2030. An aspiration to become a world-leading country in health and healthcare would be an admirable complementary goal.

As the data below will show, Mexico currently scores poorly across most of these eight measures relative to its OECD peers. That does not necessarily indicate that Mexico’s healthcare system is “worse” than those of wealthier nations. Consider the United States: It spends 17.2% of GDP on healthcare — nearly double the OECD average of 9.3% and more than any other country in the world — yet its life expectancy of 78.4 years is 2.7 years below the OECD average. Its avoidable mortality rate is higher than the OECD average despite that spending. High spending, in other words, does not automatically translate into better outcomes. Instead, the data points to where Mexico has clear room to improve, and gives policymakers, researchers and citizens a shared, measurable framework for tracking whether that improvement happens and how they can contribute.

For practical reasons — and to ensure a more consistent comparison — this analysis is limited to OECD countries, among which are nations that are richer than Mexico in per capita terms, but which have significantly smaller economies. We acknowledge that Mexico’s relative performance on health and healthcare would likely appear more favorable in a comparison with all countries worldwide.

Below you will find a snapshot of health and healthcare in Mexico. In parentheses after each indicator is Mexico’s comparative position among the countries for which comparable OECD data was available, expressed as a decile where the size of the comparison group allows for one.

It is worth remembering that the majority of Mexicans access healthcare through Mexico’s public system rather than the private system. Patients’ experiences in the two systems can vary significantly.

An MND survey conducted earlier this year found that 92.9% of respondents — mainly foreign residents of Mexico — rated the quality of private healthcare they have received in Mexico as “excellent” or “good.” As you’ll see below, a poll conducted by Gallup found a much lower satisfaction rate vis-à-vis healthcare in Mexico.

As always, we are interested in hearing about your views on health and healthcare in Mexico. Please comment below.

For now, though, let’s get into the data.

LIFE EXPECTANCY AT BIRTH (bottom decile)

According to the OECD’s “Health at a Glance 2025” report, life expectancy at birth in Mexico was 75.5 years in 2024.

That was 5.6 years below the OECD average of 81.1 years.

Among the 49 countries included in “Health at a Glance 2025”, Mexico ranked 46th — one place below Latvia and one above India. It therefore ranked in the bottom decile of the countries assessed.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

According to the OECD’s “Health at a Glance 2017” report, life expectancy at birth in Mexico was 75 years in 2015. Therefore, life expectancy increased by just six months over the ensuing nine years.

In 2015, Mexico’s life expectancy was also 5.6 years below the OECD average, then 80.6 years. The gap was therefore unchanged by 2024.

Among the 44 countries included in “Health at a Glance 2017,” Mexico ranked 36th — one place below Hungary and one above Brazil. It was therefore in the second-lowest decile of the countries assessed.

MORTALITY FROM AVOIDABLE CAUSES (second-lowest decile)

According to the OECD, “Indicators of avoidable mortality offer a general ‘starting point’ to assess the effectiveness of public health and healthcare systems in reducing deaths from various diseases and injuries.”

“Avoidable mortality includes deaths from preventable causes that can be avoided through effective public health measures and primary prevention interventions, and treatable deaths that are amenable to policy action through timely and effective healthcare interventions,” the OECD says.

Among “avoidable” causes of death are tobacco-related cancers and cardiovascular conditions as well as diabetes, which is highly prevalent in Mexico.

In 2023, Mexico’s mortality rate from avoidable causes was 418 deaths per 100,000 people, according to the OECD.

That was almost double the OECD average of 222 deaths per 100,000 people.

Among the 44 countries included in “Health at a Glance 2025,” Mexico ranked 40th — fifth worst — on this measure, placing it in the second-lowest decile of the countries assessed.

Mexico’s avoidable mortality rate was made up of a preventable mortality rate of 243 deaths per 100,000 people and a treatable mortality rate of 175 deaths per 100,000 people.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

No. Mexico’s preventable and treatable mortality rates both increased between 2013 and 2023.

The preventable mortality rate rose by approximately 10% during the period, while the treatable mortality rate increased by about 15%.

OBESITY RATE (second highest rate)

According to data in the OECD’s “Health at a Glance 2025“ report, 36% of Mexico’s population aged 15 and over is obese. A broadly similar share is overweight but not obese, pushing Mexico’s combined overweight-and-obesity rate above 70%.

The OECD average obesity rate is 10 percentage points lower, at 26%.

Among the 14 countries for which measured data was included in the OECD report, Mexico had the second-highest obesity rate. Only the United States had a higher rate, at 41%. Mexico’s rate was more than seven times that of Japan, which recorded the lowest rate, at 5%.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

No.

In 2015, Mexico’s obesity rate was 33.3%, almost three percentage points lower than it is today. However, the overweight rate was higher, at 39.2% in 2015. Mexico’s combined overweight-and-obesity rate has therefore remained broadly stable over the past decade.

In 2015, Mexico also had the second highest obesity rate among OECD countries, lower only than the United States.

POPULATION COVERAGE FOR HEALTHCARE (bottom decile)

Mexico’s population coverage for what the OECD calls a “core set of health services” was 78% in 2023.

The OECD average was 20 points higher at 98%.

Among 40 countries included in the “Health at a Glance 2025” report, Mexico ranked last on this measure, placing it in the bottom decile.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

No.

In 2015, 92.3% of the Mexican population had “total” public health coverage, according to the OECD.

Among 37 countries included in the “Health at a Glance 2017” report, Mexico ranked 33rd on this measure, one spot below Lithuania and one position above Chile.

A 2025 academic paper states that “between 2000 and 2015, Mexico reduced the uninsured population from 55% to 6.2%, largely driven by Seguro Popular (SP) expansion benefiting Indigenous peoples, rural and low-income households in high-deprivation states.

Seguro Popular was a universal healthcare program that was established during the 2000-2006 presidency of Vicente Fox.

The aforesaid academic paper says that after “SP’s dismantling in 2019, the launch of Health Institute for Welfare (INSABI), and the COVID-19 pandemic, uninsured rates rose sharply to 29.1% by 2023.”

HEALTH EXPENDITURE AS A PERCENTAGE OF GDP (second lowest decile)

In 2024, Mexico’s public and private sector health expenditure as a percentage of its gross domestic product was 5.9%, according to the OECD.

The OECD average was 3.4 percentage points higher at 9.3% of GDP

Among 49 countries included in the “Health at a Glance 2025” report, Mexico ranked 42nd on this measure, placing it in the second lowest decile.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

Yes and no.

In 2016, Mexico’s health expenditure as a percentage of its GDP was 5.8%. Thus, health spending as a proportion of GDP increased 0.1 percentage points between 2016 and 2024.

There was a difference of 3.2 percentage points between the OECD average (9% of GDP) and Mexico’s health expenditure in 2016, slightly lower than the gap in 2024.

Among 44 countries included in the “Health at a Glance 2017” report, Mexico ranked 38th on this measure, placing it in the second lowest decile.

HEALTH EXPENDITURE PER CAPITA (second lowest decile)
