“Nails are actually very useful. I’ve used them to fix a car and even to pull a fragment out of my leg.”

“I barely see my child these days,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

Injuries and attitudes toward sexism

Bihari has not officially reported her injuries. She says she feels uncomfortable going to a military hospital with a minor shrapnel wound when there are soldiers there who have undergone amputations.

She also says her hearing has deteriorated following concussions.

Asked about sexism in the military, Bihari says she tries to analyze not the comments themselves but the reasons behind a person’s behavior.

She responds to flirting and inappropriate compliments with a direct question.

“What do you want? Why did you say that? Are you trying to build some kind of relationship with me, or do you just want to chat?”

She says such conversations usually stop after that.

Bihari also uses her public profile to raise money. One charitable campaign raised six million hryvnias for winter uniforms for female service members.

She considers financial independence essential. She started working at the age of 12.

“If you want to see people around you rather than resources, you need to be able to stand on your own. And that is the principle I live by.”

Exchange

World.title: Experts warn of pesticides in Armenian food, inspectors see no issues
World.content:
Pesticides in Armenian food

Pesticides in fruit and vegetables, antibiotics in farmed fish and nitrates in melons and watermelons. These are just some of the problems highlighted in a report by Armenia‘s Food Safety Inspection Body.

Opposition Strong Armenia faction MP Harutyun Mnatsakanyan raised the issue from the National Assembly rostrum, citing the report itself. However, the Food Safety Inspection Body responded by accusing the MP of spreading false information:

“In 2024, it was not 192 but 179 samples that were tested for pesticides. Pesticides were detected in 91 of them, but in only six did pesticide levels exceed the permitted limit established by the relevant EAEU regulations [the economic union of which Armenia is a member].”

The agency also said pesticides could have been found not just in every second sample but in all the fruit and vegetable samples tested. It explained that “these substances are used during cultivation, and it is impossible to produce a healthy crop without them”.

Meanwhile, experts described the data contained in the agency’s report as “appalling and shameful”.

“We are literally living on an experimental testing ground where all kinds of chemicals are being tested on us,” food safety expert David Pipoyan said.

What hazardous substances were detected?

As part of its 2024 report, the Food Safety Inspection Body tested 179 food products for pesticide residues in products of plant origin. A further 19 products were tested for genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

The products tested included apples, peaches, strawberries, plums, grapes, potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, aubergines, watermelons, melons and corn.

Nitrates were detected in samples of melon, watermelon and potatoes.

GMOs accounted for 5.2% of one corn sample brought from Lori Region.

The highest pesticide levels exceeding permitted limits were recorded in products from Ararat, Armavir, Aragatsotn and Kotayk regions.

Of 696 samples tested, heavy metals were detected in nine — including potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and aubergines.

According to the inspection body’s report, unacceptably high levels of antibiotic contamination were found in honey from Vayots Dzor, Gegharkunik and Lori regions.

The report also says that consuming fish farmed in artificial ponds may pose health risks:

“The antibiotics detected in the samples, particularly compounds from the nitrofuran and metronidazole groups, have a cumulative effect and may have carcinogenic and mutagenic effects.”

‘We are putting our children at risk’

MP Harutyun Mnatsakanyan highlighted the presence of nitrates in potatoes, watermelons and melons:

“Our children are the most vulnerable to nitrates. In other words, by consuming products made in Armenia, we are putting the health of our children and our parents at enormous risk. I am not even talking about ourselves.”

He said farmers should not be blamed, as they cannot establish clear standards for pesticide use themselves. Mnatsakanyan said strict controls were needed:

“Controls must extend all the way to the market. The inspection body is proposing legislative amendments to establish pesticide controls throughout the supply chain. This needs to be done now, not after the next round of monitoring.”

The MP proposed taking the following steps urgently:

publishing all of the inspection body’s 2024 monitoring results;

holding parliamentary hearings involving representatives of the inspection body and the Economy Ministry, as well as scientists and MPs.

Inspection body: ‘No banned pesticides detected’

The inspection body said it was unacceptable to “mislead the public with unfounded and panic-inducing headlines”.

It also responded to the opposition MP’s claim that “what is banned in Brussels and Washington ends up on the plates of our elderly parents and children”. The body’s experts said some pesticides may be banned in one country while being permitted in another:

“Armenia is a party to the Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions and, in accordance with its international obligations, prohibits the registration, import and use of pesticides covered by these conventions. No banned pesticides were detected in the products tested in our country.”

Expert commentary

Food safety expert David Pipoyan recalled that industry experts had raised concerns about food quality a year earlier, but the Food Safety Inspection Body had dismissed their claims as defamatory.

“Last year, this same body denied everything at a news conference, saying there had been no violations. This year, it published — effectively hid — this appalling report on a little-known platform,” he said.

According to Pipoyan, if 47 out of every 100 samples tested were contaminated, this would mean that roughly every second purchase could potentially involve a contaminated product. In other words, he said, consumers would face a 47% chance of buying fruit or vegetables contaminated with pesticides.

Pipoyan said the problems went beyond the risk of consuming products containing carcinogenic substances:

“If you look at the range of pesticides being used, you can find neurotoxic substances, as well as pesticides that affect children’s health.”

He stressed that the report’s findings pointed to an ongoing risk for all consumers. In Pipoyan’s view, the publication of such a report in other countries would inevitably have led to those responsible for quality control being held accountable.

Social media reaction

Social media users also expressed outrage over the situation. Here are some of their comments:

“Every day you pay money to eat poison. And then you wonder why Armenia has ranked among the world’s leaders in cancer cases for decades.”

“This shows complete disregard for the health of the country’s own people.”

“We are demanding not token legislative ‘initiatives’ and justifications, but strict, genuine laboratory controls — from the fields to the shops.”

“Agricultural producers, are you happy with what you are doing? Let’s say there are no controls. But what about your conscience? Don’t you understand that you are committing a crime by poisoning people?“

“I’ve been saying it: we eat poison every day. Meanwhile, environmentalists are only concerned with shutting down mining operations. Environmentalists, what do you have to say now?“

“Whatever you feel like eating, pray first and then eat.”

“Everyone who doesn’t care about people’s health should be held accountable.”

World.title: Abkhaz experts discuss Georgian opposition’s proposals, EU stance on conflict resolution
World.content:
The EU on Abkhazia

Statements by Western officials and initiatives of the Georgian opposition surrounding the status of Abkhazia are once again drawing attention to the region. Abkhaz analysts commented on attempts to intensify Abkhazia’s isolation and evaluated the roles of the EU, Russia, and internal Georgian forces in this process.

Key arguments:

The Abkhazian question is being used by the Georgian opposition as a tool in their struggle against the ruling Georgian Dream party. Attempts to harden their stance and achieve the withdrawal of recognitions, as seen in the case of Nauru, are aimed at accusing the current government of a lack of patriotism and of making concessions to Moscow.

The European Union leadership’s focus on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia is driven not so much by concern for peace as by a desire to weaken Russian influence and maintain levers of influence over Georgia amid a crisis in bilateral relations.

A peaceful or forceful “return” of Abkhazia to Georgia is an unacceptable paradigm for Abkhaz society. Pressure from the EU and Georgia only destroys trust and narrows the possibilities for a diplomatic settlement.

Here are the questions posed to the experts and their responses.

Why would the Georgian opposition, which already faces plenty of problems in its relations with the authorities, choose at this moment to step up efforts toward the further isolation of Abkhazia, following the successful outcome with Nauru?

Respondent 1

It is difficult to judge the motivation of the Georgian opposition in this matter. I can only assume that, as always, the issue of Abkhazia and the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict serves as a bargaining chip in domestic political processes. Regarding Abkhazia, Georgian Dream behaves with more restraint than previous Georgian authorities, at least at the level of public statements. In contrast to it, and as if to demonstrate greater patriotism, the opposition—which lacks broad support among the population outside of Tbilisi—speaks out much more harshly. Apparently, in its largely ineffective struggle against the current government, the Georgian opposition has decided to weaponize the issue of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, or as they call it, the “Abkhazian question”.

At the same time, other voices are also being heard within the Georgian opposition. For example, Nika Gvaramia recently gave an interview in which he called on Georgian society to move past the traumatic memories of the past. In his view, conflicts should not act as weights tied to Georgia’s feet on its path toward the European Union.

Thus, within opposition circles, there are proponents of both a forceful “return” of Abkhazia and those who advocate for its “peaceful return”. Another matter entirely is that few in Georgia understand that for the Abkhaz people, peace and a “peaceful return” are by no means the same thing. In Abkhazia, such an approach is perceived as achieving the same end by hook or by crook.

Instead of trying to turn back the clock and forgetting everything we went through in the recent past, we ought to accept reality and seek common ground on issues of mutual interest. And such issues do exist, considering that we are neighbors.

To speak of returning Abkhazia, whether by peaceful or violent means, belongs to an entirely different paradigm. The Abkhaz people will resist either of these two options. However, at least a mindset focused on peaceful solutions makes it possible to maintain stability. Unfortunately, if circumstances develop in a way that favors Georgia, those parties advocating a forceful solution will gain the upper hand.

Respondent 2

I believe that the situation surrounding the revocation of recognition by Nauru undoubtedly emboldened Georgian super-patriots. But it also seems to me, paradoxical as it may sound, that the more liberal, pro-democratic forces in Georgia—meaning the current opposition, parts of which were once in the Georgian leadership—have always been and remain more hardline, nationalistic, and hawkish regarding frozen conflicts.

We have always paid attention to this hawkish rhetoric, which was heard back during Mikheil Saakashvili’s rule. On the one hand, he seemed to democratize Georgia’s governance system, but on the other, he approached conflict resolution in a way that was entirely unliberal and disregarded human rights. The current demands of the opposition appear to be a continuation of that policy.

Another factor relates to the fact that relations between the European Union and Georgia—specifically the ruling Georgian Dream party—have deteriorated so sharply that the European Union has no remaining levers of influence over processes taking place inside Georgia. Since the EU is deprived of the ability to affect Georgia’s internal political matters, it compensates by responding to this narrative to cater to the Georgian opposition, which Europe views as pro-democratic and liberal.

Respondent 3

The Georgian opposition raises this issue with a tactical objective: to demonstrate that the current government lacks principle regarding the problem of Georgia’s territorial integrity and is willing to compromise on it. In doing so, it heightens the level of friction between Western countries and Ivanishvili’s government by framing the latter as conduits for Moscow’s global agenda.

In reality, the approach across the entire political spectrum in Georgia toward relations with the former autonomous entities is identical: restoring the territory of the Georgian SSR either by force or through diplomacy.

Respondent 4

In my view, the Georgian opposition has quite a few problems not only in its relations with the government, but also in internal relations within itself; there is no single, clearly defined leader there, and it appears to me to be fragmented and non-united.

The “Coalition for Change” consists of several parties and is headed by a council of four leaders. That is to say, the Georgian opposition has problems with the authorities, within itself, and with the European Union as well.

To both questions, I would answer the same way: the appeal to Ursula von der Leyen lies within the perspective of Georgia’s domestic political problems and its relations with the European Union.

We see that the Georgian opposition has been protesting for a very long time, people are taking to the streets, but these protests yield no visible results; in my view, Georgia’s tilt away from the European Union towards Russia is growing, public support for the Georgian opposition is falling, and its ratings are falling too.

We often hear that the Abkhazian issue currently sits on the periphery of the international agenda and is virtually invisible against the backdrop of other crises. Why, then, do we see such active support from the European Union for the initiative demanding that Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia?

Respondent 1

There are two factors here. One is that Abkhazia is indeed at the very bottom of their agenda, if present at all. Russia and Georgia, however, are present. Therefore, the issue of revoking recognition represents, on the one hand, a policy of countering Russia, and on the other, a step toward trying to regain Georgia’s loyalty. Ursula von der Leyen’s support for the Georgian opposition’s demand on such a sensitive, patriotic issue also serves to bolster the position of opposition forces within Georgian society.

On the whole, the fact that against the backdrop of highly acute global and regional problems, the President of the European Commission finds time for the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia reflects political bias and the double standards associated with such bias, which, unfortunately, have always been displayed toward us by Europe and the international community at large.

It would be appropriate here to ask von der Leyen a question: if EU representatives claim to be committed to a peaceful resolution of the conflict, what does revoking Syria’s recognition have to do with it? How does it bring us any closer to peace? If anything, it does the opposite. Such steps certainly do not help the negotiation process, the building of trust, or any of the other goals declared by the Europeans. What they certainly do is call into question the EU’s role as a mediator, further shrinking its already dramatically reduced presence in the region.

Respondent 2

It is true that in words we often hear that amid the major wars taking place around the EU, the Georgian-Abkhaz context is irrelevant. In practice, however, whenever decisions are made that restrict the rights of Abkhazia’s residents, EU officials quickly spring into action.

Interestingly, Ursula von der Leyen herself, who intends to address the revocation of Syria’s recognition of the Republic of Abkhazia, appears to be going through a difficult period within the European Union. From news sources, we can see how European Parliament sessions unfold, with MEPs from various countries harshly criticizing von der Leyen’s actions, raising many grievances and questions.

In this situation, it is remarkable that despite serious internal problems and challenges, she finds the time to attend to the requests of certain political forces in a non-EU country, Georgia, regarding pressure on another non-EU country, Syria. We have always noted the European Union’s special attitude toward Georgia—an attitude I would describe as unrequited love.

The European Union contributed greatly to the development of the modern Georgian state and supported the reform of its state institutions. It seems to me that Georgia was forgiven for things that were never forgiven in other countries. What is happening now appears to be the lingering, phantom feelings toward Georgia at a time when its official representatives have ceased to reciprocate.

Of course, the factor of relations between the European Union and Russia also plays a role that cannot be ignored. Here, the EU operates on the principle of “the friend of my enemy is my enemy”. Perhaps that is why they show little concern for how EU decisions will be received by the government and civil society in Abkhazia, how these decisions impact the protection of Abkhazia residents’ rights, or how they might ultimately affect the state of the conflict.

Respondent 3

I think it is premature to speak of overly active support for this issue on the part of the European Commission. Although, on the whole, a moderate level of activity aimed at having Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia’s sovereignty would not surprise me. First and foremost, it is an effort to undo political acts of the Assad era and further weaken Russian influence in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The complaints of the Georgian opposition are of minor importance in this context. What is interesting, however, is whether it is truly in the West’s own interest to indulge Georgia, given the country’s systematic and deliberate drift toward the East. That remains an open question, and I doubt I am the only one considering it.

Respondent 4

Against the backdrop of these problems in relations between the Georgian opposition and the European Union, a certain reboot is required. Running slightly ahead and trying to answer the second question about why the European Union needs this, I think that such a reboot is needed for the European Union as well.

The chosen tactic and strategy of the European Union—not to engage in contacts with the Georgian government, but rather to cooperate more actively and closely with the Georgian opposition on the assumption that it will sooner or later manage to take power in Georgia—seems to me not to be working or to be working poorly, and it requires a new impetus. Yet no visible tracks on which success could be achieved are in sight.

By success, I mean the need to boost the rating of the opposition itself among the Georgian population and to raise its status. After the regime change in Syria, the new leadership of that country needs some assistance from the European Union, and the EU holds certain leverage over it.

If, at the request of the Georgian opposition, it manages to achieve some progress on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia, this could sharply boost the rating of the opposition in general and of this opposition bloc in particular. The exact same thing, in my opinion, is required for the European Union itself, since the previous tactic is not working and the opposition forces in Georgia are not gaining, but on the contrary are losing strength and influence.

The European Union put forward eight or nine conditions to the Georgian government so that it could return to the previous course of relations with the EU; Georgia is not fulfilling these conditions, and what is more, the tilt towards Russia has already turned into a stable trend toward rapprochement between these countries against the backdrop of the war with Ukraine and in the Persian Gulf, where Europe has a great deal of problems.

Naturally, the European Union needs to restore relations with Georgia, especially since Georgia is located in that region and used to be a partner of the EU, but is no longer one now.

In this context, I allow that the appeal of the opposition bloc to Ursula von der Leyen is necessary for all the purposes I have mentioned.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Baku-Paris-Moscow: What links French national’s release in Azerbaijan to Russian billionaire’s sanctions relief?
World.content:
Aliyev pardons French citizen

On 23 September, Ilham Aliyev pardoned French citizen Martin Ryan, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for espionage.

A day earlier, the European Union agreed, at France’s request, to remove Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list. According to the Financial Times, citing diplomatic sources, the two decisions form part of an agreement between Baku and Paris on the release of prisoners.

After years of confrontation over issues involving Armenia, Nagorno-Karabakh and France’s overseas territories, Baku and Paris reached an agreement on specific issues: France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan secured the lifting of European sanctions against the billionaire it had supported.

From a 10-year prison sentence to a pardon

The French citizen, identified in the pardon decree as Ryan Martin Richard, has been released from serving the remainder of his sentence. Authorities detained him on 4 December 2023, and on 16 March 2026 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 10 years in prison.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Ryan, the head of Merkorama, was supposed to collect military and other information for France’s Directorate-General for External Security. Paris rejected the allegations. On 30 July, France’s Foreign Ministry condemned the appellate court’s decision to uphold the sentence, called the conviction arbitrary and demanded Ryan’s immediate release.

The 10-year sentence, which the court upheld in July, was therefore brought to an end in September by a presidential decision. Ryan’s fate took a decisive turn not in the courtroom, but as part of diplomatic negotiations over sanctions.

What did Paris do for Usmanov?

On 14 September, the Financial Times reported that France was seeking to have Usmanov removed from the EU sanctions list in exchange for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. Paris and Bratislava called for his sanctions to be lifted and vetoed the extension of the restrictions for another 12 months. The EU initially granted a one-week delay to allow negotiations to continue.

On 22 September, the sides reached a compromise: Mikhail Fridman was also removed from the sanctions list alongside Usmanov, while the remaining individual sanctions were extended for 36 months instead of the previous six. For Usmanov, this means the lifting of the asset freeze and EU travel ban.

The mechanism allowed Baku’s demand to reach the level of European policy. Azerbaijan, as a non-EU country, could not take part in the sanctions decision-making process. However, France’s interest in securing the return of its citizens allowed Paris to pursue this concession within the European Union.

Why is Usmanov important to Baku?

Azerbaijan’s support for Usmanov did not begin in recent days.

On 18 September, a senior Azerbaijani diplomat told Reuters that between November 2023 and March 2025, Baku and other members of the Organisation of Turkic States had sent letters supporting Usmanov to the leaders of the United States and European countries. The diplomat described him as a philanthropist who helps strengthen ties between the West, Central Asia and the Turkic world.

The same diplomat denied reports that Azerbaijan had pressured France. A French Foreign Ministry representative, meanwhile, declined to disclose details, saying the matter concerned national security.

On 21 September, Euronews also reported that Uzbekistan had played a role in reaching the agreement. According to the report, the proposed deal involved releasing two French citizens detained in Azerbaijan in exchange for removing Usmanov from the sanctions list, with Aliyev expected to sign a pardon decree. The EU made its sanctions decision the following day, after which Ryan received a presidential pardon. The events unfolded in the same sequence that Euronews had previously described.

Confrontation from Nagorno-Karabakh to New Caledonia

The political significance of the agreement becomes clearer against the backdrop of relations between Baku and Paris in recent years. France criticised Azerbaijan’s military actions in Nagorno-Karabakh and expanded defence cooperation with Armenia. Baku, in turn, viewed Paris’s military support for Yerevan as interference in the regional balance of power.

Azerbaijan also extended the confrontation to issues sensitive for France itself. The Baku Initiative Group, established in 2023, held events involving supporters of independence for New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Martinique and other territories. Links were established between these movements and Azerbaijani political structures.

When unrest broke out in New Caledonia in May 2024, France accused Baku of interference. Azerbaijan rejected the allegations. Changes to electoral rules and fears among the indigenous Kanak people of losing political influence lay at the heart of the domestic crisis. At the same time, the crisis became a new source of mutual accusations between Baku and Paris.

The current agreement points not so much to a resolution of these disputes as to the sides’ willingness to set them aside in order to achieve specific results. For Paris, the priority was securing the release of its citizen; for Baku, it was securing a decision on Usmanov, whom Azerbaijan had supported for years.

The cost of the concession for Europe

France is not the only party to face political costs from the agreement. Ukraine’s leadership opposed removing oligarchs from the sanctions list. Within the EU, there were also concerns that making exceptions to the bloc’s common sanctions policy for national interests could set a dangerous precedent.

The political outcome of these events is that the release of a prisoner in Baku became part of negotiations over European sanctions against Russia. France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan brought one of the EU’s most influential members into supporting a billionaire backed by Baku. This points more to diplomacy based on mutual concessions under pressure than to a restoration of trust between the two countries.

Aliyev pardons French citizen

World.title: Azerbaijani FM highlights Azerbaijan’s transformation into a key logistics and transit hub (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Minister Jeyhun Bayramov addressed the Twenty-Fifth Annual Ministerial Meeting of Foreign Ministers of Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs) on the sidelines of#UNGA81.

This was stated in a post shared by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on its “X” social media account.

He emphasized that through long-term strategic investments and sustained regional partnerships, Azerbaijan has successfully transformed its landlocked geography into a key logistical, transit, and energy nexus connecting East-West and North-South corridors.

The Minister highlighted the need for transit digitalization, simplified customs procedures, and integrated energy-digital links like the Central Asia–Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor. He stressed that combining transport, energy, and digital infrastructure creates a far more resilient global trade architecture.

Underlining that peace is an indispensable prerequisite for sustainable connectivity, he showcased how the 8 August 2025 Washington agreements between Azerbaijan and Armenia and the TRIPP initiative that will expand regional and global transit networks.

World.title: Azerbaijan and Côte d'Ivoire discuss regional issues (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 24. Azerbaijan and Côte d’Ivoire discussed regional issues during a bilateral meeting today in New York.

This was stated in a post shared by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on its “X” social media account.

The discussions were held during a meeting between Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Jeyhun Bayramov and Côte d’Ivoire’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Niale Kaba on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA81).

“The sides noted the dynamic development of bilateral relations between Azerbaijan and Côte d’Ivoire, emphasizing the important role of interparliamentary ties, high-level visits, and regular political consultations in strengthening both bilateral and multilateral cooperation.

During the discussions, the sides also exchanged views on Azerbaijan’s active participation and chairmanship in international platforms, our expanding partnership with African countries, as well as key regional developments,” the post said.

World.title: Insane catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
World.content:
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an insane catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.

The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.

Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.

After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.

"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."

Mitchell Marsh got Australia's run chase off to a fast start with a rollicking knock of 60, but his departure was followed by a collapse. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.

Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.

He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.

The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.

Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.

The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.

So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.

The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.

Matthew Breetzke's brilliant 112 off just 106 deliveries allowed South Africa to post a score of 8-297 in the first innings. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.

All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.

All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.

The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

AAP

World.title: Sydney's '$78 million question': Why two wharves still have no ferry service
World.content:
It is something Kurnell resident Allison Casey has called the "$78 million question".

Since early last year, two grand ferry wharves have sat on picturesque pieces of headland in Sydney's Kamay Botany Bay National Park ready to welcome boats.

But after a cost blowout of tens of millions of dollars, and two failed attempts to attract a private operator, passengers are still waiting.

It has prompted calls for the NSW government to offer a financial sweetener to any company willing to run a ferry service there.

Passengers are still waiting for a ferry service from the Kamay Wharf at La Perouse. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

"What a lot of the community is asking for is a government-subsidised, or a government-supported ferry, like the one that runs in Bundeena to the Royal National Park … they [the government] haven't offered that support," Ms Casey said.

"I think that's one of the main reasons why we've got wharves that go to nowhere, essentially."

The Kamay Ferry Wharves officially opened in February 2025 at La Perouse in the city's east and Kurnell in the south — areas of cultural significance to the Kamaygal and Gweagal people.

Kurnell Wharf sits metres from Captain Cook's landing place, and both sides of Kamay/Botany Bay hold history of Europeans' early contact with Aboriginal Australians.

Kurnell Wharf is just metres away from Captain Cook's landing place. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

If an operator is found, a ferry trip between the two wharves would take about 20 minutes.

NSW Transport Minister John Graham said the government's latest call for expressions of interest (EOI), which opened earlier this year, had not been a success.

"We got some good information from the market, but we haven't been able to find something that works as a commercial service," he said.

" So it's back to the drawing board. "

The latest effort followed an earlier failed EOI attempt in 2024.

Exploding costs and promises made

Ferries ran between Kurnell and La Perouse for more than 80 years, but that service was brought to a halt in 1974 when severe storms damaged the original wharves.

Ms Casey said bringing back a ferry connection would make a difference for local tourism.

"Essentially, you could walk the coast, jump on the ferry here and then keep walking along the coastline until you get on the ferry at Bundeena, and then continue to walk in the Royal National Park.

"It really is the missing piece of the puzzle."

Ms Casey says a ferry service would attract tourism. (Supplied)

The plan to rebuild the wharves was first announced by the NSW Coalition government in 2018, at a forecast cost of $18 million.

Liberal member for Cronulla, Mark Speakman, said by the time final planning approval was granted in 2023, that figure had grown to $78 million.

"During COVID, costs exploded, including material costs and the engineering costs of building something that would stand rough seas at Kurnell," he said.

"But by that time, we had made the promise to build the wharves."

Some locals are calling for a subsidised service similar to the ferries that go to the Royal National Park. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Ruth Griffiths, a longtime resident of La Perouse's neighbouring Little Bay, was among those who wrote a submission against the wharves in their planning stages.

"There's no reason to go over to the other side from either the north or the south really, other than just for a picnic," she said.

" And that seems a lot of money just to provide picnic trips for people. "

Ms Griffiths said despite recreational vessels also being allowed to use the wharves, she was yet to see anyone taking advantage at La Perouse.

"They say it's great for fishing, but I've never heard anyone say anything else good about it.

"A lot of people aren't against it, but they don't really see any use."

For more than 80 years, ferries operated between Kurnell and La Perouse. (Supplied: NSW government)

'Beautiful wharves without a concrete plan'

Almost all of the project's value had been locked into contracts by the time Labor unseated the Coalition in the 2023 state election.

With the estimated cost of cancelling at least $46 million, the new government said it had been "left with no option" but to proceed with construction.

"They're remarkable wharves, but it really was beautiful wharves without a concrete plan as we came into government," Mr Graham said.

Fisherman can regularly be seen at the wharves. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Action for Public Transport spokesperson Graeme Taylor said he was not surprised the government had been struggling to find an operator.

"It's in a part of Sydney that's not terribly visible for tourists and day trippers, so you would need to promote it heavily," he said.

"The types of fares that a private company would need to charge … might be upwards of eight or nine dollars in each direction, and those sorts of fare levels do discourage patronage."

According to the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal, all private ferry operators in NSW receive some form of subsidy from the state government.

Private ferry operators in NSW receive a subsidy from the state government. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Most are reimbursed the difference if they charge discounted fares for locals, pensioners or students.

Three operators had also recently received a "viability payment", which is designed to keep them figuratively, and literally, afloat.

Mr Taylor noted that buying new ferries to service the Kamay Wharves would likely be out of reach for most companies.

"If you look at the older ferries, they were very simple boats.

"You're not allowed to build like that anymore … the regulations are much stricter around safety, everything has to be alarmed now, [and] you have to have CCTV everywhere," he said.

"It just adds up to an eye-watering cost."

Mr Taylor says safety regulations are much stricter nowdays. (Supplied: NSW government )

Government needs to step in

The Coalition's original plan had only budgeted for the cost of building the wharves themselves.

But Mr Speakman said the state government now needed to step in.

"There's this massive piece of infrastructure sitting there not being used," he said.

"When $78 million has been spent building the wharves, the quantum of government subsidy to have ferries operating is pretty small."

Ms Casey says a ferry service would be a positive for the community. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Ms Casey said despite the lack of ferries for now, the Kamay Wharves had been a "positive addition".

"I know a lot of the community was a bit divided about it, but I love the wharf.

"Having that ferry service run and connecting the sacred Gweagal people, the traditional owners, so the national park can be joined again, would be something that I look forward to seeing."

World.title: What keeps Fremantle's purple army going?
World.content:
In the cold, hard light of day, supporting your favourite footy team is a deeply illogical exercise.

For six months each year, you place your mental health and emotional wellbeing in the hands of 40-50 players who wouldn't know you from a bar of soap.

Some of us have forked out tens of thousands of dollars over the years for the privilege of doing so.

Thirty years of Fremantle membership badges. (Supplied: Ivo Da Silva)

It's questionable enough when it's a side that's delivered decades of success.

But investing such time in an organisation like the Fremantle Football Club often prompts the question: "Why do it to yourself? Why keep coming back each year?"

Sam Tomlin and Ivo Da Silva prior to Fremantle's rain-hit win over Richmond in round 3. (Supplied: Ivo Da Silva)

Ivo Da Silva flies in from Kalgoorlie-Boulder for every home game, while I've driven approximately 15,000 kilometres getting to and from games from my home in the South West.

In a week that's seen thousands of Fremantle supporters cross the state and country for just the second grand final in our history, it's a question the two of us thought we'd attempt to answer.

'From woe to go'

Ivo, born and bred in Fremantle, can present all the required credentials: support for South Fremantle in the WAFL; an education at St Patrick's Primary School and CBC Fremantle.

For me, a product of Perth's northern suburbs, it was sitting in the outer in 1996 with my brother, my dad and my grandad, somehow watching Fremantle completely dismantle Carlton, who were then just months off their 1995 premiership.

Ivo Da Silva and his sister Jacquie Preston outside the MCG on grand final day in 2013. (Supplied: Ivo Da Silva )

Peter Mann at centre half forward? Unstoppable. Scott Chisolm, the prince of pockets? Dynamic. The anchor. The rope crew. I was hooked.

Geraldton's David Shea definitely has the both of us beaten for road miles, routinely driving a 900km round trip over 15 years to get to home games.

"When I take on something, you take it on from woe to go, through the good and the bad, the ups and downs," he said.

Geraldton's Dave Shea has invested years of his life in the Fremantle Dockers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"And there's been plenty of downs, when you're driving home on a Sunday night and you get thrashed and then you meet your fax machine in the morning from all my very good Eagle friends."

David watches more games at home these days, but has turned his house into a beacon for the Dockers.

Dave Shea has transformed parts of his Geraldton home into a shrine for the Dockers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He's apprehensive about tomorrow, but confident that if a win comes, it'll be the start of something special.

"Shut my blue and yellow [West Coast-supporting] mates up," he said.

Dave Shea's "Freo room" features a huge collection of Dockers' memorabilia from over the years. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"We must have three cups for a starter and then four cups and they will get reminded daily if we have one more cup than them."

Further south in Collie, Annette and Steven Annandale are part of a group routinely making the 400km round trip to home games via bus.

Fremantle supporters Annette and Steven Annandale flew out of Busselton Airport for the grand final in Melbourne. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

They were feeling confident as they flew out to Melbourne from Busselton on Thursday.

"I've tipped the Dockers by 15 points, I think it'll be a close game," Steven said, while Annette was anticipating some momentum swings.

"I think the third and fourth quarter will be ours, and we'll come out 16-17 points in front," she predicted.

In these high-pressure situations, superstition also comes to the fore.

Brian Saggers and Bianca Benioni are contemplating matching tattoos if Fremantle win. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Broome father and daughter Brian Saggers and Bianca Benioni were jokingly worried about wife and mum Angie.

"She's been banished from watching Freo games with us for a few years now," Ms Benioni said.

"When she is in the room with us, Freo starts to lose … when we kick her out, Freo wins again," Mr Saggers explained.

The prospect of a Fremantle flag, at a grand final party alongside all their friends and family, has the pair contemplating matching Dockers tattoos.

The little things

It's the moments like these, good and bad, that keep you coming back.

It's that first final in 2003, when the Freo chant rang out in the final quarter despite being down by six goals against Essendon.

It's Jeff Farmer, the one true wizard, kicking a goal after the siren to seal a game against Melbourne.

It's sitting through a wooden spoon season in 2001, only for a young ruck-forward from Koorda named Justin Longmuir to kick five goals against Hawthorn to keep us from going the year winless.

Can now-coach Justin Longmuir deliver a maiden premiership tomorrow? (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

It's Nathan Fyfe going from a skinny kid out of Lake Grace to a superhuman playing some of the most sublime football we've ever seen.

And it's rising as one with the people around you, whether with 15,000 at the WACA, 25,000 at Subiaco or 60,000 at Perth Stadium.

Fremantle supporters line the boundary at the open training session this week. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

For the "Wharfie Time" bell.

Or for those, like Milli Lucas and Cam McCarthy, who are no longer with us.

Faith and belief

But back to 30 years ago, September 1996, when Fremantle hosted Fitzroy's final ever game before their merger with Brisbane.

The rendition of Auld Lang Syne, sung by Perth soprano Sarah Macliver from the roof of the grandstand at Subiaco, still gives me chills when I think about it.

The devastation of the Fitzroy fans there also taught me that, as tough and frustrating as losing can be, having it all ripped away from you is worse.

Loading...

For some Lions supporters, the merger was one betrayal too many, and they walked away from the AFL forever.

Others stuck fast, and have since experienced two eras of unparalleled success, culminating in tomorrow's bid for a second Brisbane three-peat.

Our road since then has had a few more detours, but the faith and belief that the good times will come is hard to shake.

It's surely no coincidence Fremantle coach Gerard Neesham's address to supporters, after his unceremonious 1998 sacking, came to be known as the "Sermon on the Mount".

Supporters chase an autograph from Luke Jackson. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"The best steel is made in the hottest furnace," he told supporters gathered in the outer at Subiaco.

Keep the faith, in other words, and the rewards will follow.

What happens tomorrow? The heart says Freo. That's all that matters; logic has no place here.

What I can guarantee is that we'll all be back for more next year.

It's what we do.

Additional reporting by Natasha Harradine, Chris Lewis, Neve Brissenden and Natasha Clark.

World.title: Fiji's HIV epidemic is surging and babies are paying the price
World.content:
Berenadeta* was 23 when she tested positive for HIV.

She had lost weight and discovered boils that wouldn't go away.

She suspected she'd picked up an infection, one that was likely sexually transmitted.

Her father told her not to panic, suggesting she visit the sexual health clinic near where she lived.

"They tested me three times, and all came up positive," she said.

" I had to accept it. "

But the same visit uncovered something else she didn't know — she was three months pregnant.

Berenadeta found out she was three months pregnant on the same visit she tested positive for HIV. (ABC News)

Her partner, who was also HIV-positive, had been on tablets to suppress the virus, but had stopped taking them and hadn't told her.

Berenadeta's father advised her not to blame herself or her partner, telling her the virus could be managed with medication.

But her wellbeing wasn't her only concern.

"That's the only thing I was curious about, was the baby's result, not mine," she said.

Her medication consisted of one tablet a day, which she never missed.

The antiretroviral tablet suppresses the virus to a level that protects the mother's own health and reduces the risk of passing it on to their baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

Berenadeta's medication consisted of one tablet a day, which she never missed. (Getty Images: Michel Lunanga)

When Berenadeta gave birth months later, doctors found no sign of the virus in her baby.

"When the result came out, they told me it's negative. I was so happy," she said.

Since then, Berenadeta, now 25 years old, has had a second child and is pregnant with her third.

Watch the episode The Pacific goes inside Fiji’s growing HIV emergency where as many as 1 in 60 adults now have the virus.

The ABC has changed her name and masked her identity to protect her from the social stigma involved with being HIV-positive in Fiji.

The young mother has bottle-fed both her children on medical advice and kept them safe from the virus.

But others haven't been as lucky.

Last year, 59 babies were born with HIV at Fiji's largest hospital, 18 of which died before their first birthday.

Colonial Memorial Hospital is Fiji's largest hospital. (Supplied: Australian High Commission Fiji)

They were born to pregnant women living with HIV, many of whom weren't taking medication out of fear of being stigmatised.

National infection rates meanwhile are skyrocketing, with new statistics showing one in 60 adults are living with the virus.

Five years ago it was one in 167 people.

The crisis has prompted Fiji's government to declare a national HIV emergency, with officials predicting it would take "upwards of five years" to bring the epidemic under control.

Growing crisis

According to Fiji government figures, 2,016 people were diagnosed with HIV in 2025, representing a 27 per cent increase in positive cases from the previous year.

UNAIDS estimated that 9,100 Fijians were living with HIV last year and only 39 per cent knew their status.

Transmission between mothers and babies is also on the rise.

Priya Kaur, who leads Fiji's work on eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, said the 59 babies who tested positive in 2025 was the highest number in a single year.

Priya Kaur is Fiji's national lead for elimination of mother-to-child transmission. (ABC News)

"They were born to about 332 women who were pregnant and had HIV infection," she said

"That puts a vertical transmission rate at 18 per cent."

Vertical transmission is the term used when HIV passes from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.

The World Health Organization's recommended rate is below 5 per cent where mothers breastfeed, and below 2 per cent where they do not.

Behind Fiji's sun and sand, this is the dark side of the islands Almost a million tourists come to Fiji every year. But behind the sun and sand, there's a dark side to the islands, with cartels using Fiji to import drugs into lucrative markets — a drug problem that has now spread into communities.

Dr Kaur said Fiji's high transmission rates were preventable because HIV testing and treatment were free to access.

"If you are positive, go on treatment and your children will be negative," she said.

But many people aren't taking the medicine.

Social stigma

Nationally, only 22 per cent of people living with HIV are receiving antiretroviral treatment.

This means many people with HIV are unable to suppress the virus to a level that protects themselves and any baby they might be carrying.

A computer illustration of the HIV virus infecting human embryo. The embryo is eight weeks old. (AFP)

Berenadeta, who is due to give birth to her third child early next year, said accessing treatment was not always easy.

She said for many HIV-positive women, it could require multiple consultations and transportation costs.

"You have your first check-up, and then you go back home, and you are coming back in a week or two, provided you have bus fare to come and your husband has given you money and you don't have four other children to look after at home," she said.

Privacy and confidentiality are also issues.

In the antenatal clinic at Fiji's largest hospital, one-on-one counselling takes place in booths that seat four or five women next to each other.

Dr Kaur says the lack of privacy in hospital counselling booths can deter women living with HIV from seeking treatment. (Supplied)

The booths are divided by a partition, but Dr Kaur said much of what was said could be overheard by the person next to them.

She said the lack of privacy could deter women living with HIV from seeking treatment or getting tested because of the risk of being exposed.

Privacy can also be an issue at home, where it's common for women to live with relatives.

A bottle of tablets can invite unwanted questions from aunties, cousins, in-laws and grandparents, discouraging women from taking treatment and placing their babies at risk of infection.

"They don't want the other family members to know that they are taking this particular medication," Dr Kaur said.

Lethal injection

Stigma and a lack of privacy are not the only barriers driving Fiji's HIV crisis.

About half of all new infections are due to intravenous drug use, mainly methamphetamine, while the other half were linked to sexual transmission.

Fiji health authorities are rolling out more public messages raising awareness of HIV. (ABC News: Sairusi Tabualuma)

Much of it arrives in Fiji through international drug traffickers, who use Fiji as a transit point to access lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand.

For many people who inject drugs, there is no easy, anonymous way to access clean needles.

Fiji sex worker Nora, who chose not to give her real name, said she contracted HIV after sharing a needle with her cousin.

'Bluetoothing': The shocking new trend fuelling HIV in Fiji Health authorities are scrambling to stem an HIV outbreak in Fiji, where alarming needle-sharing trends have accelerated the spread of the virus.

She said many drug users shared needles and were unaware of the dangers.

"We just do it, and then wash it with the water, and then pass it to somebody else to use it," she said.

Fiji's government recently announced plans to introduce a needle and syringe program (NSP) as part of its response to the growing epidemic.

The program, which is used in more than 90 countries, will make sterile needles and syringes available to people who use drugs to reduce the risk of HIV transmission.

Meanwhile, a national sexual and reproductive health and HIV unit was created 18 months ago, and HIV testing is moving out of laboratories and onto cartridges, similar to the way COVID-19 tests work.

HIV testing is moving out of laboratories and onto cartridges, similar to the way COVID-19 tests work. (AFP)

Dr Kaur said a national list of HIV positive mothers had been developed so their treatment could be monitored.

"We know who they are, where they are, what phone numbers they have," Dr Kaur said.

"We go to that extent to look for them if they have missed clinic [appointments]."

World.title: Live: Albanese to urge world leaders to band together on AI
World.content:
An unprecedented breach of a government website by a rogue OpenAI agent will sharpen Australia's push to impose stricter safety, transparency and reporting requirements on artificial intelligence companies.

Findings from a "rapid" forensic investigation into the incident will feed into the federal government's existing work to develop national AI standards governing how the technology operates in Australia.

Despite resistance from the Trump administration, Australia will impose "guardrails" on AI, with Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton declaring tech companies should not unleash unsafe models.

"I think what we're observing at the moment is that a number of the AI models … that they have inside their companies are not safe and they have a lot more work to do to make them safe before they release them to the public," he told the ABC.
