Tips & adviceKnow how The Mexican chef’s guide to making excellent nachos at home With a few small tweaks to what you’re probably already doing, you can take your nacho game to the next level. Dani Valent September 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As homemade snacks and easy meals go, there aren’t many that beat nachos. They cover a few food groups, they’re gluten-free, you can proteinmaxx them, there’s melted cheese involved, and you can eat them with one hand while watching the footy on TV. So what are the nachos basics and are there any hacks or rules? Nachos from Hotel Mexico. Chris Hopkins Are nachos Mexican? They were invented in the northern Mexico town of Piedras Negras in 1943 by a waiter called Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya. A gaggle of US Army wives descended on his restaurant before the chef arrived, and Nacho threw together a baked tortilla dish from ingredients he had to hand. The women approved and took the dish across the border where it was amped up, becoming a Tex-Mex staple and baseball game essential. “We do eat nachos in Mexico,” says Luis Sanchez, chef at Hotel Mexico in Yarraville in Melbourne’s inner west. “They’re usually simpler than the Tex-Mex versions, with just cheese, pickled jalapeno and chipotle mayo. We put them in the centre of the table at the start of a meal. For us, nachos means family and sharing.”



1 / 5 Use a mix of coloured corn chips for flavour variation and for aesthetics. Chris Hopkins 2 / 5 Scatter nachos with lots of grated mozzarella cheese. Photograph by Chris Hopkins 3 / 5 Melting the mozzarella cheese on the grill at Hotel Mexico. Chris Hopkins 4 / 5 Load with pickled jalapeno slices and sour cream. Photograph by Chris Hopkins 5 / 5 Don’t forget the salsa and guacamole! Chris Hopkins Previous Slide Next Slide The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up How does a Mexican chef make them in Melbourne? Freshly fried tortilla triangles (a mix of yellow and blue corn) are placed in a bowl, then scattered with grated mozzarella cheese before being melted under a grill. The oozy mess is loaded with guacamole, pico de gallo (tomato salsa), pickled jalapeno slices, sour cream and fresh coriander. “We put Mexican ingredients on it so we could say it’s more Mexican than anything else,” says the chef, who is from Puebla, south-east of Mexico City. There’s the option to load up with meat too. “You can turn our nachos into a meal by adding chorizo, chicken, birria or a vegetarian version with mushrooms,” he says.



Your nachos are served! Chris Hopkins What are the shortcuts? You can buy corn chips instead of frying tortillas but you should still use a mix of white corn and blue corn for flavour variation – and because it looks cool. Any melting cheese can be substituted for mozzarella. There are plenty of good jarred salsas, but if you want to make your own, it’s just finely chopped tomato, onion, coriander, lime juice and pickled jalapenos. Guacamole is worth making yourself – at its simplest, it’s just avo, lime juice, salt and pepper – but you can use a store-bought version too. Dorilocos is a Mexican street food served in the Doritos bag. iStock



Is there anything else I could try? “Nachos are getting popular in Mexico and changing a little bit,” says Sanchez. In his central region, dorilocos or tostilocos (“crazy corn chips”) are street food that you can modify as desired. Often made directly inside a cut-open bag of Doritos or Tostitos, they’re loaded with ingredients such as roasted peanuts, white corn kernels, pickled pork rind, fresh carrot and cucumber, and chamoy (a pickled fruit condiment) or Salsa Valentina, a bottled hot sauce. In northern coastal parts of Mexico, baked tortilla chips are sometimes topped with seafood, such as garlic shrimp or crab. In summary, go forth and mod your nachos. I’m thinking chilli crisp … Related Article EASY Adam Liaw’s jalapeno guacamole < 30 mins Related Article EASY Mexican salsa < 30 mins Related Recipe collection Mexican recipes: tacos, burritos, fajitas, nachos and more

World.title: Police officer killed in Redfern crash
World.content:
A police officer has been killed and another hospitalised in an early morning crash in inner Sydney. The female constable was a passenger in a fully marked police vehicle travelling under lights and sirens along Gibbons Street, Redfern, when it crashed into a tree about 1.30am on Friday. She died instantly, police said. Police comfort one another after a female constable died in a crash in inner Sydney. TNV The female constable died instantly, police said. TNV A male constable – the driver – has been taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in a stable condition.



Officers were seen hugging and comforting each other at the scene, about 100 metres from Redfern police station. “It’s just a tragic day for all police in NSW where two young officers were doing their job as police across the state do 24/7,” Police Association of NSW president Kevin Morton said. Premier Chris Minns said it was devastating news. “My thoughts are with the family, friends and colleagues of the officer who has lost her life,” Minns said. “Every day our police officers put themselves in harm’s way to keep the rest of us safe, and today the entire NSW police family will be grieving.



“I’m also thinking of the officer injured in the crash and everyone who responded to this terrible scene.” A male constable was also taken to hospital. TNV NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said police officers dedicates themselves to looking after others. “Today the NSW Police family is mourning one of its own,” Catley said. “My heart is with her family, her loved ones and her colleagues on this dark day.”



Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she was heartbroken. “She was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community,” Sloane said. “Our police put themselves in harm’s way every day to protect us. Today, we stand with them as they mourn one of their own.” A crime scene has been established and a critical incident has been declared. Detectives have removed several bags of evidence from the crash site. Police at the scene in Redfern where a NSW Police officer died after the fully marked vehicle she was a passenger in crashed into a tree. A male constable driving the car has been hospitalised. Riley Walter



A large section of Gibbons Street, where the crash occurred, down to Cleveland Street, remains closed as crash investigators examine the scene. Regent Street is closed in both directions north of Lawson Street. Wyndham Street has also been closed. Bus routes are being diverted and motorists are advised to avoid the area as the police investigation is expected to take some time. More to come Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Children pay the price’: Child safety workers to walk off job, citing ‘mismanagement’
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government ‘Children pay the price’: Child safety workers to walk off job, citing ‘mismanagement’ Julius Dennis September 25, 2026 — 7:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of child safety workers will walk off the job today to protest outside the offices of local MPs, as their union continues to scrap with the government over pay and conditions, and officers complain of caseloads that double the safe amount. The Together Union, which represents the workers, said more than 100 child safety officer positions remain vacant around the state, and the government has engaged in a quasi hiring freeze. The union claimed there were also at least 60 youth justice jobs empty. Loading As of March, there were 2819 children in residential care, a 25 per cent jump from the same time in 2025.



Together assistant secretary Dee Spink said workers were pushed to the brink, and it was taking a toll on the children under their care. “We keep coming back to the same basic question: how much time does a child safety officer actually have for each child?” Spink said. “When a worker is responsible for 30 children instead of 16, when experienced staff are leaving and vacancies can’t be filled, and when workers are staying back late because there is nowhere safe for a child to go, children pay the price.” The workers will strike for 2½ hours on Friday afternoon, carrying blow-up mattresses to MPs’ offices to represent reports of children in state care sleeping on the ground of government offices when they cannot be placed somewhere safe. The union has been undertaking protected action since early August, and claim they have been left without a clear minister with whom to work through issues, while Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has been on six weeks of leave.



Finance minister Ros Bates has been backfilling the child safety portfolio during Camm’s leave, but Spink said it was unclear if she had the authority to sign a new deal. Related Article Child safety Labour hire firm had six child safety complaints in mandatory scheme’s first month “That is not good enough for a child safety system already under enormous pressure. The mismanagement needs to stop,” Spink said. “Our members have given the government every opportunity to act before reaching this point. Now workers are going to their local MPs because every MP should understand what is happening in the child protection and youth justice systems in their community.” The union had previously raised concerns about vacant positions not deemed “key frontline” needing approval from the deputy director-general to be filled.



In particular, Spink said business and administrative roles in child safety centres, key to supporting frontline officers, were being left unfilled. “These roles are critical to frontline child protections, and they should be treated as critical workers when it comes time to fill them,” she said. “The department says this isn’t a recruitment freeze, but for some workers it can feel like one.” A department spokesperson said the plan was part of efforts to balance the books and all vacancies were weighed against workforce needs. World.title: ASX set to retreat after shaky day on Wall Street
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to retreat after shaky day on Wall Street Stan Choe Updated September 25, 2026 — 6:34am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After whipping through a couple sudden reversals, stocks ended a shaky day of trading on Wall Street roughly where they began. The S&P 500 finished nearly flat and edged down by less than 0.1 per cent following several turns between losses and gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added less than 0.1 per cent. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to slide, with futures at 6.18am AEST pointing to a loss of 32 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.7 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.12¢. Stocks have slowed their rally since the S&P 500 climbed to the brink of its all-time high earlier this week as pressure from the bond market has cranked higher.



Related Article Opinion

Weight loss How McDonald’s is grappling with the Ozempic boom Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.20 per cent from 5.11 per cent late Wednesday and is back to where it was in 2007. High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive to borrow money, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Yields climbed through the morning, which pushed stocks downward, until they took a sudden turn lower in the midday hours. The 10-year yield dropped from nearly 5.17 per cent to less than 5.13 per cent in about 20 minutes before ultimately turning higher again. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude in the most actively traded part of the market went from $US102 to roughly $US99 in a matter of minutes midday Thursday. It later rose to settle at $US100.22, up 2.1 per cent from the prior day.



It’s not just worries about expensive oil and inflation that have sent Treasury yields higher. The US economy continues to expand, which also supports yields. On Thursday, a report showed fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week and further strengthened expectations for the economy. Such numbers could convince the Federal Reserve that the economy can withstand more hikes to short-term interest rates. The Fed raised its main interest rate last week for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the economy and removing some of the fuel for inflation. Traders now see better than a coin flip’s chance that the Fed could raise rates twice more by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. So far, the solid overall economy has helped US companies continue to deliver strong growth in profits. That in turn has helped their stock prices remain relatively strong despite worries about war, inflation and tariffs.



“The headlines have turned more ominous, but the underlying drivers of growth remain intact,” strategists at Barclays wrote in a report. “As long as AI-related investment, US corporate profitability, and consumer spending continue to beat expectations, the economy and markets seem capable of absorbing tighter central banks and higher rates.” Stitch Fix became one of the latest US companies late Wednesday to report better quarterly results than analysts expected. But its stock nevertheless tumbled 21.6 per cent after it said “a more challenging consumer environment” could hold back its revenue growth this upcoming fiscal year. Related Article Opinion

World markets The Trump effect: Why cracks are widening in financial markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse, fell 3 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter that matched analysts’ expectations. High yields in the bond market hurt prices for all kinds of stocks, and they often hit hardest on those seen as the most expensive. That puts the target on AI stocks, which soared for years in the frenzy around the technology.



Higher yields also make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build AI data centers, which could slow their construction and restrain demand for AI chips. Nvidia slipped 0.4 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. On the winning side of Wall Street was Everpure. The data storage and management company’s stock jumped 11.2 per cent after it stood by its financial forecasts for this fiscal year and said it expects revenue growth to accelerate in the following one. All told, the S&P 500 fell 1.90 to 7,704.13 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161.61 to 51,349.98, and the Nasdaq composite rose 3.34 to 26,939.37. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell modestly around much of the world. A drop of 1.2 per cent in Shanghai and gain of 0.8 per cent in Tokyo were two of the bigger moves.

World.title: The Sam Walker files: Why the NRL’s greatest minds love this one-man mystery
World.content:
Sam Walker: a sight to behold in the eyes of rugby league’s best modern halves.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Johnathan Thurston lets loose that trademark machine-gun cackle. Then lets slip a dirty little secret. Sam Walker isn’t quite the mercurial, playmaking version of a small dog chasing cars in the street. “And I got that sense very early on from watching Sammy,” one of the greatest halfbacks of all time says. “It’s not like he goes out there and plays everything off the cuff at all. It just looks like it.” Daly Cherry-Evans has played 377 NRL games, and would have had as many teammates, too. None have read the game like his latest, and last, NRL halves partner. Andrew Johns hasn’t seen a halfback from the same mould as Walker in 15 years.



In total, the champion playmakers the Herald canvassed boast more than 1500 games of NRL experience between them, along with 14 premierships, 109 Origins and 124 Test matches. And they all agree. Sam Walker – who will make a remarkable 27-day recovery from a syndesmosis injury to take on the Dolphins in Friday night’s grand final qualifier – is a playmaker unlike any other. Organised chaos: Breaking down the beauty in Sam’s game Eyes always on the prize: Roosters half Sam Walker watches a conversion attempt sail toward the uprights against Newcastle. NRL Imagery Ben Walker is the old playmaker who knows Sam best. Though Ben’s own two grand final wins in those all-conquering Broncos outfits of the late 1990s and successful Queensland coaching career pale next to his efforts as a family man and father. Especially when he welcomes you into his favourite father-son catch-up with one of the NRL’s best halfbacks. “The beauty of being able to talk to him after a game is asking what he saw in a moment before executing a pass or a kick,” Ben explains.



“And I know the way he plays looks a bit chaotic and off the cuff, but those explanations of, ‘I know this defender has a habit of turning in on this play’, or, ‘The fullback can drift too far across field late in a half’ – that’s where you learn he’s far more considered and more calculating than people would think. “He’s certainly more methodical than most halfbacks that I’ve come across or coached, and I played with some great ones. He’d do it as a kid, too. Friday night footy at home, we’d be forever pausing, rewinding, asking why a play had happened or analysing it. “So those big highlight plays, most times I’d say he would have been thinking about that well before the game during the week, if not two weeks beforehand.” For Thurston, one skinny, silky and supremely skilled halfback can see another working out how to thrive, not just survive, in a sport of car-crash collisions with a Steeden pinballing about in the middle. “I got the sense he knew how to handle a rushing defensive line, mostly because he had to,” Thurston says of his early encounters with Walker in his junior representative days.



“Sam’s quite comfortable in that uncomfortable space – when you’re digging deep into the line with the ball, he can react to the defence, make a good decision, knowing he could get whacked. “You learn how to adapt to that. Because when you’re the smallest player on the field, you just have to.” Johns, meanwhile, adores the risk-taker in Walker. The last-bob gambler who will take those calculations and considerations – all those weeks, months and years of pre-game legwork – and still try something most players wouldn’t dare dream of. Like the cross-field, 50-metre kick that landed smack bang on the chest of Daniel Tupou against the Warriors in 2024. “No one has played the game anything like the way Sam does – he treats the NRL and Origin like his own backyard,” Johns says. “The closest I have seen is Alfie Langer, and they’re so similar in so many ways: risk-taking, impulsive, attacking halves. He’s just a breath of fresh air.”



Especially so for Cherry-Evans, who will line up alongside Walker at Suncorp Stadium on Friday night, knowing he may have only 80 minutes left in the NRL after 16 years at the top level. How two of the game’s great freewheeling halves would combine and conduct Trent Robinson’s small galaxy of attacking stars posed one of this season’s curliest questions. Cherry-Evans’ signing at Bondi brought scrutiny on both sides of the scrum base. Happy halves: Daly Cherry-Evans and Sam Walker. NRL Imagery “I might be the senior half in the combination,” Cherry-Evans says, “but I really love listening to Sam talk about footy. And what he sees in the game, I’d say it’s a bit different to anyone else I’ve come across. “I’ve definitely learned things from him this year and considered things I probably never would have because the way he approaches the game is so unique. It’s the little things he sees, and they’ll stay in-house, but I’ll take them with me as a playmaker, for sure.” Those who encounter Walker, 24, around Roosters HQ, or his and Langer’s old Norths Tigers stomping ground, notice two things: the ready smile, and seemingly never too far behind, a ready Steeden. A perusal of photos from any pre-game scene shows the No.7 with football seemingly glued to his hands. Johns notes: “Sam will carry and pass with his left hand, but kick long with his right foot, and kick short with his left and right. I haven’t seen too many players ever with that much skill.”

World.title: ‘I’d feel ill after interviews because I said too much’: How Julia Jacklin eased into her new gem
World.content:
‘If you brace against time, your life is just so much harder’: .Julia Jacklin loosens up on new album The Gem.

Out of contract and flush with time, Julia Jacklin – one of Australia’s most celebrated songwriters – decamped to a pub for her new album.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s very possible Julia Jacklin has watched Looking For Alibrandi more than any other person in the world. While crammed in a small Collingwood studio making her fourth album The Gem, Jacklin and producer Robert Muinos would sit and fiddle with recordings while Pia Miranda’s Josephine Alibrandi flitted on a TV screen stuck near the mixing desk. “I would be scared to know how many times we watched [that film],” Jacklin says with a smile, sipping tea in a hotel lobby bar in Sydney’s Surry Hills. Serendipitously, the film played in cinemas as part of its 25th anniversary celebrations while the band was recording; Jacklin and Muinos went to a screening and snapped a photo with actor Kick Gurry, who played Alibrandi’s love interest Jacob Coote. “I never ask people for photos,” Jacklin laughs. “He was in the bar area, and I was like ‘I have to get a photo’. I’ve seen that movie a thousand times, and it’s a perfect movie … We either watched that or The Muppet Christmas Carol.” If recording for The Gem sounds low-key, that’s because it was. After three acclaimed records recorded in various studios around the world – Don’t Let the Kids Win (2016), Crushing (2019), and Pre Pleasure (2022) – Jacklin wanted to embed herself in her beloved Melbourne, which she’s called home since moving from Sydney in 2017. Jacklin, one of Australia’s most celebrated contemporary songwriters, was also out of contract with her label for the first time in her career, allowing her precious time to look around and find a place to whittle away at a new record. She settled on a pub called The Gem.



Located in Collingwood, The Gem is a local institution filled with quirky decor and a devoted local crew who will pile in to push the furniture against the walls so bands can play in the corner. When Jacklin first moved to the city, she became a regular. Handily, Muinos’ Rat Shack studio is right above The Gem, a small but mighty space with a piano packed in the old laundry and a constant drip coming from the ceiling. Jacklin completely loved it. “We had to ask the kitchen staff if they wouldn’t mind turning down the radio when we were doing a vocal take,” Jacklin says. “We had to think about the neighbours if we were going to do a drum take. We had to just ask people not to walk down the hall [sometimes] ... It was really tight. Some of my most favourite memories of recording music are from that little room, just all playing together.” Julia Jacklin outside The Gem, the Collingwood pub that inspired her new album. The ramshackle room also afforded Jacklin the environment to make the album she truly wanted to make. Her last album, Pre Pleasure, was a rich mix of orchestral and electronic elements. For The Gem, she wanted to strip back those elements and pursue something lo-fi, like some of her favourite records by Gillian Welch and Emmylou Harris. “Sometimes you can get into this headspace of like, ‘Oh, but I’m not allowed to make a record like that’,” she says. “That ‘I’m not good enough to do something that’s lo-fi.’ It’s hard to explain… I love Pre Pleasure, but I thought I had to elevate the production so it was a very different process. Whereas with this one, I allowed myself to make something that I actually enjoy listening to and gave myself the permission to not feel like I needed each record to go up in production standards.” It was also the longest time Jacklin has spent recording an album, stretching over a year and a half. She would turn up to the studio – waving hello to the hairdresser and tattooist that also worked above the pub – and get to work. “It felt like I was in the world while making music instead of tucked away in a hidden studio, which is usually how it goes,” she says.



The Gem sounds alive and live, like you’re hanging in that cramped laundry while someone hammers on the piano right next to you. There are lovely intrusions of the outside world – some street noise and sirens waft through the mic on certain tracks – and each instrument feels physical and near; you hear the scratches of nails on guitar strings and fretboards, you hear the full reaches of Jacklin’s distinctive, warm voice. Lyrically, Jacklin has dug deeper into her constant study of love and relationships, how they can support and clash with personal liberation. God, or the idea of an omnipotent being (another lifelong theme throughout her work), is also present on The Gem. “My use of God is not in any way tied to a Christian God,” she says, slowly picking her way through her sentences. “On this record in particular, I think I’m using God as a metaphor for having the ability to have more knowledge and power than I can have as a human being with my two feet on earth … and feeling so frustrated by the limitations of that. “In particular,” she continues, “If I Had the Hand of God is about how intense this job can be and how much it takes me away from my family, my life at home, for a majority of my adult life. Because it’s all-encompassing when you’re doing it … It’s truly just very relentless. ‘I was actually talking to people in my life through interviews. You’re just desperately trying to be understood.’ “An album cycle can last for two years. As you get older, you can come out of a two-year album cycle and be like, ‘Oh my God, this person had a baby. This person’s been really struggling with something, but they didn’t tell me about it because they didn’t want to stress me out because I’m doing this’. “I’ve gotten better at it, but I have found it quite difficult to do this work that I do feel services people in many ways. I do believe that I’m doing something good with my life, and I am communicating with people and helping myself and therefore others feel. But it means that you also can’t be the best person at home, which I’ve always struggled with.”



We’re meeting in the middle of a busy promotion schedule for The Gem. Jacklin would be the first to admit she’s not necessarily comfortable with press and promotion – particularly during this album cycle when nearly every interview is filmed and clipped to become short-form content. The somewhat grim reality of having to sell a product – herself and her work – weighs on her mind. But certain things have become easier over the years. “I think when I was younger, I was so desperate to be understood,” she says. “So then sometimes the press cycle would actually seem like this way to talk about myself. If I was being really honest, I think a lot of the time I was actually talking to people in my life through interviews. You’re just desperately trying to be understood constantly … I used to feel ill [after interviews] because I would’ve said too much, I would’ve given too much away, because it felt good in the moment. “The thing is I love music journalism,” she continues a bit later on. “I’m genuinely so passionate about it and I’m not one of those people that talk shit about Pitchfork, for example … I love that people take what we do seriously enough to write about it and to interrogate it. That’s the biggest compliment and it’s such an important part of such a symbiotic relationship of art.” Aside from a new album, 2026 also marks the 10-year anniversary of Jacklin’s debut album, Don’t Let The Kids Win. It’s been on her mind today, in fact, while driving past her old school and university. “I played [the title track] recently and one of the verses choked me up that used to not choke me up,” she says, smiling. “Things have happened in my life since I wrote it that made one of the things I was talking about feel a lot more intense … I don’t think I even fully understood it, but I was able to articulate that you never get used to time passing. If you brace against time, your life is just so much harder. You just have to relax in whatever way you can.” Julia Jacklin’s The Gem is out now. Jacklin performs at the album’s namesake, The Gem in Collingwood in Melbourne, on Saturday and Sunday.

World.title: After two days with Evonne Goolagong Cawley, I couldn’t help but text her one final question
World.content:
Not only that but she was a transcendent joy within the sport – a player of legendary lightness, more poetic than prosaic. She did not storm the court, they said, but danced across it, more ballerina than baseliner. Study her closely and Evonne Goolagong Cawley begins to feel like an inexorable sporting truth – an Australian athletic exemplar and source of immense Aboriginal pride.

Card after card came and there was no escaping her exploits, which is no surprise once you take an even cursory glance at the gravity of her career. Eighty-six titles. Eighteen Grand Slam singles finals. Female world No. 1 in 1976. Australian of the Year in 1971.

Who was the first mother to win a Wimbledon singles title in the open era, achieving the feat in 1980, 66 years after Dorothea Lambert Chambers? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Holding the Wimbledon trophy in 1971 after winning the first all-Australian women’s singles final in straight sets against defending champion Margaret Court.

Who was the first Indigenous woman to win Wimbledon , in a career featuring seven Grand Slam singles titles? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

I was playing Trivial Pursuit at the time – specifically, a sun-weathered 1980s edition – and between sips of Singha and tom yum goong, it became unmistakably clear that the Australian tennis legend was my key to victory. Time and again, whether going for an orange wedge (sport and leisure) or a yellow one (history), “Evonne Goolagong Cawley” was the correct answer. I can’t remember the exact questions but her name – that instantly recognisable and unforgettable name – just kept coming up.

One magical muggy night, many moons ago, under the thatched roof of a beachfront backpacker bar on a quiet island off the coast of Thailand, I came to understand the fulsome greatness of Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who takes me into her home and laughs and laughs and laughs – joyously and uproariously – 47 times (by my count) over the course of three hours? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who says hello at the front gate wearing a blue linen shirt and colourful sheer skirt, with wavy brown hair framing a face of ineffable vitality? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Scoff if you will, dear reader, but I am here to tell you that I won that game, and handsomely so. And now, many moons later, I am in another beautiful, humid setting, approaching a modest suburban house near Noosa, to interview this tennis icon, cultural heroine and national treasure (not to mention trivia hack) – to ask new questions and see if she is still the answer.

As that Trivial Pursuit game edged closer to the death and the stars above Koh Chang came to life, whenever a question started with “Who” and I didn’t know the answer, I found myself blurting out “Evonne Goolagong Cawley!” (Related note: for questions starting with “Which”, I recommend answering “Battle of the Bulge”, and for questions starting with “What”, always consider “Coca-Cola”.)

Who played in the singles final of the Australian Open seven years in a row throughout the 1970s, winning four titles? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who is the only tennis player in history to defeat Margaret Court, Billie Jean King, Martina Navratilova and Chris Evert, all in Grand Slam finals? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

“Mum would always say, ‘Bye, have a lovely day!’ And then when I came back she would say, ‘Did you have a lovely day?’, because that’s what concerned her,” says Evonne. “She never asked how I’d played, and that followed me throughout my career – making sure you have fun.”

For the moment I want to go back to her Mum and Dad, Melinda and Kenny, and what Evonne got from them. Her dad, she says, was a very hard worker, which is how he ended up in the Riverina wheat-belt town of Barellan. He was a crack shearer and car- tinkerer – the great warm sun watching over his family. Her mum, meanwhile, was their placid moon – the type of person who strummed the guitar and sang her eight children to sleep every night. Every morning, she taught little Evonne perhaps the most important lesson of her life.

It’s been raining , and so everything outside has that luscious and alive feeling, but it’s damp, too, so we sit at the dining table off her open-plan kitchen and lounge. Evonne faces away from the window, chunky sunglasses handy, just in case the light becomes too much. We’ll discuss why later, along with the reason the love of her life, Roger Cawley, 76, is in an electric wheelchair, with a pair of walking sticks for getting up and down.

And who has something important to say – something to share about life, and love, and the universe – after 75 years on this planet, 51 of them married to the same lovely man?

Who is somewhat hobbled by health issues these days, yet unwaveringly pragmatic and unrelentingly positive? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

The best way to describe her play? Maybe with one of those five-dollar words that grizzled sports editors hate: insouciance. She had a legendary lightness, rarely seen since, but echoed in the proprioceptive balance of someone like Roger Federer. He was famous for that same poised, one-handed backhand (with heavy topspin). Evonne spotted the resemblance immediately. “Watching him turn his shoulder, and go over and up, I’d think, ‘Ooooh, that must have felt gooood,’ ” she says, laughing, “with that complete, fluid follow-through.”

When the ball connected with my racquet , she writes, I felt connected to everything: the court below me, the sky above me and the world around me. It was an almost spiritual experience.

The article became a treasured keepsake but also a self-fulfilling prophecy, daring her to learn the formalities and intricacies of the game, then master them. Her resulting playing style was characterised by fluid strokes, ethereal touch and graceful movement. Not for nothing did she earn the nickname “Sunshine Supergirl”.

Inspiration came next, after a trip to the Barellan General Store, where she picked up a copy of Princess magazine, featuring a fairytale about a young tennis player who wins fame and fortune at a prestigious tournament in England. The place sounded so magical that I thought it must be make-believe , she writes in her new book, Only Ever Evonne (out September 29). When I found out Wimbledon was a real place in London, I was blown away.

She was two years old when she found an old tennis ball, tattered and dirty, somewhere underneath the back seat of a junker her dad was working on in the front yard, but that ball became a treasure and totem – a magical object she squeezed for comfort. “I wonder if squeezing it strengthened my hand at an early age?” she ponders. “Later on, Dad cut a handle out of a piece of wood from an apple crate, and I used it to hit that ball against the house walls and the water tank.”

What stands out in her mind from that place and time isn’t golden fields, but the rivers that snaked through the region, from the Murray to the Murrumbidgee, and the fun her family had swimming and fishing. “Isn’t it funny, the detail that sticks out in your brain?” says Evonne, smiling. “I see the gum leaves touching the water, and sending out ripples.”

But working with him meant leaving home and boarding with his family in Sydney, where Evonne was shy and homesick, yet could at least test herself in serious junior tennis tournaments. She started living there temporarily at 11, and cried every night in those first weeks.

“The good points about him?” she says. “He was a very good coach. I really understood his directions.”

That coach, of course, was Victor Edwards. Anyone who has seen the three-part ABC miniseries Goolagong will recognise the pivotal part “Mr Edwards” played in her story. Her first impression of him, from when she was nine years old, was of a tall man wearing a white V-neck jumper and cream slacks, who looked and sounded “immaculate”.

“I never watched myself,” she points out. “That goes back to what my coach used to say, ‘Don’t believe in what you read, believe in yourself.’ I carried that with me, too.”

She remembers little about specific points, games, matches or sets, but knows exactly what it felt like in that state of flow. “I just remember the ball looked this big,” she says, holding her hands around an imaginary sphere the size of a human head, “and the line seemed so fat and wide,” her hands apart like she’s lifting a toaster. “There was no noise, and a feeling of complete slow motion. I just had so much time, and then I would hear the noise of the point finishing, with a winner.”

“The one thing that kept me going was that I just loved playing tennis. I loved it enough never to tell Mum that I cried every night, or any other thing that happened with my coach,” she says, pausing. “Basically, he was a dirty old man. But he didn’t get away with it. I stopped it pretty well.”

It started when she was a teenager, with his words – “If you want to learn about sex, come to me” – before progressing to deeds, such as the day he cornered her in the office of the local tennis club. “He gave me a tongue kiss, and I surprised myself and said, ‘You do that again, I’ll bite it off!’ ” she says, laughing. “I just walked out, and didn’t tell anyone else.”

Occasionally, his dark words and deeds coalesced, too, such as the moment in a taxi in London, when she was in her 20s and he turned to her, put his hand on her leg above the knee, and declared his drunken feelings – part affection, part threat. “You know I love you so much,” he said, with scotch on his breath, “I could rape you.”

Evonne simply turned and looked out the window, and realised she needed a plan for when they got back to the hotel. That plan was to make so much noise that people would inquire. When he followed her into her bathroom and tried to pull her into the bath, she called out loudly, and it worked. “I got a call in the room from reception – a noise complaint – and was able to say, ‘I’m sorry about that, Mr Edwards is just leaving.’ ”

With coach Victor Edwards in 1964, a consistent but controversial figure in her early life. Search Foundation/Mitchell Library

He’s a consistent figure throughout her story, scolding her both publicly and privately after losses, spreading rumours about her weaknesses as a player, while also exercising restrictive financial control. She wasn’t free of him until the late 1970s.

“I guess I’d been through enough then that I knew how to handle it, and it just ran off my back. But now I think back to everything I’ve done, and I realise I was quite tough,” she says, beaming, “in a quiet sort of way.”

Evonne Goolagong Cawley, perhaps more than anyone I’ve ever met, sees the good over the bad. This is a conscious choice – a kind of governing philosophy for living. She was given elocution lessons as a young woman in Sydney, for example, and where many might see a transplanted Indigenous girl being forced to walk in a white world, all she saw was preparation for her travels and the adventure of life.

The culture shock was real, but largely a source of fun, not fear. Like the time she was flummoxed on a trip to Newcastle, when it was her turn to make tea. A group of women called out and asked what was taking her so long: “I said, ‘It takes a long time to get the tea out of these stupid little bags!’ ”

Nothing seemed to weigh her down. At Willoughby Girls High School in Sydney’s lower North Shore, she had to write an essay in which she pretended to be an early settler, and described her day in the new colony. “What happened during my day was I tended my sheep, smoked my tobacky, and when the Aboriginal people came on my land, I shot ’em,” she says. “I got 10 out of 10!” If that strikes you as inherently racist – that an Aboriginal child be asked to write an imagined account of bloody dispossession and is rewarded for doing so – it was nothing compared to facing her first overtly racist comment, after playing doubles against two older ladies.

At her wheat-belt childhood home with her early trophies: “Mum made me pose with them in the backyard,” she says. Courtesy of Evonne Goolagong Cawley

“When it was time to shake hands, one of them said, ‘This is the first time I’ve had the pleasure of playing against a n-----.’ And I did get really upset,” she says. “I didn’t tell Mum until later, and she said, ‘Don’t worry bub, they’re just ig-or-ant’. Mum never went to school – ig-or-ant – but she knew everything. And she knew that’s what racism is about: ig-or-ance.”

Evonne knew that she had a platform for presenting Indigenous Australians in a positive light, but she felt no pressure to do so. “Being a role model never entered my mind,” she says. “Mum always said, ‘Just be yourself,’ and I just loved playing so much, it was all I ever wanted to do. I loved travelling to different countries, meeting different people.”

That became harder when she toured South Africa. Many felt let down by the decision to go, given the Apartheid policy, but the decision was made by her coach. She does remember, however, the stark dichotomy in the grandstands. “It did scare me when I first went there, to see all the crowds – people sitting in the black section and the white section, all in suits and hats.” But she also remembers a black woman approaching her to share a thought. “I don’t know what the fuss is about,” Evonne, laughing now, recalls her saying. “You’re not even black!”

Tennis great Margaret Court looked after her well on that visit, she recalls, eating with her every night. Court also used to invite her to stay at her home in Perth whenever they were playing against one another in Western Australia. Court, of course, has more than courted controversy in recent years, with her conservative faith compelling her to oppose same-sex marriage and compare transgender acceptance to “the work of the devil”. Long before that, she resisted calls to better compensate female players, and for good measure asserted that “lesbianism has ruined women’s tennis”.

Playing doubles with Margaret Court in London in 1971. Getty Images

Evonne doesn’t agree with those sentiments. But equally, she finds it hard to hang someone who showed her such kindness. Her husband, Roger, explains: “Margaret was just someone who had a religious experience,” he says. “God spoke to her at a time when she was feeling really down. But that point of view she has is so unnecessary, for such a great person.”

Evonne feels sad not just for the hurt caused to the LGBTQI+ community, but to those within their shared tennis community, like her good friend Billie Jean King. “I don’t agree with many of the things Margaret has said, but my main thing is that love is the main thing,” she says. “I believe that God is love for everyone.”

On the second day that I interview Evonne Goolagong Cawley, she comes armed with a prop. It’s a deck of “angel cards” – one of many so-called oracle decks (like tarot cards) enjoyed by people who consider themselves searchers. She bought them in a local crystal store. “Every few days, I do them before I go to sleep,” she says. “And last night after we spoke, this card came up.”

The title says Learning Experience, and it has a picture of a hooded figure holding a lantern, meant to convey inner peace and security, derived from overcoming hardships. Without the challenges that life has presented to you, you wouldn’t be the person that you are today, it reads. This is a time for you to reflect upon the incredible strength you have.

‘When I saw her something went “click” and from that moment on, I was besotted.’ Roger Cawley on meeting Evonne in 1970

“I agree with that,” she says. “I feel that all these hardships in my life have made me a strong person.”

She shuffles the deck, fans them out, and I pluck one from the middle. The card is Holy Love: You are blessed to receive this card today, for it shows that you are being surrounded by loving energy, and the cup of your heart will be filled, until it overflows with goodness.

How nice.

“Oooh, I’ve never had that one,” she says. “Well there you go!”

The holy love story of Roger and Evonne begins in 1970 at a wine and cheese party on the outskirts of London, when the young man with long hair and roguish charm spotted the self-conscious tennis star on the fringe of the soirée. “I remember you coming in,” says Roger, “and I remember you staring, and I remember me staring, and that was it.”

That night, after a short drive through town, they found themselves dancing on the seventh green of Guildford Golf Course, at one point looking up from their giggling moonlight waltz – an English boy and an Aboriginal girl – to find a cow gazing up at them in puzzlement.

With husband Roger Cawley at an Australian Open Inspirational Series event in 2025. Tennis Australia/Fiona Hamilton

“I had read all about her in magazines,” Roger says. “But when I saw her, something went click, and from that moment on I was besotted, and by the end of the year I was totally in love.”

“He seemed really nice, this man – and funny! That’s what got me. He definitely knew how to make me laugh,” Evonne says. “We’ve been married 50 years now. Actually, 51!”

I wonder what they’ve learnt about love – or if they have any advice for people hoping to last that long?

Roger: “You’ve got me!”

Evonne: “I’ve forgotten!”

They devolve momentarily into cackles and guffaws.

Evonne: “You’ve gotta have a sense of humour – about everything. That’s what keeps us going through the really bad times.”

Roger: “We laugh at the silliest things, and the same things, at the same time.”

Their daughter, Kelly Inala Cawley, was born in 1977 – Inala meaning “peace” or “peaceful place”. Then son, Morgan Kyeema Cawley, was born in 1981 – Kyeema being “the dawn” or “new beginning”. And that was a beginning, in a way, of a whole new chapter in their mother’s life.

Evonne with son, Morgan Kyeema, daughter Kelly Inala, and husband Roger Cawley. Courtesy of Evonne Goolagong Cawley

Evonne retired in 1983 and, as with almost any top-tier athlete, she went through a period of mourning – re-evaluating her reason for being. “It was so depressing,” she says. “It was like going into a dark space.” She was given medication but unfortunately has allergic or adverse reactions to many drugs, including antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and yes, anti-depressants. “I think I just sulked. I was miserable.”

Emerging slowly, she found a new way to enjoy life, and spent a lot of time fishing where they lived in South Carolina. “It’s so relaxing and beautiful. It’s calming. And being Aboriginal, you’re connecting to the land, the water, the trees – the beauty of the place – and you’re very much a part of it.”

Evonne’s father had passed away in 1974 at the absolute peak of her career, but when her mother finally died in 1991, it became the catalyst for a move home from the United States. She had seen and done so much. Had her hair styled by Vidal Sassoon and her photo taken in the Oval Office with [former US president] Ronald Reagan. She counted Kenny Rogers among her close friends, even travelling to the Bahamas to go scuba diving with the country star. “One time when Kenny came to stay with us in South Carolina, I called up Mum – who was a big fan – and I said ‘Mum, I’ve got someone here to talk to you.’ It made her so happy.”

With close friend, singer Kenny Rogers, in 2015 at the Australian Open. Getty Images

Evonne wanted to be back on her mother’s country, too. Very early in her career, Edwards had disparagingly attributed any lack of focus on court as Evonne going “walkabout” – now she wanted to do so properly. She went to mission shacks and rock-art sites, always meeting with elders and gaining their permission to visit sacred places. She camped by rivers and slept under the stars and drove down a dirt track in South Australia, headed for the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands, where she was allowed to do sacred women’s business.

“It was amazing. I can’t talk about it, but they were all laughing at the expressions on my face,” she says, laughing yet again. “That answered a lot of questions that I had. Very powerful. Good for the soul. I felt stronger and more connected to everything – to the universe.”

The tale of Roger and Evonne doesn’t end here, in this living room in southern Queensland, but their story is – at least right now – confined to this place. Ordinarily an active couple, this is the first year in many that they haven’t been able to travel, due to an array of health concerns.

First, Roger. He had a heart attack in both his 50s and 60s, and a third one only recently, along with a diagnosis of distal dystrophy – a genetic disorder characterised by the slow weakening and eventual atrophy of his muscles. “I woke up one morning and couldn’t move,” he explains. “Every muscle in my body was throbbing. I was scared stiff.”

His doctor had no idea what it was, but specialists at the Mayo Clinic eventually identified the problem and suggested vague forms of mitigation and preparation. “The thing they were putting off saying is that I can’t get rid of it,” he says. “There’s no way it goes away. It just gets worse. That took some adjustment.”

And Evonne?

“Here’s my bag of health issues,” she says, plonking a big plastic folder on the table between us, filled with notes and prescriptions. Her most pressing condition is the fallout from a concussion last year, after catching the toe of her shoe on a step outside her front door. “I just fell flat on my face and body, really hard, and I remember seeing stars. But I got up straight away.”

Fooled into a false sense of security, it wasn’t until a trip to Darwin in support of her charity – the Evonne Goolagong Foundation – that she felt the brunt of the blow. She was thirsty, and so tired, too, with vertigo. She shows me a leaflet about concussion in which she’s underlined in biro all the symptoms she experiences.

Trouble focusing. Trouble remembering things. Slow and foggy. Sensitivity to light and noise. Having trouble sleeping. Feeling dizzy. Feeling tired. Feeling anxious or worried. Feeling more frustrated.

I find it hard to picture her frustrated.

“I keep it to myself,” she responds, laughing.

The other issue is giant cell arteritis – an inflammatory condition causing everything from stiffness to soreness to throbbing headaches. She doesn’t know if it’s progressive or temporary. She knows she’s supposed to take Prednisolone for the concussion and Tocilizumab for the giant cell arteritis, but she has bad reactions to both drugs, including a bloated face and raised cholesterol. Oh, and she’s recently had a nasty bout of respiratory syncytial virus, and hip surgery to boot.

“It’s just been one thing after another, and all of it confusing,” says Roger. “One thing affects another, and that affects another, but when you’ve got five or six things going on in the body and you can’t take all the medicines required, it’s complicated.”

Meanwhile, they still have responsibilities with the Evonne Goolagong Foundation, which uses tennis to help Indigenous children access education, providing scholarships and encouragement and guidance. It’s hard for them to attend foundation events, but that means more time at home with their grandchildren.

“I make the popcorn, and I buy those little two finger Kit-Kats,” says Evonne, grinning. “They go straight to the other room, to watch what they want.”

It doesn’t really matter what they choose either, or even if it’s something she’s seen before.

Evonne: “That’s one of the good things about memory loss …”

Roger: ” … You can watch something again on Netflix because you don’t remember it!”

Time and again, “Rog” and “Gong” finish one another’s thoughts, almost like they’re playing a game of tennis, each exchange between them a serve and return, drop shot to net volley, lob followed by smash.

Roger: “We can’t play any more, or run, but we go out to lunch and laugh together.”

Evonne: “We’ve both got an illness, so we look after each other!”

Roger: “I think that when something happens, you just …”

Evonne: “… live with it, and try to laugh.”

I take that as my cue to leave the happy couple to their life, but later, after they’ve enjoyed a day of more giggles and angel cards – after they’ve been to the local golf club for a counter meal with the grandkids, and sat down to watch something new or old on Netflix, I text Roger one final question.

Not a Trivial Pursuit question, but a question that might sound trivial to anyone but Evonne. I want to know the answer to the question that used to greet her when she walked in the front door every night as a child – the one her mother asked: Did you have a lovely day?

Roger replies immediately: “She did, and thanks for asking!”

Then three text message dots appear, and they pulse like the ripple of a gum leaf on the surface of the river. Evonne has a return shot for me – one of those graceful and gracious single backhand winners down the line: “And she hopes you had a lovely day, too.”

Only Ever Evonne by Evonne Goolagong Cawley (Allen & Unwin) is out September 29.

World.title: Why this man owns a Dolphins trademark – and what he wants in exchange for giving it up
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandIntellectual property Why this man owns a Dolphins trademark – and what he wants in exchange for giving it up Cameron Atfield September 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As the Dolphins continue to make a splash in the NRL finals series, the club is fighting a quiet, multi-year battle to legally own its name on team merchandise. And it’s in no small part down to one man. Larry Kershaw, 72, has owned the “Dolphin” trademark in the class that deals with sporting equipment since November 2018. He successfully registered the trademark to protect a surfboard fin he designed. Larry Kershaw is a holdout for the Dolphins, who are trying to trademark their brand. Photos by Natalie Grono and Phil Walter/Getty. Composite by Stephen Kiprillis. The Dolphins NRL club applied for its trademark three years later, almost to the day.



Another nearly five years on, the NRL club on the cusp of its first grand final appearance has been unable to achieve protection for the Dolphins name and logo. The Dolphins have been battling to trademark their logo for five years. Dolphins NRL Other owners of dolphin-themed trademarks, such as Swimming Australia, have consented to the NRL club’s application, but Kershaw has held out, leading IP Australia to defer the application until the dispute is resolved. Kershaw is not a big rugby league fan, although he does have a soft spot for the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks. So his brush with the NRL was unexpected. “I’m not really privy to rugby league clubs and how they operate and all that, but I’m assuming these people are used to getting their way, one way or another,” he said.



“But what’s the point of anybody having a trademark if some big company can just come in and just roll somebody over? You’re trespassing on my property, really, aren’t you?” Speaking to this masthead from his Tenterfield home, Kershaw said the first he became aware of the NRL club’s interest was in February 2024, when he received a legal letter asking him to waive his rights to the trademark, with no mention of compensation. Kershaw said he countered with a $50,000 offer, which “in today’s value of money, doesn’t seem like a lot”. Since then, in March 2024, official records show the Dolphins formally filed an application to IP Australia to have Kershaw’s mark forcibly struck off the register. “People have said to me, ‘You know, you can make a motza out of this,’ which you probably could if you really wanted to be hard-headed and pull in some big-shot lawyers – and if you had the money to back you up,” Kershaw said.



“But I’d just like to get something sorted out where they say to me, ‘here’s a cash payment.’ “Or, if they wanted to pay me royalties on what they were selling – maybe that might be a more reasonable way of going. I mean, if I got 5 per cent on everything that was sold, I’d be doing all right, wouldn’t I?” Larry Kershaw holds the Dolphin trademark thanks to a surfboard fin he designed. Natalie Grono Intellectual property lawyer Chris Round, from the Melbourne office of international law firm K&L Gates, has had a long history in sports trademark law – including the AFL’s infamous stoush with Warner Bros over the Tasmanian Devils branding. Round said the Dolphins’ registration was “about 95 per cent” there, with IP Australia offering to accept the trademark if the club abandoned certain trademark categories.



“For whatever reason, the Dolphins have decided they’re not going to do that, and they’ve decided to take on Mr Kershaw’s registration,” he said. “Mr Kershaw is only registered with respect to surfboard fins, longboard fins, and stand-up paddleboard fins – that’s a really small thing, but the problem is, the Dolphins have filed for sporting goods. The Dolphins are one win away from the NRL grand final. Getty Images “Now, sporting articles is a universe of goods, and surfboard fins are part of that universe.” But Round said people should think twice before getting any big ideas about selling counterfeit merchandise outside Suncorp Stadium on Friday night.



“Whether you take seven months or seven years to get registered, it’s registered from the date it was filed,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2025 Brisbane Broncos sport fresh rebrand after 25 years “So if you went out there on Friday night and sold a counterfeit shirt, at the moment, the Dolphins don’t have a course of action for trademark infringement. “But eventually, they will have one, and they will predate your behaviour.” Round said it was unusual that the application had taken so long, but he would not be drawn on Kershaw’s chances of a financial windfall.



“Those who own trademarks are entitled to seek whatever compensation they want from an applicant asking for a letter of consent,” he said. “You have been given a monopoly by IP Australia for your trademark with respect to your goods and services, and it’s up to you as the trademark owner to decide whether someone else can come along and register their brand. “If you look on the register, Mr Kershaw only got registered because somebody else consented to him getting on the register. So he understands a letter of consent because he got one.” Kershaw said he hoped the matter would be resolved soon, and in a way that helped his retirement. “I’m not asking for a million dollars or anything like that,” he said.



“I just want what I feel is fair, because they’re obviously going to make a lot of money out of this.” Citing an ongoing legal matter, the Dolphins declined to comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The Mexican chef’s guide to making excellent nachos at home
World.content:
Tips & adviceKnow how The Mexican chef’s guide to making excellent nachos at home With a few small tweaks to what you’re probably already doing, you can take your nacho game to the next level. Dani Valent September 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As homemade snacks and easy meals go, there aren’t many that beat nachos. They cover a few food groups, they’re gluten-free, you can proteinmaxx them, there’s melted cheese involved, and you can eat them with one hand while watching the footy on TV. So what are the nachos basics and are there any hacks or rules? Nachos from Hotel Mexico. Chris Hopkins Are nachos Mexican? They were invented in the northern Mexico town of Piedras Negras in 1943 by a waiter called Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya. A gaggle of US Army wives descended on his restaurant before the chef arrived, and Nacho threw together a baked tortilla dish from ingredients he had to hand. The women approved and took the dish across the border where it was amped up, becoming a Tex-Mex staple and baseball game essential. “We do eat nachos in Mexico,” says Luis Sanchez, chef at Hotel Mexico in Yarraville in Melbourne’s inner west. “They’re usually simpler than the Tex-Mex versions, with just cheese, pickled jalapeno and chipotle mayo. We put them in the centre of the table at the start of a meal. For us, nachos means family and sharing.”



1 / 5 Use a mix of coloured corn chips for flavour variation and for aesthetics. Chris Hopkins 2 / 5 Scatter nachos with lots of grated mozzarella cheese. Photograph by Chris Hopkins 3 / 5 Melting the mozzarella cheese on the grill at Hotel Mexico. Chris Hopkins 4 / 5 Load with pickled jalapeno slices and sour cream. Photograph by Chris Hopkins 5 / 5 Don’t forget the salsa and guacamole! Chris Hopkins Previous Slide Next Slide The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up How does a Mexican chef make them in Melbourne? Freshly fried tortilla triangles (a mix of yellow and blue corn) are placed in a bowl, then scattered with grated mozzarella cheese before being melted under a grill. The oozy mess is loaded with guacamole, pico de gallo (tomato salsa), pickled jalapeno slices, sour cream and fresh coriander. “We put Mexican ingredients on it so we could say it’s more Mexican than anything else,” says the chef, who is from Puebla, south-east of Mexico City. There’s the option to load up with meat too. “You can turn our nachos into a meal by adding chorizo, chicken, birria or a vegetarian version with mushrooms,” he says.



Your nachos are served! Chris Hopkins What are the shortcuts? You can buy corn chips instead of frying tortillas but you should still use a mix of white corn and blue corn for flavour variation – and because it looks cool. Any melting cheese can be substituted for mozzarella. There are plenty of good jarred salsas, but if you want to make your own, it’s just finely chopped tomato, onion, coriander, lime juice and pickled jalapenos. Guacamole is worth making yourself – at its simplest, it’s just avo, lime juice, salt and pepper – but you can use a store-bought version too. Dorilocos is a Mexican street food served in the Doritos bag. iStock



Is there anything else I could try? “Nachos are getting popular in Mexico and changing a little bit,” says Sanchez. In his central region, dorilocos or tostilocos (“crazy corn chips”) are street food that you can modify as desired. Often made directly inside a cut-open bag of Doritos or Tostitos, they’re loaded with ingredients such as roasted peanuts, white corn kernels, pickled pork rind, fresh carrot and cucumber, and chamoy (a pickled fruit condiment) or Salsa Valentina, a bottled hot sauce. In northern coastal parts of Mexico, baked tortilla chips are sometimes topped with seafood, such as garlic shrimp or crab. In summary, go forth and mod your nachos.
