World.title: Mayors left stunned by Government's council amalgamation U-turn
World.content:
Audio player for " Mayors ‘blindsided’ by govt delay on council amalgamations " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1564050%2Fmayors-left-stunned-by-government-s-council-amalgamation-u-turn

Mayors ‘blindsided’ by govt delay on council amalgamations Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Mayors say a decision to delay amalgamation was completely unexpected, and leaves plans - some discussed for years - contingent on an election.

Wellington's mayor is pointing to a lack of support inside government as the reason for the U-turn - but the local government minister has rejected this.

In May, the Government gave councils a three month deadline to submit plans to simplify and reform, known as Head Start proposals, or it would make plans for them.

But that's changed - with the local government minister deferring decisions until after the election.

Wellington mayor Andrew Little blamed a lack of support around the Cabinet table.

"They clearly didn't have the numbers to enact reform, so consequently after all the effort that local government has put into it, we don't have reform."

Local Government Minister Simon Watts. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

That was put to Local Government Minister Simon Watts on Checkpoint.

"No, look I do my job, and I'm part of a government that thinks about fixing the basics and building the future, and I want to build a future that's enduring."

Watts said the decision was made after Cabinet on Monday.

Porirua mayor Anita Baker said the decision came completely out of the blue, and there was no hint of change at a zoom meeting she attended with Local Government New Zealand and the minister on Monday.

"At no point did we get an indication they would be cowards and not step up to this, and push it to the ... election, well how do we know they are even going to be there?"

Audio player for " Porirua mayor responds to amalgamation delays " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1564050%2Fmayors-left-stunned-by-government-s-council-amalgamation-u-turn

Porirua mayor responds to amalgamation delays Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Watts said this local government reform was the most significant in decades, and it couldn't be rushed.

"I don't think it's sensible ... that the New Zealand public would expect the government to rush a decision, we've got to get this right."

Watts said all 18 Head Start proposals had gaps - including about financial details, representation issues, and none had unanimous support across regions.

Baker said she'd been discussing amalgamation in Wellington for 16 years and was deeply frustrated it had been put off again.

Porirua mayor Anita Baker. RNZ/Dom Thomas

Marlborough District Council's deputy mayor David Croad said he was relieved the council had more time to consider amalgamating with Kaikōura District Council.

Councils already had a high workload dealing with challenges like extreme weather, he said.

"[Local government reform] should be well thought out, it should be well structured, and for me frankly the government needs to respect local government and the role that they play and the challenges we have all round in that decision making."

In Waitaki - where residents are facing a 16.9 percent rates rise - mayor Mel Tavendale said she desperately wanted to cut the costs of duplication from straddling both the Canterbury and Otago regional councils.

"There's still so much in the way coming down the barrel at councils, and for us being across two regions we're just getting some of it doubly.

"It's just not sustainable - it has me really concerned."

Watts said officials would continue to work through Head Start proposals through the election campaign and none of the time or money spent was wasted.

World.title: What's going on with fuel prices?
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1563982%2Fwhat-s-going-on-with-fuel-prices

The cost of fuelling up your car has gone up again, and experts say it's unlikely to drop any time soon.

New Zealand fuel prices have been volatile since conflict broke out in the Middle East earlier this year. There was a reprieve when a ceasefire looked to be taking effect, allowing more oil to travel out of the area, but that has reversed.

Audio player for " The home loan factor that banks are reluctant to shift on " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1563982%2Fwhat-s-going-on-with-fuel-prices

The home loan factor that banks are reluctant to shift on Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Oil prices have edged back up over US$100 a barrel, taking 91 petrol above $3 a litre across the country.

So what's going on?

The price that you pay at the petrol pump is made up of the dated Brent physical oil price, plus refining margins, shipping costs, and the exchange rate. (Then there is the fuel excise tax and other levies on top of that.)

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said oil prices had been volatile in the 24 hours to Thursday.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"They were under US$100 [a barrel] because there was talk from the Qataris and the Iranians that there were some kind of talks going on … but then later in the day it came out that the Iranians had a list of demands they wanted satisfied before they could commit to significant negotiations, including opening the Strait [of Hormuz].

"Most of those were quite difficult things for the United States to agree to, for example around the nuclear programme. So we've seen the prices go back up again. They're continuing to rise."

He said there was a period in June and July where it was relatively easier to get oil out of the region but it had subsequently tightened up.

"It's like any market where if people think there is less risk in the future and that things are going to get better, then they'll be happier to sell their oil now. But if they think that it's going to be tight in the future, if you've got oil, you're going to be less willing to sell it because you don't really know what it will be worth in a week's time. So there's quite a strong sentiment impact that on these commodity markets."

It's more than just the oil

AA spokesperson Terry Collins said while oil prices used to be a reasonable indicator of what retail fuel prices might be, other factors had started to play a much larger part.

AA principal policy advisor Terry Collins. Supplied / AA

He said, when fuel prices lifted earlier in the year, they were being pushed up by very high refining costs. "Record high, that we hadn't seen before and it really distorted the market. We've got high ones now but not so high."

But he said it was costing more to get fuel out of the Middle East.

"I've seen quotes of to insure a ship or get it through the Strait, of US$1 million for insurance … some of the large tanker rates have gone up nearly 1000 percent … We're seeing these distorted elements externally occurring around the refining costs and the shipping costs."

Another thing that counts against New Zealanders is the exchange rate, because all trading happens in US dollars. Our dollar has fallen recently, from almost US$0.60 in late August to US$0.56 now.

"When we model what petrol prices are going to do, we take the futures price in US dollars, then we adjust it by the exchange rate to bring it back to NZ dollars," Eckhold said.

"Then typically there will be a lag between when those prices have adjusted and when you start to see it at the pump here. That looks to us to be around a two-week lag these days."

He said, at roughly $3.40 a litre on average, it looked like much of the expected change in prices had already happened. "Obviously, it's very variable."

But Infometrics managing director Gareth Kiernan said he thought there might be more to come. "I'm not entirely sure we've seen the full effect of the life internationally over the last two or three weeks come through yet. It's probably most of the way through, but there might still be a bit of upward pressure."

Infometrics managing director Gareth Kiernan. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

He said commentators might have argued that futures and oil markets were not adequately pricing in likely risk in June and July, when prices were lower.

Demand from China had also increased, he said. "They've been running down their reserves quite substantially and that's been almost artificially suppressing demand internationally. I think they've got to a point where they don't really have a lot more to run down.

"That demand and supply equation - while the supply side doesn't look any more critical than it might have four or five months ago, it is possible that demand is a little stronger going forward."

And what about diesel?

There are more concerns about the future track for diesel than for petrol.

Eckhold said in the past three or six months, there had been much more difference developing between the prices for the two products, due to the degree of inventory shortage for each.

"Part of that is that for petrol, it's easier for people to substitute out of it, because it's too expensive. You know, you don't drive a car, you take the bus, all of those sorts of things, whereas with diesel, it's predominantly used for commercial purposes and is typically non-substitutable.

"If you want to run your tractor or your bus or something like that, your only real choice is to not run it at all."

There are more concerns about the future track for diesel than for petrol. 123RF

Eckhold said diesel prices still looked not to have fully adjusted to what occurred in the last few weeks. "There is a relative shortage of diesel globally, particularly in Europe. United States and European inventories of diesel have fallen to quite low levels and that's forced the price of diesel up relative to other refined fuels.

"That has meant the US diesel price has gone up through US$6.50 a gallon, which is a very painful level for American business. It's become an increasingly important political issue, bearing in mind that they have an election themselves coming in a month. So the US authorities have been talking about the potential of imposing limitations on exports of diesel from the United States to preserve more supply domestically.

"If that was to occur, that would have quite a significant impact on global diesel markets because the US is an important supplier of diesel to places like Mexico, but also Europe, which means that if those countries could not get their diesel from the United States, they would then go into the open market and start bidding for whatever else is available around the world, including coming out of the Middle East. And that would be how it would translate through to high diesel prices and potentially a shortage of availability down in this part of the world."

He said US President Donald Trump was facing heavy criticism. "But it is totally up Donald Trump's street. He's famous for doing stuff that is dangerous and has adverse consequences. Just because you probably shouldn't do it doesn't mean it won't happen."

What next?

Collins said he did not see any indication that prices would fall. "The rises may slow down, they may stabilise. But actual downward pressure occurring … I think there is too much uncertainty and volatility internationally."

He said there needed to be better leadership from the world's superpowers. "That'll be the number one thing. The rule of law internationally would sort a lot of that out."

World.title: Dannevirke residents demand accountability over state of healthcare
World.content:
Audio player for " Dannevirke residents hold meeting over health care in region " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1563980%2Fdannevirke-residents-demand-accountability-over-state-of-healthcare

Dannevirke residents hold meeting over health care in region Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Dannevirke locals have echoed calls from other towns in the Tararua region for a return to a local ownership model of healthcare.

About 200 locals turned out to a meeting about the future of the Dannevirke Community Hospital on Thursday.

Health New Zealand has put a temporary halt on the hospital taking new patients while it finds more clinical staff, following a number of resignations.

The hospital and a number of medical centres in the region are owned by the Tararua Health Group, which is in turn owned by OmniHealth - a network of about 17 practices around the country.

OmniHealth has been contacted for comment.

Retired sonographer Annie Poulton worked for Tararua Health Group for 23 and a half years.

The culture at the hospital changed dramatically and staff morale declined during the time Omni were majority shareholders, she said.

"They were holding these big team corporate meetings trying to boost staff morale, and I'd been away, and so many staff had left in that time. And I made a comment at the meeting, you know, 'It feels like a block of Swiss cheese. There's so many holes in this place now'. We've lost so much experience, so much knowledge, you know, really amazing people. And the comment was, 'no one's irreplaceable'."

Poulton said she wanted to see some accountability from Omni.

"We'll get through this and I think this is just what's needed, actually. It had to come to a head and we'll move forward from here, I think we will.

"It'll be a new, different look, hopefully it'll still be Tararua Health Group, but it won't be owned by Omni. It'll be a community-based, whatever, a new entity, but not with a corporate leading it."

Tararua District Mayor Scott Gilmore. RNZ / Pokere Paewai

Tania Chamberlain is chief operations officer at Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tamaki-nui-a-Rua, she oversees Te Kahu Hauora GP clinic and formerly worked at OmniHealth.

Things had gotten so bad at the hospital that clinicians were sending patients to the emergency department instead, she said.

"No clinician worth their salt and has got into health for that reason would ever choose to send an elderly patient to ED where the wait might be 27 hours when they could be safe and warm and cosy down the road at their own community hospital. But sadly, that's how unsafe they felt that it is."

Representatives from both Health New Zealand and the Primary Health Organisation, which managed Omni's contract, attended the meeting.

Geoff Gwyn, the regional director planning, funding and outcomes for the central region at Health New Zealand told the crowd it had no plans to close the hospital.

Health New Zealand was providing additional clinical workforce support at Dannevirke Community Hospital for the next 30 days and as a precautionary measure during that period, put a temporary pause on new admissions to the hospital.

"It's clear that at the moment the services aren't sustainable due to some staff resignations. So, we are bringing in additional Health NZ clinical staff in order to ensure the services remain available to the community," he said.

The health agency also carried out an audit of the hospital this week.

"We're taking this seriously. There was an audit done on the Tararua Community Hospital, a regular audit in June. I've listened to the community, I've listened to the concern of the clinicians, and that's why the unannounced audit was done on Tuesday. I have to wait to see what that tells us before I can understand the next steps," Gwyn said.

Geoff Gwyn, the regional director planning, funding and outcomes for the central region at Health New Zealand. RNZ / Pokere Paewai

Chamberlain said she was unsure if anything would change in the long term.

"But I guess time will tell. I just hope that they don't sort of think, well, all the meetings are gone and the pressure is off now and we can go back to doing what we're doing. Something has to change."

Tararua District mayor Scott Gilmore said the turnout at all three community meetings showed just how important healthcare was to rural communities.

"Rural healthcare absolutely is difficult, but that doesn't mean we should accept not having a good safe service for people living in our areas.

"It's funded through public money, we need to make sure that one, our politicians understand what the needs are in our areas, but actually our healthcare is well managed here as well."

World.title: The election fight for Wigram is taking flight
World.content:
Audio player for " Wigram boundary changes make it a seat to watch this election " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1564994%2Fthe-election-fight-for-wigram-is-taking-flight

Wigram boundary changes make it a seat to watch this election Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Wigram is a likely two-horse race between National's Tracy Summerfield and Labour's Dominik Yanzick.

The south-west Christchurch seat of Wigram takes its name from the former airfield at its heart.

The electorate is young and diverse - but changing boundaries have also changed its character.

Why is it interesting?

While RNZAF Station Wigram - New Zealand's first military airfield - is long gone, the aerodrome has left its mark.

Street names give a nod to its aviation history along with the subdivision at its centre - Wigram Skies.

The electorate has been a left-wing stronghold for decades.

Labour MP Megan Woods inherited the seat from her mentor Jim Anderton after his retirement and has held it since 2011.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405519345112

Anderton, who was a former Progressive, Alliance and NewLabour leader, held Wigram after the current seat was created in 1996.

Labour MP Mick Connelly held an earlier iteration of the seat from 1969 to 1978.

When electorate maps were redrawn last year, Wigram lost about 10,000 voters from traditionally ruby red areas close to the central city in Addington and Spreydon and picked up more than 11,000 voters from Prebbleton and rural areas carved from the deep blue neighbouring seat of Selwyn.

Selwyn National voters have often outnumbered Labour voters by more than two to one and Labour's candidate finished third in the electorate race in 2014.

Wigram has lost voters from red inner city suburbs and picked up vast swathes previously in the deep blue seat of Selwyn. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Wigram is also diverse with only 63.3 percent of people identifying as European at the last Census, compared to 67.8 percent across New Zealand.

Data showed 10.2 percent identified as Māori (17.8 percent nationally), 4.8 percent as Pacific Peoples (8.9 percent nationally) and 28.9 percent as Asian (17.3 nationally).

The electorate is also younger with about 30 percent of potential voters aged between 18 and 34, although only 54 percent of people under 25 are enrolled to vote compared to 57.5 percent nationally.

Wigram has the lowest enrolment nationally across all age groups.

The seat will be an open race for the first time since 2011 because Woods is stepping aside after five terms to run as a list-only candidate.

Outgoing Wigram MP Megan Woods. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

What happened last election?

Woods garnered 15,590 votes, holding off National newcomer Tracy Summerfield by just 1179 votes.

The result was a steep decline from the 24,186 votes Woods picked up in 2020 and the slimmest margin by which she had ever won the seat.

National also won the party vote by 2152 votes, its best effort since the height of John Key's popularity in 2011 and 2014.

Who's standing?

With Woods standing as a list-only Labour candidate, newcomer Dominik Yanzick will represent the centre-left party in the election.

Yanzick works in the tech sector and previously worked in agritech in Lincoln. He grew up south of the Waitaki River in North Otago after his parents migrated to New Zealand in the late 1980s.

Tracy Summerfield is again standing for National after coming close to taking the seat in 2023. She previously owned and ran childhood education centres for 15 years and has more than 28 years of experience in accounting and finance across the public and private sectors.

Wigram is young, diverse and less likely to be enrolled. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

List MP Laura McClure is representing ACT after unsuccessfully standing for Banks Peninsula in the last election. A Christchurch local, she led fire evacuation planning company Fire Safety Net before entering Parliament.

Political novices Bryce Park and Shreejan Pandey will represent New Zealand First and the Greens.

Park grew up in the Christchurch suburb of Yaldhurst and studied at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. He worked as an economic adviser on his father's unsuccessful 2019 Christchurch mayoral campaign.

Pandey is an electrical engineer and father of two. He is also director of the Monash Energy Institute at Melbourne's Monash University.

It is likely to be a two-horse race between Summerfield and Yanzick with current polling giving Yanzick the edge, although boundary changes since the last election are likely to create a tight race.

What do the locals say?

Alissa Docherty does not think her vote makes a difference. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Alissa Docherty is one of the unenrolled under-25s and does not feel like her voice counts for much in the election.

"I don't see why it makes a difference if one person doesn't vote," she said.

"It just doesn't really faze me, I suppose. I don't feel like my input matters as much."

Nikita McRobert will be voting for the first time. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

First-time voter Nikita McRobert, 20, is enrolled and enthusiastic about exercising her democratic right.

"If more people my age knew the importance of it, I feel like we'd definitely get more people voting," she said.

"I think that's really important. We definitely do need, especially people my age, to be voting more."

It is tough for business owners like Neetu Saini. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Most voters told RNZ the cost of living would be the biggest issue on their minds when they go to the ballot box.

Business owner Neetu Saini said business was tough with the lack of spare cash and retail crime still a concern.

"It's still very bad. Last month I had two people stealing off my shelves.

World.title: Weather: School holidays to start with heavy rain, strong winds
World.content:
A series of cold fronts is forecasted to move up the country in a wet and windy start to the school holidays.

MetService said blue skies were seen in most of New Zealand on Thursday, but showers over the South Island would travel north and linger in the west on Friday and Saturday.

Sunday would be especially wet, it said.

Meteorologist Samkelo Magwala said it was a typical spring pattern.

"Which is why these fronts are moving through quickly, resulting in less rainfall accumulation despite the briefly heavy rain.

"Parts of the North Island will wake to frosts on Friday morning and we're forecasting showers from the southwest on both Friday and Saturday before the main band of rain arrives with the front on Sunday."

MetService said the east could expect warm and dry conditions as a feed of air from the northwest moved in, with temperatures in the upper teens and low 20s on Saturday.

It said Sunday would be the more active day of weather as a front moved up the South Island.

Heavy snow was possible above 600m for parts of Central Otago, Southern Lakes, and the Canterbury High Country in the morning.

Southwest gales were possible in coastal Clutha, Christchurch and along the Kaikōura coast.

Northwesterly gales would blow through Cook Straight and across into Wairarapa and southern Hawke's Bay as the front moved up the country.

World.title: 'Not happy': Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid 'cannot explain' OIA comments
World.content:
Audio player for " Education Secretary on OIA avoidance allegations " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/education/1567188%2Fnot-happy-secretary-for-education-ellen-macgregor-reid-cannot-explain-oia-comments

Education Secretary on OIA avoidance allegations Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The head of the Ministry of Education says she is "not happy" with a manager caught on video appearing to suggest staff skirt the law, nor a scathing internal review of the culture in its curriculum division.

It has been a tumultuous week for the ministry, just six weeks ahead of the general election.

It began with a leaked video of senior official Dr Catherine Law telling staff not to put information shared with Education Minister Erica Stanford's office in writing because it could be made public under the Official Information Act (OIA). The leaker said was not an isolated incident.

Then on Thursday, a review prompted by staff concerns reported numerous issues, including allegations of favouritism, unprofessional workplace behaviours and a fear of speaking up.

Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid told Morning Report on Friday she could not explain Law's comments.

"What she said was wrong, she should not have said it. And my expectation is that everyone within the Ministry of Education should be meeting the obligations under the Official Information Act, including that staff member."

MacGregor-Reid said she had commissioned another review and would be meeting with the chief ombudsman after the interview to provide him the terms of reference.

"I'll be providing the ombudsman with our OIA track record. We have responded to a wide variety of OIA's and I'll be fully working with the ombudsman into whatever matters he wishes to look into as well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405522238112

She said to the best of her knowledge, no directive to avoid writing material down to escape potential discovery under the OIA had been made.

Host John Campbell put it to MacGregor-Reid that Law's instruction was a reminder of a "pre-existing concept", not a policy she was introducing herself.

"Is this video emblematic of our culture?" he asked.

"What Dr Law said in that video wasn't okay," MacGregor-Reid responded. "Dr Law is not a senior official. Dr Law is not a seasoned public servant. She's come into the ministry on secondment as a school principal for her expertise in education.

"I cannot explain what Dr Law was thinking, but what I can tell you is I have commissioned a review to ascertain whether there is a wider problem."

Minister for Education Erica Stanford (L) and Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor Reid (R) with IHC chief executive Andrew Crisp. Lillian Hanly / RNZ

MacGregor-Reid said those claims had not been put to her, and did not want staff to fear speaking up.

"I always welcome people pushing matters of concern to me… I commissioned that review of the workplace because I could see the pressure the group has been under. It has been working extraordinarily hard. And I commissioned that review because I wanted to hear from people…

"They can speak to me. They will be safe. And if action is needed to be taken as chief executive, I will absolutely take it."

World.title: Ōrewa beach sauna hopes for reprieve as deadline looms
World.content:
Auckland councillor John Watson, "in a kind of statement of defiance to my ongoing years", leapt into the sea after a hot sauna at Ōrewa beach last month in late winter.

"I'm still here ... It's really quite invigorating," Watson said.

"That's been one of the key things from people is there's a real health and mental wellbeing benefit to it."

But the sauna has been facing a deadline to move on by next Thursday from the council-owned campground despite 4000 people signing a petition backing it to stay there.

The council gave it advance notice as summer approached on the basis the business could not operate when sites were in high demand.

Sauna Collective owner Cam MacKinnon said he outlined a new proposal to council last Friday but had not heard back.

Sauna Collective owner Cam MacKinnon. Supplied / Sauna Collective

"They're definitely leaving me hanging," he told RNZ on Thursday.

The council was expected to offer a temporary reprieve on Friday.

It told RNZ on Thursday, "We met with Mr MacKinnon last Friday to discuss options for future occupation at the holiday park, including a short pre-summer extension to enable him to make alternative arrangements.

"We expect to communicate our decision on the length of the extension by tomorrow [Friday]."

But any decision on future occupancy depended on how it managed the impacts, after fielding complaints about smoke, smell and obstruction of beach views, and increased car and foot traffic from non-campground guests.

MacKinnon said he - and his five casual staff or "firekeepers" for the wood-fired sauna as he called them - remained in limbo.

"Like every day I have to let my guys who work for us, our firekeepers, who we care deeply about, [know] like, but 'Sorry, I don't have any more information'. And then they're having to answer all our regulars and our people who care about the sauna who ask them the same question."

He had proposed a year-long trial of a new arrangement where he shut down from December to Waitangi Day, paid more for the site and compensated campers nearby.

Albany ward councillor Victoria Short said MacKinnon was not being pushed out or treated unfairly.

Albany ward councillor Victoria Short. Supplied

"We're trying to work with him to come up with a solution for him to be somewhere else with this agreement that we've kind of had in place where he's going to be there during off-peak season and on peak season he has to find a new location," said Short.

They had to work "just to make sure that everything is kosher, especially when it comes to the safety and liability aspects".

MacKinnon ran two other mobile saunas though Ōrewa was his mainstay. He said Friday's meeting left him uncertain about its long-term future.

"We might be under the assumption that we might be able to come back but they definitely weren't indicating anything like that," he said.

"That's not a given, not at all ... The only thing that is certain is that ... not only have we had the petitions, we've had hundreds and hundreds of emails."

Watson was not party to the discussions but said the council should be trying to keep the sauna in place at the campground as long as possible each year, and find an alternative site on the long beach for the Christmas holidays.

"The starting point should be this has been a huge, big success. The local people want it to stay ... Make that happen."

Short said alternative sites for the peak season were being looked at, such as within the regional parks network or involving land governed by the Hibiscus and Bays local board.

The chair of the local board was approached for comment.

It is understood it could be complicated for the private sauna business, that needs power and other amenities, to operate from reserve or park land.

The council's head of specialist operations Martin van Jaarsveld said, "As a Holiday Park, a primary focus is on providing an enjoyable holiday experience that meets the expectations from paying guests at what is a very popular regional destination.

World.title: Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know
World.content:
The Socceroos will play their first internationals since the 2026 FIFA World Cup against five-time world champions Brazil in Queensland this week.

It is the team's first meeting since they played at the MCG in June 2017.

The Socceroos have only ever beaten Brazil once, a 1-0 victory in the 2001 Confederations Cup third-place play-off thanks to Shaun Murphy's 84th-minute strike.

Here's everything you need to know about the Queensland Series.

When are the Socceroos playing?

The Socceroos are back in action on home soil. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The first game is on Friday, September 25 at Townsville's Queensland Country Bank Stadium.

The second is on Tuesday, September 29 at Brisbane's Lang Park.

For both games, kick-off is 8pm AEST, meaning Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, kick-off is 7:30pm and in Western Australia, it's 6pm.

How can I watch the Socceroos?

Friday night's game in Townsville is available to watch across Network 10 on free to air and Paramount+, you just need to check your local guides.

Tuesday night's game in Brisbane is only available on subscription streaming service Paramount+.

Alternatively, you can follow both games in full on the ABC Sport live blog.

Who is in the Socceroos squad?

Lucas Herrington is back on home soil for the first time since his move to Hull. (Getty Images: PA Images/Annabel Lee-Ellis)

With July's Round of 32 penalty shootout defeat to Egypt in Dallas firmly in the rear-view mirror, coach Tony Popovic's eyes are now gazing forward towards January's AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.

As such, Popovic has called up seven uncapped youngsters: Dylan Leonard (19 years old), Marcus Younis (21), Kasey Bos (22), Kealey Adamson (23), Yaya Dukuly (23) and Eli Adams (24), while Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek, who both missed the World Cup through injury, return.

Nestory Irankunda will hope to lead the line and test himself against some of the sport's biggest names.

Hull City centre back and Brisbane local Lucas Herrington has had a superb start to life in the Premier League and will look forward to play in front of his friends and family.

Only one player, Sydney FC's Aziz Behich, plies his trade in the A-League Men.

Socceroos squad: Goalkeepers: Patrick Beach (Troyes), Paul Izzo (Randers), Jacob Chapman* (St Mirren). Defenders: Kealey Adamson* (QPR), Aziz Behich (Melbourne City), Alessandro Circati (S.L. Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Touré, who has been on fire for Norwich in the Championship, has a shoulder injury which could lead to a lengthy lay-off, while Robertson is reportedly being rested by Cardiff after a heavy workload at the start of their campaign.

Several other World Cup players were not selected, namely Cammy Devlin, Awer Mabil, Kai Trewin, Mat Leckie and Ajdin Hrustić.

After the shambolic way his World Cup ended, keeper Mat Ryan has also been dropped, despite playing well for Levante in La Liga.

Cameron Burgess and Jordan Bos are out with long-term injuries, while Cristian Volpato was left out with a hamstring strain.

Volpato was also charged by police over driving with cocaine in his system, a charge he says he will challenge.

Vinícius Júnior headlines Brazil's squad. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti copped a fair amount of criticism for the Seleção's last-16 exit at the World Cup, but just as much flack for his erratic approach to selection.

The five-time Champions League-winning coach was adamant that he would not pick players based on reputation for the World Cup, only to surprisingly select a desperately out-of-form and unfit Neymar Junior, whose only contribution to Brazil's poor performances in the USA was to embarrassingly taunt Norway's goalkeeper Ørjan Nyland after slotting a consolation, stoppage time penalty in their 2-1 defeat.

Neymar has since retired from internationals and Brazil is now firmly on the rebuild.

"Friendlies are used to have a look at different players … players who I don't know really well," Ancellotti said this week.

Of the 26-man squad, Ancelotti has selected 10 from the domestic Brasileirão Série A, including all three goalkeepers, leaving Liverpool's Alison Becker at home.

There are eight players from the English Premier League in the squad though and a collection of experienced stars from Italy, Spain and France, which Ancelotti said was crucial to Brazil's revival.

"I chose these players — Marquinhos, Gabriel [Magalhães], Bruno [Guimarães], Raphinha and Vini Jr. — to help with this change in direction. They are crucial for the future," Ancelotti said.

World.title: The AFL's gut feel to Neale's gut punch leaves fans dazed and confused
World.content:
It was a gut-feel approach to a gut punch that has left AFL fans baffled by the circus surrounding it.

Brisbane Lions superstar Lachie Neale is indeed free to play in the grand final tomorrow after successfully arguing that his impeccable character was enough to forego tribunal precedent.

But by the end of the whole drawn-out saga, the AFL's case against Neale was part Balogun, part popgun, and part Raygun in its absurdity and futility.

Folarin Balogun was allowed to play at the World Cup despite being red-carded in the previous game. (Getty Images: ISI Photos/Robin Alam)

Part Balogun, in that fans could be forgiven for once again tasting that hint of bitterness in their mouths that accompanied FIFA's decision to allow US striker Folarin Balogun to play a knockout match despite being handed a red card in the previous game.

Part popgun, in that the AFL's approach all season of stamping out behind-the-ball gut punches with an instant one-week suspension ended with a whimper when it mattered most.

And part Raygun, in that they all flailed around indiscriminately in front of a captivated audience, who couldn't decide whether what they were watching was actually kind of brilliant in its blinding nonsense.

Nobody saw this coming, but everyone still somehow suspected it might arrive.

To compare it to the Balogun decision, where US President Donald Trump made a direct phone call to FIFA boss Gianni Infantino, is potentially unfair, yet the comparisons will come, and they already have.

This was not a sneaky phone call, or a threat, or a back-scratching exercise that so often permeates the world of sport, but a cartoonish widening of the eyes and a dimpling of the cheeks accompanied by an innocent, "Who, me?"

Using a precedent set earlier in the season when the AFL allowed Scott Pendlebury to escape with a fine for an offence that would usually attract a suspension via a "compelling and exceptional circumstances" provision, Neale's team argued that the 320-gamer was just as worthy as the Collingwood veteran for the same provision.

In Pendlebury's case, he was on the verge of becoming the most-capped AFL player in history, had never come close to a suspension, and was fronting the tribunal for an incident that happened in play and was deemed careless rather than deliberate.

In Neale's case, he had played 100 fewer games than Pendlebury, was fronting the tribunal for an incident that was clearly deliberate and behind the play, and, crucially, had been fined on three prior occasions for striking an opponent off the ball.

The decision to compare the two cases and conclude that Neale's case was on par with Pendlebury's will most baffle fans and open doors to veterans in future seasons to argue that their records need only compare to Neale's for them to all receive the "good bloke" discount when push comes to gut punch.

Meanwhile, the nine players who were suspended this year for similar actions to Neale's must question whether the AFL is as serious about body strikes as it says it is, or is only serious about it when the players don't have a couple of Brownlow Medals to their name and a grand final to play in on the weekend.

Make no mistake though, this is not a decision that comes with a bona fide outrage guarantee.

In an ABC Sport poll accompanying yesterday's live blog of the appeal, 42 per cent of the 47,000 respondents said they believed Neale should be free to play.

Footy legends from Matthew Richardson to Tony Shaw bemoaned the idea that a footballer could miss out on a grand final for a whack that in yesteryear would be considered a bit of a rib tickler, a gentle reminder to an opponent to stay out of your way and stop being a goose.

But 2026 is not yesteryear, and the AFL decided long ago that striking a player to the body behind play was not something that it would stand for.

Six things to know ahead of the AFL grand final The Brisbane Lions and Fremantle are preparing for an historic AFL finale at the MCG on Saturday. Here's everything you need to know.

Neale knew this, and did it anyway.

Yet he will lace up the boots and run out onto the MCG tomorrow after the AFL flipped and flopped, turned and tumbled, and kangaroo-bounced its way to a decision that has left at least half of the AFL world with its collective mouth agape, questioning whether what they just witnessed was real.

The Fremantle players standing across from Neale tomorrow will likely be torn as they attempt to win their club's first flag in 31 years of existence. On the one hand, not having Neale out there would have been a major leg up. On the other hand, they surely want to claim the premiership knowing they beat the Lions at their very best.

A Fremantle victory now becomes the most palatable result for the AFL.

Because if the Lions win a close one, and Neale goes on to star as he is wont to do, that victory will leave a sour taste in the mouths of those who believe the AFL should have stuck to its guns.

And for long-suffering Dockers fans, that prospect would be the greatest gut punch of all.

World.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua boxing megafight announced
World.content:
A long-awaited boxing match between British former heavyweight world champions Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua has been confirmed for December 11 in Cardiff, according to an event promoter.

The two boxers will meet at the Principality Stadium, promoter Turki Alalshikh said on social media on Thursday.

Earlier media reports had suggested promoters were initially proposing to stage the fight at New York's Madison Square Garden.

The long-awaited fight has been anticipated for more than a decade. (Reuters: Supplied/Action Images/Andrew Couldridge)

“For 15 years no one has been able to make this fight,” he posted on X.

" I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over… "

A clash between the British rivals has been one of the most anticipated fights for more than a decade.

Fury and Joshua ruled the heavyweight division for much of the past decade, but a bout between them to unify all the major belts never came to fruition.

Both were later beaten by Oleksandr Usyk, who became the undisputed heavyweight champion.

In an Instagram post on Thursday, local time, Joshua's announcement of the fight and message to fans was short: "I am inspiring a generation."

Fury stepped out of retirement this year and made his return to the ring for the first time in more than a year with victories against Arslanbek Makhmudov and Mariusz Wach.

Joshua’s only fights since losing his IBF world title fight against Daniel Dubois in 2024 were against YouTuber Jake Paul and Kristian Prenga.

Mr Alalshikh is a Saudi Arabian adviser who organises boxing events for the Middle Eastern kingdom.

While Fury and Joshua are arguably past their peak, it is a fight that is still likely to garner global attention and will be streamed worldwide on Netflix.

“THE WAIT IS OVER. Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua finally collide,” Joshua's promoter Matchroom posted on X.

Matchroom's Eddie Hearn told The Independent last month they had insisted on the fight taking place in the United Kingdom.

"We don’t want the money, we’d rather it was in the UK," he said.

World.title: Neale freed to play by AFL Appeals Board as grand final teams named
World.content:
Lachie Neale has succeeded in his bid to overturn a one-game striking suspension at the AFL Appeals Board and is free to play in the grand final.

Neale lost on Tuesday with the AFL Tribunal upholding his ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.

In a hearing that took nearly two hours, the panel of chair Richard Loveridge, Steven Jurica and Wayne Henwood took less than half an hour to return with their verdict.

Neale's defence team chose not to challenge the decision of the Tribunal to uphold the grading of intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which resulted in the one-match ban.

The case turned on the question of the "exceptional and compelling circumstances" clause in the rules, which allows the Tribunal discretion to not apply a ban, and whether the Tribunal considered Neale's record of 320 games without suspension and two Brownlow Medal best-and-fairests in reaching their decision.

Neale's counsel Adrian Anderson said the exceptional circumstances should have been reached because of Neale's amazing record, the fact that Ginnivan had not been injured in what he said was a "pretty minor" incident, and the fact that the consequences of the decision were that Neale would miss a grand final.

"We find that the Tribunal did err in having regard to whether the conduct was intentional," Loveridge said in the Appeal Board reasons.

"We accept the position of Neale in his written submissions that the intentional aspect was an element of the charge which had already been established.

"The relevant inquiry was whether, despite the charge having been established, there was exceptional and compelling circumstances.

"In this case, that was Neale's record.

"We find that Neale's record is exemplary, and that he should be afforded the benefit of the provision.

"In conclusion, we allow the appeal."

Neale was fined $10,000 and he will be able to play in Saturday's grand final.

Both teams released their line-ups for the decider, with no changes for either Brisbane or Fremantle.

Look back at how all the proceedings and team news unfolded in the live blog.

World.title: Would you travel over 50 hours for your team? This Dockers fan is
World.content:
Would you go to the ends of the earth for your favourite team?

That's pretty much what Rafe English is doing.

The university student, originally from Perth, is undertaking a journey of more than 50 hours across the globe — from Illinois in the US to Melbourne — to see his beloved Fremantle Dockers play in the grand final.

Purple army heads east The Nullarbor has turned purple this week as Fremantle Dockers supporters make the long journey to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

"I would fly from anywhere to see Freo play in this grand final," English told the ABC during a seven-hour layover in Dallas, Texas, one of many stops on his epic journey.

"I say every year is our year, but in the back of my mind, I did have that sense that we were going to Docker it up.

"I knew when we strung together those last couple of games that I was going to be flying to Melbourne."

Love and devotion

From his university in Normal, Illinois, English has watched fervently as his team climbed to the top of the ladder.

Footy fans filthy as airfares soar ahead of grand final Return airfares to Melbourne have hit $6,000 ahead of Saturday's AFL Grand Final as Fremantle and Brisbane fans scramble for seats.

"Early mornings, but it's all worth it in the end when you love the club this much," he said.

His journey started with a two-hour train ride from central Illinois to Chicago, where he spent the night.

English then took a bus and a train for an hour to the airport, followed by a two-and-a-half hour flight to Dallas, where he boarded his final 17.5 hour flight to Melbourne.

This is the second ever grand final for the Dockers. They face the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Saturday. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Dockers and dad

During his stopover in Dallas, English explained why the Dockers meant so much to him.

"Obviously what the club has built, and what they mean and stand for, but for me it's the memories that I've had with my dad, and growing up, and that real connection," he said.

Mr English is posting about his more than 50-hour journey on social media. (Supplied: Instagram)

He recalled how sad he was when the Dockers lost the 2013 grand final against the Hawthorn Hawks by just 15 points.

"I don't think I spoke for about two or three days, as a nine-year-old, I was devastated," Mr English said.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership.

Many fans are traversing more than 3,000 kilometres across Australia to catch the grand final, but English's journey makes the drive across the Nullarbor pale in comparison.

As the crow flies, the distance between Normal, Illinois and Melbourne is more than 15,000km — which is roughly five times the distance between Perth and Victoria's capital.

English's flight is scheduled to land in Melbourne at 5am on Saturday, where he will reunite with family and watch his team try to take the premiership.

"It would mean the world to me to see Fremantle lift up that cup after all these years of devotion," he said.

World.title: Matildas name three uncapped players in squad for October friendlies
World.content:
After suffering a gut-wrenching ACL injury on the eve of her potential Matildas debut, midfielder Hana Lowry has been handed a national team recall.

Coach Joe Montemurro has named three uncapped players for his 26-player squad, which will face world number three Germany and world number 47 Haiti in Europe in October.

One of them is Lowry, who was previously selected in 2024 but was ruled out with a knee injury, and has been building ever since.

The 23-year-old signed a deal to move from A-League Women's club Sydney FC to Norway earlier this year and has impressed, scoring a goal and assisting another in her first seven games with the new club.

"We've been watching her games and [she's] just really grown game by game, really stabilised as a player that's comfortable with the ball, but also someone that I believe has a great attitude and character to really be a top-level footballer," Montemurro said.

Former Sydney defender Tori Tumeth has also received a maiden call-up after shining for the Vancouver Rise in Canada's Northern Super League. At the same time, Melbourne Victory's Courtney Newbon is the third potential debutant.

But the Australians will be without stars Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule due to injury, while Teagan Micah continues her recovery from concussion earlier this year.

"Teagan has recovered really well. I think [she] just needs a little bit more time with the team ... to feel comfortable coming in," Montemurro said.

"She joined Lyon fairly late in the pre-season, so she's back with the team and doing well. So we'll just keep monitoring that."

Arsenal midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross also won't join the team as she continues her return to football following her mother's death.

"We said from day one that we were going to make sure that she's supported and given every opportunity to come back at her time and when she feels right," Montemurro said.

"She was thinking about coming [back] in October. We discussed it and we just felt it was a little bit too early. And we've got the opportunity now to let her just be herself and grow and go through this difficult period.

"She's in a really good space at the moment, and she'll be back with us."

Midfielder Isabel Gomez and goalkeeper Ilona Melegh have been dropped after they were part of the side for their two-game series against Mexico in June.

Superstar Sam Kerr has been named to feature in the friendlies. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Defenders Charli Grant and Alexia Apostolakis, along with midfielder Daniela Galic, will return to the national team set-up.

European stars Mary Fowler, Caitlin Foord, Ellie Carpenter and Steph Catley have also been named, as well as Gotham City's Sam Kerr.

The October international window marks a crucial stage in the Matildas' preparation for the FIFA Women's World Cup, which gets underway in Brazil next June.

There are only a handful of international breaks before the showpiece tournament, meaning every game is crucial for Australia as they look to build on their fourth-place finish in 2023.

"We have a good mix of experience, players returning to the squad and players earning their first senior call-ups, which is important as we build towards the Women's World Cup," Montemurro said.

"We want to use these games to strengthen our connections, build confidence and continue developing as a team.

"Germany will test us against one of Europe's leading teams, while Haiti will provide a different style and perspective."

World.title: Six things to know ahead of the AFL grand final
World.content:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the 2026 AFL grand final?

The game starts 2.30pm (AEST) on Saturday, September 26 at the MCG.

That's 12.30pm for those watching in Western Australia, and 2pm for South Australia.

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

How can you watch watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire AFL season that is exclusive to Channel 7.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

When will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

The Wiggles will be performing at Friday's grand final parade through Melbourne.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

At this point we don't know.

Teams will be announced about 6pm (AEST) today, but before that we'll have to see if Lions superstar Lachie Neale's tribunal appeal against a one-match ban gets up.

ABC Sport's Andrew McGarry will be live blogging every moment of the appeal, with the case set to get underway at 4pm.

Should Neale miss out, Noah Answerth is the most likely player to come in for the Lions. The injured Brennan Cox is a chance to come in for the Dockers, but it looks odds on that the Dockers will be unchanged from their preliminary final victory over the Swans.

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

World.title: 'That's why Taliban is scared': Cyclist's incredible journey to silver
World.content:
The easy part for Fariba Hashimi was winning a silver medal in the women's cycling road race at the Asian Games.

The nearly impossible part for the cyclist from Afghanistan was trying to train in her country. To do that, she dressed as a man in a place where women have few rights.

"All the time when I was going to training I was dressing as a guy," she said.

She said she also hid her face to avoid being recognised.

"Because sometimes when they recognised me, they were trying to throw … stone[s] or hitting me," she said.

Hashimi, who is 23, won silver overnight AEST in a time of 2 hours, 50 minutes, 5 seconds, which marked another leg in a journey that began in 2021 when she left Afghanistan, escaping to Italy with the help of former road racing world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Hashimi (left) with gold medallist Guo Li of China and bronze medallist Leung Wing Yee of Hong Kong. (Getty Images: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhu)

"In 2021, when the Taliban moved into my country, I escaped my country because I wanted to follow my dream," she said.

"I want to show the Afghanistan women in the world that … we can have an opportunity."

Hashimi talked about having many dreams for women in Afghanistan, dreams for herself and dreams that might take time to be realised.

"I'm really, really happy and I'm full of emotion. I don't know how I can explain it for you," she said.

"I hope one day I come back in my country and ride the streets of Kabul — and riding with the women side-by-side to share the same passion.

"And I hope in the future changing some things.

"I think we are really tired of the situation of our country and I hope the Taliban is watching. I know how much one woman can be powerful, and that's why Taliban is scared [of] women."
